n: What is React, and why does it exist?
t: Start Here — What is React and Why Does it Exist?
x: Updating the DOM by hand gets slow, tedious, and error-prone as an app grows. React solves this with a component model: you describe what the UI should look like, and React works out how to update the DOM efficiently. Facebook open-sourced it in 2013. What problem does React solve? What was wrong with updating the DOM manually? Declarative you say "the screen should look like this" and React decides how to get there Imperative you spell out every step: grab this element, change this text, remove this class UI = f(state) the UI is the output of a function whose input is the state Definition: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. Its core idea fits in one line: UI = f(sta

Bundler makes your files runnable in the browser (Vite, webpack) HMR Hot Module Replacement: the browser updates instantly when you save a file, with no full reload Meta-framework a framework built on top of React that includes routing and SSR (Next.js) Definition: There are three common ways to start a React project: Vite (fast and simple, ideal for SPA

n: Your first React component: Hello World
t: Start Here — What is React and Why Does it Exist?
x: A React component is just a JavaScript function that returns JSX. function App() { return Hello World ; } is a complete component. React renders it into the DOM with createRoot(document.getElementById("root")).render( ). What is a React component? How does React turn a component into actual HTML on the page? Component a function that returns UI (JSX) Root the DOM element where the entire React app is rendered Render running a component so React knows what to show on screen Definition: A React component is a plain JavaScript function that returns JSX. There is one naming rule: the name must start with a capital letter . function Button() is a component. function button() is treated as an HTML

x: JSX looks like HTML, but it's really JavaScript. Babel compiles Hello into React.createElement("h1", null, "Hello"). Rules: className instead of class, camelCase attributes (onClick, not onclick), and every tag must be closed ( not ). What is JSX? Is it valid JavaScript? How does it work under the hood? JSX a way to write HTML-like syntax inside JavaScript Transpile converting JSX into ordinary JS function calls (at build time) Expression slot the { } inside JSX, where you can put any JS expression Definition: JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript that looks like HTML. Browsers don't understand it. During the build, it is transformed into React.createElement(...) calls (into jsx() calls i

n: Props vs State: passing data and managing change
t: Start Here — What is React and Why Does it Exist?
x: Props are data passed FROM a parent TO a child. They're read-only, like function parameters. State is data that lives INSIDE a component, and when it changes, React re-renders the component. Props are for configuration; state is for things that change. function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return setCount(c => c+1)}>{count} ; } What is the difference between props and state in React? Props data passed from parent to child; the child cannot change it State a component's own data that can change; changing it triggers a re-render Re-render the component function runs again to produce new UI Definition: React has two kinds of data: Props come from outside, like function arg

JSX is syntactic sugar. Babel compiles it into React.createElement() calls that return plain JS objects called React Elements. What does JSX actually compile to? What is the difference between a React Element and a React Component? React.createElement the function JSX was compiled into (classic runtime) Automatic runtime the newer approach in React 17+: a jsx() function, with no import needed React Element the result of JSX: a plain, immutable object Definition: JSX compiles into a function call that returns a plain object . That object is a "React Element": a description of what should appear on screen, not an actual DOM node. Before React 17, the compiler produced React.createElement calls

An in-memory tree of JS objects that mirrors the real DOM. React diffs the new tree against the old one and applies only the minimal changes to the real DOM. What is the Virtual DOM, and why does React use it? Does it always make things faster? Virtual DOM a lightweight copy of the real DOM, held as JavaScript objects Diffing comparing the old and new trees to find the differences Reconciliation applying the minimal set of changes to the real DOM based on the diff Definition: The Virtual DOM is a lightweight JavaScript representation of the real DOM. When state changes, React builds a new virtual tree, compares it with the old one, and applies only what changed to the real DOM.

Class components use lifecycle methods and this; functional components use hooks. Hooks give functions everything classes could do, and more. What are the key differences between class and functional components? Why did the React team move to hooks? Class component the old way: class extends React.Component with a render() method Functional component the current standard: a plain function plus hooks Lifecycle methods a class's special methods, such as componentDidMount and componentDidUpdate Definition: React components used to be written in two ways. Class components (the standard before hooks arrived in 2019) rely on this.state , this.setState , and lifecycle methods. Functional components

Props are read-only inputs that flow from parent to child. Mutating props directly breaks the one-way data flow contract. Why are props immutable? What happens to child components when a parent re-renders? Immutable cannot be changed children a special prop: the content written between the tags Spread passing all props at once with {...obj} Definition: Props are the data a parent passes to a child. React treats them as read-only , so a child cannot change its props. React's rule: "every component should behave like a pure function with respect to its props."

State is private, mutable data. Changing it schedules a re-render, and React batches state updates for efficiency. What triggers a re-render in React? What does NOT trigger one? useState the hook that creates state; it returns [value, setValue] Batching combining multiple setState calls into a single re-render Functional update setX(prev => ...): computes the new value from the previous one Definition: State is a component's private data. It persists across re-renders, and changing it makes React re-render. const [x, setX] = useState(initial) . Two important truths: (1) setX does not change the value immediately; the new value appears on the next render. (2) React batches all the setSt

Keys help React identify which items in a list changed, were added, or were removed. They are critical for correct reconciliation. Why does React need keys? What happens if you use the index as a key? When is an index key actually safe? Key a unique identifier given to each item in a list Index key using the array position (0, 1, 2) as the key; often wrong Remount the component is replaced with a brand-new one, and all its internal state is lost Definition: A key is a special prop that tells React which item is the same item across two renders of a list. Without keys, React matches items by position, which goes wrong when items are added, removed, or reordered.

Controlled: React state owns the input's value. Uncontrolled: the DOM owns it, and you read it through a ref. Both have legitimate use cases. What is the difference between controlled and uncontrolled inputs? When would you use each? Controlled the input's value comes from React state Uncontrolled the input keeps its own value in the DOM, and React reads it through a ref defaultValue the initial value of an uncontrolled input Definition: There are two ways to handle a form input: Controlled uses value={state} plus onChange . React always holds the source of truth. Uncontrolled uses defaultValue plus a ref . The DOM holds the truth, and React reads it only when needed, such as on submit.

A development-only tool that double-invokes render functions and effects to surface side-effect bugs and deprecated API usage. What does StrictMode do? Why does it call some functions twice in development? StrictMode a wrapper component that performs extra checks in development Double invoke intentionally running render and effects twice in development Idempotent gives the same result when run twice, with no extra side effects Definition: <StrictMode> is a development-only wrapper. It renders nothing itself. It just tells React to "check extra strictly." The most visible effect: components render twice and effects run twice (mount, unmount, mount again). In a production build, it does

A complete rewrite of React's reconciler (React 16+). Fiber turns the render tree into a linked list of units of work that can be paused, aborted, and resumed. What is React Fiber, and why was it a complete rewrite? What problem does it solve compared with the old stack reconciler? Fiber a JS object that represents a unit of work for a component Stack reconciler the old reconciler (React 15): it used recursion and could not be paused Interruptible able to pause work in the middle and resume later Definition: Fiber is the reconciliation engine in React 16+. For each component, React creates a fiber node : a plain object holding the component's type, props, state, and pointers to its parent, c

React's O(n) algorithm for comparing two trees, built on two heuristics: elements of different types produce different trees, and keys identify stable elements across renders. Explain how React's diffing algorithm works. What are the two assumptions that make it O(n) instead of O(n³)? Reconciliation comparing the old and new trees to work out the DOM changes Heuristic a shortcut rule that isn't always perfect but works well in practice O(n) n steps for n items: linear, so fast Definition: Reconciliation is the algorithm that compares the old fiber tree with the new element tree. A perfect tree diff is O(n³) : for 1,000 nodes, that's around a billion operations. React applies two heuristics t

Render phase: pure, interruptible work where React builds the new Fiber tree. Commit phase: synchronous and uninterruptible, where React applies DOM mutations and runs effects. What is the difference between the render phase and the commit phase? Why must the render phase be pure? Render phase React works out what changed; pure and interruptible Commit phase React actually changes the DOM; synchronous and uninterruptible Effect list the list of fibers that have DOM work or effects to run Definition: Every update happens in two phases: Render (thinking) — component functions run, a new tree is created, and diffing happens. Nothing touches the DOM. React can pause, restart, or throw away this

React's scheduler assigns each update a priority lane (SyncLane, InputContinuousLane, DefaultLane, IdleLane) and processes the highest-priority work first. How does React decide which updates to process first? What are lanes in React? Scheduler React's own module that decides which work runs when Lane a priority bit; React 18 has 31 lanes Starvation low-priority work never getting a chance to run Definition: The Scheduler is React's priority system. Every update gets a lane . More urgent lanes are processed first, and less urgent work waits. Priority order, most urgent first: Sync (discrete events like click or keypress) → InputContinuous (hover, drag) → Default (normal setState) → Transitio

The Fiber work loop processes one Fiber node at a time and yields back to the browser every ~5ms so frames aren't blocked, which makes rendering interruptible. What is time slicing in React? How does the work loop render without blocking the browser? Work loop the loop that processes one fiber at a time Time slicing splitting work into ~5 ms chunks Yield handing the main thread back to the browser Definition: The work loop is React's main engine. It is a while loop that processes one fiber at a time and, after each fiber, asks: "Have my 5ms run out?" If so, it yields (lets the browser run) and resumes from the same spot later.

React 17 batches state updates only inside React event handlers. React 18 batches ALL updates automatically, including those in setTimeout, promises, and native events. What is state batching? How does React 18's automatic batching differ from React 17? How do you opt out? Batching combining multiple state updates into a single re-render Automatic batching React 18 feature: batching everywhere, not just in event handlers flushSync opts out of batching and forces an immediate render Definition: Batching means combining all setState calls made in the same tick into a single re-render. In React 17 , batching happened only inside React event handlers. Inside setTimeout , promises, or native list

n: React Element vs Component vs Instance
x: Element: a plain object describing what to render. Component: a function or class that returns elements. Instance: the live record of a mounted component. Only class components expose one (this). What is the difference between a React element, a React component, and a React instance? Element a plain, immutable object describing "what should be shown" Component a function or class that produces elements Instance the fiber node: the live record of a running component (state, effects) Definition: Three different things that people often mix up: Component = the recipe (the function Card ) Element = the order slip ( <Card title="Hi"/> : just an object, nothing has run yet) Instance = the ac

Hooks must be called at the top level and only from React functions. React stores hook state in a linked list on the Fiber node, matched by call order. Why can't hooks be called inside conditionals or loops? What would break internally if you did? Hook a special function whose name starts with use and that gives you a React feature Call order the order in which hooks are called; React uses it to identify each hook Linked list nodes linked one after another; React stores hooks this way Definition: Two rules: Call hooks only at the top level , never inside an if, a loop, or a nested function. Call them only from a React function component or a custom hook . The reason in one line: React identi

useState stores its value in a hook queue on the Fiber node. The setter enqueues an update and triggers a re-render. Functional updates avoid stale closure problems. How does useState work under the hood? What is the difference between setState(value) and setState(prev => value)? Hook node the object inside the fiber that holds the state for that hook Update queue a circular list of pending setState calls Bailout if the value is the same, React skips the render Definition: useState creates a node in the memoizedState linked list on the fiber. That node holds the current value and an update queue containing pending setState calls. During render, React applies each update in the queue in order

Runs after paint, asynchronously. The dependency array controls when it re-runs. The cleanup function runs before the next effect and on unmount. Explain useEffect's full lifecycle: when does it run, when does cleanup run, and what is the dependency array contract? Side effect work that happens outside of render: fetch, timer, subscription, DOM Dependency array the values whose changes cause the effect to re-run Cleanup the function returned by the effect; it runs before the next effect Definition: useEffect(fn, deps) tells React: "after the commit and paint, do this work." The deps array says when to run it again. No array → after every render [] → on mount only (and twice in development un

useLayoutEffect fires synchronously after DOM mutations but before paint, matching the timing of componentDidMount/componentDidUpdate. useEffect fires after paint. When would you use useLayoutEffect instead of useEffect? Give a concrete real-world example. Paint the browser drawing pixels on the screen Layout thrashing repeatedly measuring and mutating the DOM, which is very slow Flicker the user sees incorrect UI for a single frame Definition: Both run after the commit, but their timing differs: useLayoutEffect — after the DOM update, BEFORE paint . Synchronous; it blocks the browser. useEffect — AFTER paint . Asynchronous; it doesn't block the browser. Default to useEffect . Reach for useL

useRef returns a stable { current } object that persists across renders without triggering re-renders. Use it for DOM access, timers, previous values, and mutable instance variables. What are the three main uses of useRef? How does it differ from useState for storing values? Ref a mutable box: { current: value } Mutable can be changed directly Instance variable a value that persists between renders without triggering one Definition: useRef(init) gives you an object { current: init } that stays the same object for the component's entire life . Changing .current does not cause a re-render . It has two jobs: (1) grabbing a DOM node, and (2) holding a value that must be remembered but has nothin

n: useMemo — When to Use & When Not To
x: Memoizes the result of an expensive computation and recalculates only when dependencies change. It costs memory and adds complexity, so it's only worth it for genuinely expensive work. When should you use useMemo? What is the overhead of useMemo itself? When does it hurt performance? Memoize remember a result so it doesn't have to be recalculated Referential stability getting the same object reference on every render Premature optimization optimizing without measuring, which is often harmful Definition: useMemo(fn, deps) remembers the result of a calculation. If the dependencies haven't changed, fn doesn't run again and the previous result is returned. There are two valid reasons: (1) the ca

Returns a memoized function reference that changes only when its dependencies change. Critical when passing callbacks to memoized child components. Why does useCallback exist? When does it actually improve performance, and when is it wasted? useCallback keeps the function reference stable Reference equality whether two values are the very same object; it compares identity, not content Definition: useCallback(fn, deps) is equivalent to useMemo(() => fn, deps) . It remembers the function so you get the same reference on every render. In JavaScript, every render creates a new function object for () => {} . It looks identical, but the reference is different. That defeats a chil

An alternative to useState for complex state transitions. Takes (state, action) => newState, which keeps state logic testable and in one place. When would you choose useReducer over useState? Implement a cart with useReducer. Reducer a pure function: (state, action) => new state Action an object describing what happened: { type: "...", payload } Dispatch the function that sends an action Definition: useReducer(reducer, initial) — when several state values are related, keep them in a single reducer instead of separate useState calls. Every change is described as an "action". Rule of thumb: 3+ related pieces of state , or one event that changes several of them → use useReducer.

Subscribes a component to the nearest context value. Every change to the context value re-renders ALL consumers, even those that use only part of it. What is the performance problem with useContext? How do you prevent unnecessary re-renders from context changes? Context a way to pass data down the tree without props Provider the component that supplies the value Consumer a component that reads the value via useContext Definition: Context is a way to avoid prop drilling. A Provider supplies a value, and anywhere below it in the tree you can read that value with useContext . Performance trap: when the context value changes, all consumers re-render, even if they only use a small part of it.

Functions starting with "use" that call other hooks — encapsulate and reuse stateful logic without changing component hierarchy. What is a custom hook? How does it differ from a utility function? When should you extract one? Custom hook a function that starts with use and calls other hooks Stateful logic logic that involves state or effects Composition building larger hooks by combining smaller ones Definition: A custom hook is a normal function that (a) starts with use and (b) calls other hooks inside. It lets you pull stateful logic out of a component and reuse it. Important: each component gets its own separate copy . Custom hooks don't share state; they share logic .

Local state → component. Shared UI state → lift up or context. Server state → React Query/SWR. Global app state → Zustand/Redux. How do you decide where state should live? Walk me through your decision framework for a real app. Server state data owned by the server, of which you hold a copy (users, posts) Client state data that exists only in the browser (modal open, form draft) Derived state data that can be calculated from other data; it shouldn't be stored as state Definition: Where state lives is a decision, not a default. The most important question is: is this server data or client data? Server state → React Query / SWR / a framework loader. Don't put it in useState. Client state → use

Context is designed for low-frequency, global data (theme, auth, locale) — not high-frequency state updates that should use a dedicated store. What is Context good for and what is it NOT good for? What performance problems does heavy Context use cause? createContext creates a context object Default value the value consumers get when no Provider is above them Custom hook wrapper your own hook around useContext, for safety Definition: The right way to use Context is to wrap it in a custom hook that throws when the Provider is missing, memoize the value with useMemo , and keep data and actions in separate contexts .

Single store, pure reducers, actions as intent. Middleware (thunk, saga) handles side effects. Selectors compute derived state. DevTools enable time-travel debugging. Explain the full Redux data flow. What role does middleware play, and when is Redux overkill? Store the single place where the whole app's state lives Action a plain object describing what happened Middleware a layer between dispatch and the reducer, used for logging, async work and so on Definition: Redux is a predictable state container built on three rules: (1) a single store , (2) state is read-only , so you can only change it by dispatching actions, and (3) changes are made by pure reducers . Data flows in one direction: d

RTK eliminates Redux boilerplate: createSlice merges actions+reducers, createAsyncThunk handles async flows, RTK Query handles server state. What problems does Redux Toolkit solve over vanilla Redux? Explain createSlice and createAsyncThunk. createSlice creates the reducer and its actions together Immer a library that lets you write "mutating" code but produces an immutable copy under the hood RTK Query RTK's data-fetching and caching layer Definition: Redux Toolkit (RTK) is the official, recommended way to write Redux. createSlice defines state, reducers and actions in one place. Immer is built in, so you can write state.count++ . It looks like mutation, but it produces immutable updates un

A minimal store based on closures and subscriptions. Components subscribe to slices — only re-render when their subscribed slice changes, unlike Context. How does Zustand work under the hood, and how does it avoid the re-render problem that Context has? Store a hook that provides state, created with create() Selector picks one part of the store, so the component re-renders only when that part changes Shallow compare compares only the top-level keys of an object Definition: Zustand is a tiny (~1KB) state library. You create a store with create() and get back a hook. No Provider, no boilerplate. The biggest difference from Context is selector support . You can subscribe to a single field of th

Manages server state: caching, background refetching, stale-while-revalidate, pagination and optimistic updates. Removes the loading/error/data boilerplate. What problem does React Query solve that useState+useEffect doesn't? Explain stale-while-revalidate. Query key the unique identifier for a cache entry, written as an array Stale the data is old and will be refetched in the background Mutation an operation that changes data on the server (POST/PUT/DELETE) Definition: TanStack Query is a cache for server data, not a general state manager. It handles caching, deduplication (two components requesting the same data trigger one request), background refetching, stale-while-revalidate, retries,

Atom-based state: tiny, composable units of state. Components subscribe only to the atoms they use, giving minimal re-renders through a graph-based dependency model. What is atomic state management? How do atoms differ from a single global store like Redux? Atom the smallest piece of state Derived atom an atom computed from other atoms Bottom-up building from small pieces upward, the opposite of a top-down store Definition: In atomic state libraries (Jotai, Recoil) there is no single large store. Instead there are many small atoms , and each component subscribes only to the atoms it uses. Derived atoms are computed from other atoms and recompute only when one of their dependencies changes.

A component re-renders when its state changes, its parent re-renders, a context it consumes changes, or its key changes. Receiving the same props is NOT enough to prevent a re-render. List every cause of a React re-render. What is the most common source of unnecessary re-renders in production apps? Re-render the component function runs again Repaint the browser redraws pixels, which is a separate thing Bailout React skips the render Definition: A component re-renders for only four reasons: Its own state changed Its parent re-rendered A context value it consumes changed A hook it uses (useSyncExternalStore, etc.) triggered an update Changed props are not on the list. Props only change when th

Wraps a component to memoize its render. Skips re-render if props are shallowly equal. Fails silently with object/array/function props created inline. How does React.memo work? Why does it often fail to prevent re-renders with object or function props? React.memo a higher-order component that skips re-rendering when props are the same Shallow compare compares each prop with Object.is without looking inside Custom comparator your own comparison function Definition: React.memo(Component) wraps a component. When the parent renders, React first does a shallow comparison of the props. If they're all the same, it skips running the component. Shallow means each prop is compared with Object.is . It

React.memo + useCallback is the classic pattern: memo prevents the re-render, and useCallback keeps the function reference from changing on every parent render. Explain the React.memo + useCallback pattern. When is it necessary, and when is it premature optimization? Triad the three tools working together Memoization chain if one link breaks, the whole chain is useless Definition: These are three separate tools that work together: React.memo — skips re-rendering a component useMemo — keeps a value reference stable useCallback — keeps a function reference stable Rule of thumb: without React.memo, the other two do nothing for rendering (except for

React.lazy() enables dynamic import() for components. Suspense shows a fallback while the chunk loads. This reduces the initial bundle size and time to interactive (TTI). How do React.lazy and Suspense work, and what network request pattern do they produce? Bundle all your JS in one file; if it's large, the page loads slowly Chunk a separate piece of the bundle that is downloaded independently Lazy load only when needed Definition: Code splitting means breaking a large bundle into smaller chunks that are downloaded only when needed. In React you do it with React.lazy() + <Suspense> . lazy(() => import('./X')) is a dynamic import, so the bundler emits a separate file for X .

Only render DOM nodes for visible items. Libraries like react-window and TanStack Virtual keep a constant-size DOM regardless of list length. What is list virtualization? Explain how react-window implements it. What are its limitations? Virtualization create DOM nodes only for what is visible Window the portion of the list currently visible Overscan a few extra rows above and below the window to keep scrolling smooth Definition: Rendering 10,000 rows into the DOM can freeze the browser. With virtualization, only the ~20 visible rows exist in the DOM, and as you scroll, those same nodes are reused with new data. A spacer element fakes the full list height so the scrollbar looks correct.

The Profiler API and the DevTools flamegraph show render durations, commit counts and which component triggered a render. They are the starting point for any performance investigation. How do you identify performance bottlenecks in a React app? Walk me through your debugging process. Profiler the React DevTools tab that measures renders Flamegraph a chart where each component's render time is shown as a bar Commit an update in which React applied changes to the DOM Definition: The React DevTools Profiler records which component rendered, when, for how long, and why . It answers "why did this render?" with data instead of guesswork. You can also collect timings programmatically with the <P

Lifting static children into props.children or slot props means the parent creates them, not the stateful component, so they don't re-render when that component's state changes. How can component composition prevent unnecessary re-renders without using React.memo? Composition connecting components through props/children children as props passing JSX as a prop Element identity the React element being the very same object Definition: If you create JSX outside the stateful component and pass it in through the children prop, the element's reference doesn't change. When the wrapper's state changes, React sees the same children element and skips rendering it , without any memo .

React can now pause, interrupt, and restart rendering work. High-priority updates (user input) can interrupt low-priority renders in progress. What is Concurrent Mode? How does interruptible rendering improve user experience? Concurrent preparing more than one version of the UI at the same time Interruptible a render can be paused and resumed later Urgent vs non-urgent which updates must happen immediately and which can wait Definition: Concurrent React means React can pause, resume or discard a render. It isn't a feature you switch "on". It's a capability that comes with createRoot , and you use it through useTransition / useDeferredValue / Suspense . It is not parallel . JavaScript is stil

Suspense catches "not ready yet" signals from lazy components or data libraries, shows a fallback, and re-renders when data is ready — enabling a waterfall-free fetch-on-render model. How does Suspense work for data fetching vs code splitting? What does a library need to do to support Suspense? Suspense a boundary that shows a fallback for children that are "not ready yet" Fallback the UI shown until the content is ready Suspend a component signals "I'm not ready yet" by throwing a promise Definition: <Suspense fallback={...}> is a boundary. If any component inside it is "not ready yet" (a lazy chunk is loading, or data is still arriving), React shows the fallback , and then the real c

Mark a state update as non-urgent. React can interrupt and defer it in favour of urgent updates like typing. Returns [isPending, startTransition]. What does useTransition do? Give a concrete example where it keeps the UI from feeling sluggish. Transition an update that can be paused, i.e. non-urgent isPending a boolean that is true while a transition is in progress Urgent update typing or a click, which should appear immediately Definition: const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition() . React treats state updates inside startTransition(fn) as non-urgent . If an urgent update arrives, React pauses them, or discards and restarts them. You can use isPending to show a "loading" hint with

Returns a deferred version of a value. React shows the stale value first, then re-renders with the new value in the background. What is the difference between useDeferredValue and useTransition? When would you reach for one over the other? Deferred value a slightly older version of the value Debounce waits a fixed time, and you control the timing Throttle allows execution at most at a fixed rate Definition: const deferred = useDeferredValue(value) gives you a "lagging" copy of the value. React first updates the urgent UI with the new value, then re-renders in the background with the deferred one. The difference from useTransition : with a transition you wrap the update (so you must control

Components that run only on the server: zero JS in the client bundle, direct database/filesystem access, and no hooks or state. Client Components still render on both the server and the client. What are React Server Components? What can and can't they do? How do they differ from SSR? RSC React Server Component, which runs on the server and never in the browser Client Component the "classic" component, which runs in the browser "use client" a directive at the top of a file that creates the boundary Definition: Server Components are rendered only on the server . Their JavaScript is never sent to the browser. Only the render result (in a special serialized format) is. That means they cannot use

React 18's renderToPipeableStream sends HTML as it becomes ready. Selective hydration lets React hydrate the part the user is interacting with first. How does streaming SSR work? What is selective hydration and why does it improve interactivity (TTI)? SSR generating the HTML on the server and sending it to the browser Hydration attaching client-side JS to server-generated HTML so it becomes interactive Streaming sending HTML in chunks without waiting for the whole document to be ready Definition: Classic SSR is all-or-nothing: the server sends nothing until all the data for the whole page has arrived. With streaming SSR, the server sends whatever is ready immediately and streams the remainin

The use() hook (React 19+) reads resources such as Promises or Context during render. It unwraps a Promise and suspends automatically until it resolves. What does the use() hook do, and how does it differ from await and useEffect for async data? use() a React API that reads a promise or context Unwrap extract the resolved value from a promise Conditional call calling it inside an if, which is allowed for use() Definition: use(promise) unwraps a promise. Until it resolves, the component suspends and the nearest Suspense fallback is shown. use(context) reads context. Despite the name, use() doesn't follow the usual hook rules: it can be called conditionally and inside loops .

A function that takes a component and returns an enhanced component. It was the classic reuse pattern before hooks and has largely been replaced by custom hooks. What is an HOC? What problems does it solve and what problems does it create (wrapper hell, prop collision)? HOC a function that takes a component and returns a new component Wrapper hell when many HOCs are nested, DevTools shows 8 layers of wrappers hoistStatics copying static properties from the wrapped component to the wrapper Definition: A Higher-Order Component (HOC) is a function of the shape Component → Component . It takes an existing component, wraps it with extra props or behavior, and returns a new component. Custom

Share behavior by passing a function as a prop that returns JSX. This gives the consumer full control over what gets rendered. What is the render props pattern? How does it compare with HOCs and custom hooks for sharing logic? Render prop a prop whose value is a function that returns JSX Children as function passing children as a function Inversion of control the consumer decides what gets rendered Definition: The component keeps the logic and leaves the rendering decision to the consumer , through a function prop that receives the component's state. For example, <Mouse render={pos => <p>{pos.x}</p>} /> , or the same idea using children as a function.

A parent component implicitly shares state with a set of child components via Context — creating expressive, flexible APIs like + . What is the compound component pattern? Build a Tabs component with it. Compound components components that work together as one unit Implicit state the parent's state that children receive via context Flexible layout the user decides which part goes where Definition: A parent component shares its state with its children through context. The user writes <Tabs><Tabs.List><Tabs.Tab/></Tabs.List><Tabs.Panel/></Tabs> , much like HTML's <select>/<option> .

Class components implementing getDerivedStateFromError / componentDidCatch that catch render errors in their subtree and show fallback UI. What are Error Boundaries? What errors do they NOT catch? Why must they be class components? Error Boundary a class component that catches its children's render errors getDerivedStateFromError sets state so a fallback UI is shown after an error componentDidCatch used for logging the error Definition: An Error Boundary is a class component that catches errors thrown in its children's render, lifecycle methods and constructors , and shows a fallback UI instead of crashing. It does not catch errors in event handlers, async code (setTimeout, promises), server

ReactDOM.createPortal renders children into a different DOM node than their parent. It's useful for modals and tooltips that must escape overflow:hidden or z-index stacking. What are Portals? Why do modals use them? How does event bubbling work through a Portal? Portal rendering a child elsewhere in the DOM while keeping it in the same place in the React tree Stacking context the CSS scope within which z-index values are compared Event bubbling an event propagating upward to its parents Definition: createPortal(children, domNode) renders children into any DOM node, but they stay in the same place in the React tree . That means they still receive context and their events bubble to the React p

forwardRef passes a ref through a component to a child DOM node. useImperativeHandle customizes what the parent sees through that ref. When and why do you need forwardRef? What is the difference between forwardRef and useImperativeHandle? forwardRef passes a ref through to the inner DOM node useImperativeHandle customizes what is exposed through the ref Imperative API performing actions by calling methods (the opposite of declarative) Definition: ref isn't a normal prop. React handles it specially, so it isn't passed to the child automatically. forwardRef lets a parent reach the inner DOM node. useImperativeHandle lets you expose only selected methods through the ref instead of the full DOM

Wrap a subtree in a Provider to inject dependencies (services, config, state) without prop drilling. It's the foundation of most React library APIs. How does the Provider pattern work in React, and how is it used for dependency injection in tests? Dependency Injection supplying a dependency from outside instead of creating it inside Provider the component that supplies the dependency Composition combining multiple providers Definition: With the Provider pattern, you put services or config into the tree via Context. A component doesn't care where the API client came from; it just calls useApi() . This is React's form of dependency injection.

Separate data-fetching/logic (container) from pure rendering (presentational). Now done naturally with custom hooks extracting logic from display components. What is the container/presentational pattern, and how has it evolved with hooks? Container a component that fetches data (logic) Presentational a component that only displays (UI) Dumb component the old name for a presentational component Definition: In the original pattern, a Container fetches data and holds the logic, while a Presentational component only takes props and renders UI. Today: hooks have almost eliminated the need for container components, but the idea lives on as "logic in a hook, UI in a component". With RSC it's str

"Test the behavior users see, not implementation details." RTL queries mirror what users and assistive technology perceive, which avoids brittle tests tied to component internals. What is the React Testing Library philosophy, and why is testing implementation details harmful? RTL React Testing Library, a library that tests the way a user would Query a method for finding elements, such as getByRole or getByText Implementation detail internal code the user never sees Definition: RTL has one guiding principle: "the more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you" . So RTL doesn't touch state, props or internal functions. It only interacts with what

Test: user interactions, rendered output, async state changes, error states. Do NOT test: internal state, component method calls, or prop types. What makes a good React component test? What should you avoid testing and why? Testing trophy Kent C. Dodds's model, where integration tests give the most value Coverage how much code the tests touched, which isn't proof of quality Regression an existing feature breaking because of a new change Definition: Testing everything is wasteful. Test where the damage from a break is high : User flows — login, checkout, form submit Business logic — price calculation, permissions, validation Edge cases — empty, error, loading, very long text Past bugs — add a

MSW (Mock Service Worker) intercepts at network level — most realistic. jest.mock replaces modules. Both have their place; MSW is preferred for API tests. What is MSW and why is it better than mocking fetch/axios directly in tests? MSW Mock Service Worker, which intercepts API calls at the network level vi.mock / jest.mock replaces a whole module with a fake Handler a fake response for an endpoint in MSW Definition: There are two kinds of mocking: MSW intercepts at the network level. Your code makes a real fetch call, and MSW catches it and returns a fake response. vi.mock replaces at the module level. The entire module is faked. For APIs, MSW is the better choice .

renderHook from RTL wraps hooks in a minimal component so you can test stateful logic in isolation without building a full UI around it. How do you test a custom hook that manages state and side effects? Walk through testing useFetch. renderHook a helper that runs a hook inside a test act wraps a state update so React can process it wrapper the provider the hook needs Definition: To test a hook in isolation, use renderHook . It creates a small component that calls your hook and exposes the return value through result.current . But think first: if a hook is used by a component, testing that component is often more valuable.

waitFor retries assertions until they pass or timeout. findBy queries are async. act() wraps state updates to ensure React flushes before assertions. How do you test a component with async data loading? What is act() and when do you need it explicitly? waitFor retries until an assertion passes findBy getBy combined with waitFor Fake timers replacing real timers so the test doesn't have to wait Definition: After an async operation in React (fetch, timer, transition), the DOM doesn't update immediately. RTL's async tools are: findBy* — waits for an element to appear waitFor(fn) — retries until an assertion passes waitForElementToBeRemoved — waits for a spinner to disappear

n: Why Next.js? — SSR, SSG, ISR & When to Use Each
x: Next.js is the dominant React meta-framework. On top of React it adds server-side rendering (SSR), static site generation (SSG), incremental static regeneration (ISR), file-based routing, API routes and built-in optimizations. What problem does Next.js solve that create-react-app cannot? When would you choose SSR vs SSG vs ISR? SSR the server generates HTML on every request SSG HTML is generated at build time ISR SSG plus periodic regeneration in the background Definition: Next.js is a framework built on React. Routing, rendering strategies, bundling, image optimization and API routes are all built in. It supports four rendering strategies: SSG — HTML generated at build time. Fastest. Blogs,

x: The Next.js App Router (v13+) uses the app/ directory for file-based routing. Each folder is a route segment. layout.js persists across navigations, loading.js shows an instant loading UI, error.js catches errors, and page.js defines the page content. How does the App Router differ from the Pages Router? What are layouts, loading states and error boundaries in the App Router? File-based routing the folder structure is the URL structure Layout UI that stays rendered across navigations Route group a (name) folder that does not appear in the URL Definition: In the App Router, the folder structure inside app/ defines the routes. The special files are: page.tsx — the UI for that route layout.tsx

n: Server Components vs Client Components in Next.js
x: In the Next.js App Router, components are Server Components by default. They run only on the server, can access databases and the filesystem directly, and send zero JS to the client. Add "use client" at the top of a file to make a Client Component that runs in the browser. What is the default rendering mode in the Next.js App Router, and how do you make a component interactive (a Client Component)? "use client" a boundary that makes everything below that file run on the client Serializable can be converted to JSON, so not a function Client island a small interactive part inside a server-rendered page Definition: In the App Router, everything is a Server Component by default . Writing 'use cl

n: Data Fetching in Next.js — fetch(), Caching & Revalidation
x: Next.js extends fetch() with built-in caching and revalidation. Server Components can async/await data directly. use cache: "force-cache" for SSG-like behaviour, or revalidate: 60 for ISR. Client components use React Query or SWR. How does Next.js caching work with fetch()? What is the difference between force-cache and no-store? Request memoization identical fetches in one render pass share a single request Data cache fetch results stored on the server, persisting across deployments revalidate how long before the cached entry is refreshed Definition: In a server component you can await fetch() directly, or call your database. Next.js extends fetch with caching options: cache: 'force-cache'

n: Hydration in Next.js — Mismatches, Selective Hydration & Streaming
x: Hydration is when React attaches event handlers to server-rendered HTML. Next.js streams HTML with React Suspense boundaries — each boundary hydrates independently. Hydration mismatches (server HTML differs from client render) cause errors and hurt performance. What is hydration? What causes hydration mismatches and how do you fix them? Hydration making server-rendered HTML interactive by attaching client JS Mismatch the server and client output differing suppressHydrationWarning silences the warning for one element Definition: The server sends HTML that is rendered but not yet interactive. Then the JavaScript arrives and React attaches its component tree to that HTML and wires up the event

next/image automatically optimises images (lazy loading, responsive sizing, WebP/AVIF, CDN). next/font optimises font loading (self-hosted, no FOUT, layout-shift-free). Metadata API handles SEO (title, description, Open Graph, structured data). How does next/image differ from a regular img tag? What optimisations does it perform? CLS Cumulative Layout Shift — how much the page jumps around LCP Largest Contentful Paint — when the largest content element appears FOUT Flash of Unstyled Text — the fallback font showing before the web font loads Definition: Next.js ships with built-in optimizers: next/image — automatic resizing, WebP/AVIF, lazy loading, blur placeholders next/font — fonts self-ho

API routes (app/api/) let you build backend endpoints inside your Next.js app. Server Actions (v14+) let you call async functions directly from form actions and Server Components without creating API routes — handling mutations server-side. When would you use API routes vs Server Actions? What are the trade-offs? Route Handler app/api/*/route.ts — an HTTP endpoint Server Action a function that runs on the server and can be called from the client "use server" the directive that turns a function into a Server Action Definition: Next.js gives you two ways to run code on the server: Route Handler — create app/api/x/route.ts and export GET / POST functions from it. This is a real HTTP endpoint th

n: Deploying Next.js — Vercel, Docker & Edge Runtime
x: Vercel is the default deployment platform (built by the creators of Next.js). To self-host, use standalone output mode with Docker. The Edge Runtime runs middleware and API routes on edge (CDN) nodes for low latency. Static export works for fully static sites. What is the difference between deploying on Vercel and self-hosting with Docker? What is the Edge Runtime? Edge runtime runs on servers close to the user: fast, but with a limited API set Node runtime full Node.js, so everything works standalone a build output containing only the files needed to run, ideal for Docker Definition: You can deploy Next.js in several ways: Vercel — zero configuration, and every feature (ISR, image optimizat

Nested routes routes inside routes, sharing a layout Loader a function that fetches a route's data before it renders Action a function that handles form submissions Definition: React Router is the standard routing library for SPAs. Since v6.4 it includes data APIs : loader (fetch data before rendering), action (handle form submissions) and errorElement (a route-level error

n: React Forms — controlled vs uncontrolled, validation, React Hook Form, Formik
x: Controlled: React state owns value (onChange + value). Uncontrolled: DOM owns value (useRef + defaultValue). React Hook Form uses uncontrolled for performance with validation. Formik provides controlled model with built-in validation. Server Actions handle form state in Next.js. When would you choose uncontrolled over controlled components? What are the performance implications? React Hook Form a fast form library built on uncontrolled inputs Resolver an adapter that connects a validation schema (zod/yup) to RHF register connects an input to the form in RHF Definition: There are three common ways to build a form: Controlled with useState — fine for small forms (1-3 fields) React Hook Form —

n: Error Boundaries — catch render errors, fallback UI, componentDidCatch
x: Error boundaries catch JavaScript errors in their child component tree during rendering, lifecycle methods, and constructors. They don't catch errors in event handlers, async code, or server-side rendering. Use getDerivedStateFromError for state update, componentDidCatch for logging. What do Error Boundaries catch and what don't they catch? How do you implement one? react-error-boundary a popular library that adds reset and hooks Fallback the UI shown when an error occurs Reset key a value that resets the boundary automatically when it changes Definition: A plain class-based boundary only catches errors; it has no way to reset. In practice you also need a retry button, an automatic reset whe

prop-types: runtime type checking (legacy, replaced by TypeScript). defaultProps: default values for undefined props (deprecated in function components, use default parameters instead). refs callback: function refs for custom logic on mount/unmount. Why are defaultProps deprecated for function components? What replaces them? PropTypes an old library that checks props at runtime defaultProps the old way to give props default values Callback ref passing a function instead of a ref object, so you can run code on mount/unmount Definition: Three legacy topics that still come up in interviews: PropTypes — runtime prop type checking. Largely redundant next to TypeScript, and no longer checked in Re

Three ways to declare variables — differ in scope, hoisting, and mutability. What is the difference between var, let, and const, and when would you use each? Scope The region of code where a variable is visible. Re-assign Giving an existing variable a new value. Re-declare Declaring a variable again with the same name in the same scope. JavaScript gives you three ways to declare a variable. They differ in scope , hoisting , and whether you can reassign them . var is the old style: it is visible throughout the whole function. let and const are the modern style: they are visible only inside their own { } block.

Before execution, JS moves declarations (not initializations) to the top of their scope. What is hoisting? How does it behave differently for var vs let/const vs functions? Hoisting Before execution, JS registers all declarations at the top of their scope, but not their values. TDZ Temporal Dead Zone: the stretch from the start of a block until a let/const declaration, during which the variable cannot be accessed. Before your code runs, JS scans the whole scope once and registers every declaration . The value , however, is only assigned when execution reaches that line. That is why reading a var before its declaration gives undefined : the variable exists, but nothing has been assigned to it

Primitives are copied by value; objects/arrays are copied by reference. What is the difference between primitive and reference types in JavaScript? Primitive A simple value: number, string, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, or bigint. Reference An object, array, or function. The variable stores a reference (address) to it, not the value itself. A primitive variable holds the value itself . When you copy it, you get a new, independent value. A reference variable holds only an address . The actual object lives elsewhere (in the heap). When you copy it, the address is copied, not the object. Two names, one house.

JS automatically converts types when mixing incompatible values in operations. Explain implicit vs explicit type coercion. Why is 0 == false true but 0 === false false? Coercion JS automatically converting a value from one type to another. Implicit You didn't ask for it; JS did it on its own, as in "5" * 2 . Explicit You did the conversion yourself, as in Number("5") . When you combine two different types, JS tries to convert them to a common type, whether or not that makes sense. Remember two rules: + leans toward strings (if either operand is a string, it concatenates instead of adding), and all other arithmetic operators lean toward numbers .

== allows type coercion; === checks value AND type without conversion. When would you ever want to use == over ===? Give a real use case. == (loose) Converts the types first, then compares. === (strict) The types must match too, then it compares values. Object.is Like ===, but treats NaN as equal to itself and distinguishes -0 from +0. === is straightforward: it is true only if the types match and the values match . == first coerces the operands to a common type, then compares. That "coerce first" step is where everything goes wrong.

Three "empty" values with different semantics: intentional absence, uninitialized, and failed numeric op. What is the difference between null, undefined, and NaN? How do you reliably check for each? undefined No value was given. JavaScript assigns it automatically. null Deliberately left empty. You assign it. NaN Not a Number: a numeric operation failed. All three look like "nothing", but their meaning is different: undefined = "no value was ever given". null = "deliberately left empty". NaN = "tried to produce a number and failed".

Scope determines where variables are visible. JS has global, function, and block scopes. Explain the three types of scope in JavaScript, with examples. Scope The region of code where a variable is visible. Scope chain If a variable isn't found, JS searches the outer scopes, up to global. Lexical Scope is decided by where the code is written , not where it runs. There are three kinds of scope: global (the whole file), function (inside a function), and block (inside a { } , which applies only to let / const ). When JavaScript needs a variable, it searches from the inside out : first the current scope, then the next one out, all the way up to global. This is

A function that "remembers" variables from its outer scope even after that scope has returned. What is a closure? Give a real-world use case and a common pitfall. Scope The region where a variable is visible. Closure A function that remembers its outer variables even after the outer function has finished. When you create a function inside another function, the inner one can see the outer function's variables. That part is normal. The remarkable part is that even after the outer function has finished , the inner function still remembers those variables. They don't disappear. That is a closure .

JS creates an execution context for every function call, and the call stack tracks the current chain of calls. What is an execution context? What gets created when a function is invoked? Execution context A frame that records which code is running, what its variables are, and what this is. Call stack The stack of these frames. The top one is the one currently running. Whenever a function runs, JS creates a new frame that holds the function's variables, its scope chain, and its this . These frames are pushed onto a stack . The top frame is the one running. When it finishes, it is removed and the frame below it continues.

this refers to the object that is executing the current function. Its value depends on how the function is called. Explain how this is determined. What are the four binding rules? this The object the function is currently running on. Call-site The place where the function is called . It determines this . The value of this is not fixed when you write the function. It is determined when the function is called. That one sentence clears up most of the confusion. The same function, called in different ways, can get a different this .

Concise function syntax that lexically binds this and cannot be used as constructors. How are arrow functions different from regular functions? List at least 3 differences. Arrow function Short syntax, with no this or arguments of its own. Implicit return Without curly braces, the expression's value is returned automatically. Arrow functions are more than shorter syntax. They have no this of their own ; they borrow this from the place where they are written. That one difference decides when to use an arrow function and when not to.

Functions that take other functions as arguments or return them. They are the foundation of functional JS. What is a higher-order function? Implement map, filter, and reduce from scratch. Higher-order function A function that takes another function as input or returns one. Callback A function you pass to another function so that it can call it later. In JavaScript, a function is just a value . You can store it in a variable, pass it as an argument, or return it. A function that takes another function or returns one is called a higher-order function . map , filter , setTimeout , and addEventListener are all examples.

Transforming a multi-argument function into a sequence of single-argument functions. Explain currying. Write a curry function that works for any number of arguments. Currying Turning a function that takes multiple arguments into a chain of functions that each take a single argument. Partial application Supplying some arguments now and the rest later. Turning add(a, b, c) into add(a)(b)(c) is called currying. The benefit is that you can fill in some arguments ahead of time and get back a new, smaller function.

A function that runs the moment it is defined, used to create an isolated scope. What is an IIFE? Why was it heavily used before ES6 modules? IIFE Immediately Invoked Function Expression: a function that runs as soon as it is defined. Namespace A separate scope that keeps names from clashing in the global scope. An IIFE is a function that runs immediately after it is defined: (function(){ ... })() . Its sole purpose was to create its own scope , so that its inner variables don't end up in the global scope.

Methods to explicitly set this for a function call. bind returns a new function; call/apply invoke immediately. What is the difference between call, apply, and bind? Implement bind from scratch. call Takes this and the arguments separately, and runs immediately. apply Same, but the arguments go in an array . bind Doesn't run immediately. It returns a new function with this fixed. All three exist for the same purpose: setting this manually . call and apply run the function immediately (they differ only in how you pass arguments). bind doesn't run it. It returns a new function whose this is permanently fixed.

Caching the result of expensive function calls so repeated calls with the same input are fast. Implement a generic memoize function. What are its tradeoffs? Memoization Remembering a function's result, so that when the same input comes again it doesn't have to be recomputed. Cache The place where earlier results are stored. Pure function The same input always gives the same output, and nothing else in the world changes. If a function is expensive and the same input keeps coming, recomputing it every time is wasteful. Store the result in a cache (usually a Map). The next time the same input arrives, return the result straight from the cache.

The mechanism that keeps JS non-blocking: it takes tasks from the queues whenever the call stack is empty. Explain the event loop. What is the difference between the microtask queue and the macrotask queue? Call stack The stack of work currently executing, one frame at a time. Macrotask The normal queue: setTimeout , clicks, fetch responses. Microtask The VIP queue: Promise.then and code after await . JS can do only one thing at a time. So why doesn't a 5-second network call freeze the page? Because JS doesn't do that work itself . It hands it to the browser and moves on. When the response arrives, it goes into a queue . The event loop is the guard that keeps asking: "Is the stack empty? The

Passing a function to be executed after an async operation — leads to nested "pyramid of doom". What is a callback? What is callback hell and what problems does it cause? Callback A function you hand to someone else to run when the work is done. Callback hell Callbacks nested inside callbacks, so the code drifts further right at every step. When JavaScript has a slow task to do (a network request, a file read, a timer), it doesn't stop and wait. Instead, you hand it a function that says "run this when you're done" . That function is a callback. The trouble starts when one task depends on another, and then a third. Each step ends up nes

Objects representing eventual completion or failure of an async operation, with then/catch chaining. How does a Promise work internally? What are its three states? Promise A container that says "the answer isn't ready yet, but it will be, either a value or an error". pending / fulfilled / rejected The three states. Once a promise leaves pending, it never changes. Chaining .then() always returns a new promise, which is why chains work. A Promise is like a receipt . The work isn't finished yet, but you're holding something that says "I'll let you know when it's done". It has three states: pending (in progress), fulfilled (finished, with a value) and rejected (failed, with an error). Once a pro

Syntactic sugar over Promises that makes async code look synchronous using generator-like pausing. How does async/await work under the hood? What does await actually do? async Makes a function return a promise. await Waits for a promise's result without blocking the thread. async/await isn't a new mechanism. It's syntax sugar over promises , and the same promises run underneath. await means "pause here and continue when the result arrives". But it doesn't freeze the whole program . Only the current function pauses, and the rest of your code keeps running.

Promise.all, .race, .allSettled, .any — each handles multiple concurrent promises differently. When would you use Promise.all vs Promise.allSettled vs Promise.race vs Promise.any? all Succeeds only if every promise succeeds. One failure means total failure. allSettled Waits for every promise, even failed ones, and reports the outcome of each. race Whichever promise settles first (success or failure) decides the result. any The first promise to succeed wins. Fails only if all of them fail. There are four ways to handle many promises together. They differ in just one thing: when the group counts as finished, and what happens if something fails.

Functions that can pause and resume using yield. They're the foundation of how async/await works internally. What is a generator function? What problem does it solve? How does it relate to async/await? Generator A function that can pause in the middle and later resume from the same point. yield The point where the function pauses and hands a value to the caller. Iterator An object with a next() method that returns {value, done} . A normal function runs from start to finish without stopping. A generator ( function* ) can pause in the middle, at a yield . The key point is who controls the pause : the caller. Each time you call next() , the generator moves forward.

Microtasks (promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) run before the next macrotask (setTimeout, setInterval). What is the difference between microtasks and macrotasks? Predict the output of a tricky async snippet. Macrotask The normal line: setTimeout , setInterval , I/O, UI events. Microtask The VIP line: Promise.then , await , queueMicrotask , MutationObserver . Starvation If microtasks never finish, macrotasks never get to run and the page hangs. There are two separate queues, and the rule fits in one line: run one macrotask, then drain the entire microtask queue, then move on to the next macrotask . That's why Promise.then always runs before setTimeout(fn, 0) , even if the setTimeout is writte

Every JS object has a hidden __proto__ link forming a chain up to Object.prototype for property lookup. Explain the prototype chain. How does property lookup work in JavaScript? Prototype An object that other objects fall back to when they can't find a property themselves. __proto__ An object's link to its prototype. prototype A property of a function; it becomes the prototype of objects created with new . Every JavaScript object has a hidden link to its prototype. When you ask for obj.foo and the object doesn't have it, JS follows that link . If it isn't there either, JS goes one level further up, until it reaches null . This sequence of links is the prototype chain , and it is how inherita

Syntactic sugar over prototype-based inheritance — classes don't add new OOP semantics, just cleaner syntax. Are JavaScript classes "real" classes? What is happening under the hood? class Clean syntax for prototype-based inheritance. Underneath, it still uses prototypes. Syntactic sugar Not new functionality, just a nicer way to write existing behavior. #field A truly private field that can't be accessed from outside the class. class in JavaScript doesn't add anything fundamentally new . It's the same prototype chain with cleaner syntax. class Dog { bark(){} } actually creates Dog.prototype.bark .

JS uses object-to-object delegation, not class-to-instance copying. extends sets up the prototype chain. Explain the difference between prototypal and classical inheritance. When is composition better? Prototypal An object inherits directly from another object. Classical Class to class, as in Java or C++. JavaScript doesn't have this natively. Composition Building behavior by combining pieces instead of inheriting. In Java, a class is a blueprint and objects are created from it. In JavaScript, an object inherits directly from another object , with no blueprint in between. class ... extends looks like Java, but underneath it is the same prototype linking.

Creates a blank object, sets its prototype, runs the constructor with this , and returns the object. What does the new keyword do, step by step? What happens if a constructor returns an object? new Runs a function as a constructor and creates a new object. Constructor The function you call with new . When you call new Foo() , JS does four things, in this order: 1. Creates an empty object. 2. Sets that object's prototype to Foo.prototype . 3. Runs Foo with this set to the new object. 4. Returns the object (unless the function itself returns an object).

Built-in methods to create, copy, and lock down objects, down to the property-descriptor level. What is the difference between Object.freeze and Object.seal? When would you use each? Object.create Creates a new object with the given prototype. Object.assign Copies properties from one object to another (shallow). freeze / seal freeze = nothing can change. seal = no new properties can be added, but existing ones can still be changed. These are four utilities you'll use with objects almost daily. Note that freeze and seal only work at the top level .

Combining functionality from multiple sources without inheritance — prefer composition over inheritance. What is a mixin in JavaScript? How does it address the diamond problem of multiple inheritance? Mixin A piece of behavior that can be mixed into many classes or objects. Composition Building things by combining parts rather than inheriting. In JS, a class can have only one parent . But you often need behavior from two or three places. A mixin is the workaround: keep the behavior in a plain object or function, and mix it into whatever needs it.

Automatic memory management using mark-and-sweep: objects with no reachable references are freed. How does JavaScript garbage collection work? What can cause memory leaks? Garbage collection The engine automatically frees memory that is no longer in use. Reachable An object that can be reached from a root (global, stack). Mark and sweep A GC method: start from the roots, mark every reachable object, then clean up the rest. In JS you don't free memory yourself; the engine does it. Its rule is simple: any object that is no longer reachable gets cleaned up. "Reachable" means it can be reached from a root (the global object or the current call stack), directly or through a chain of references.

When objects remain in memory unintentionally — detached DOM nodes, forgotten timers, global variables. What are the most common memory leak patterns? How do you detect and fix them? Memory leak Memory that is no longer needed but is still being held, so it can't be freed. Detached DOM A DOM node that has been removed from the page but is still referenced by JavaScript. A leak doesn't mean "memory is full". It means something is holding on to data you no longer need . In JavaScript there are only four major causes, and all four are easy to recognize.

Debounce delays execution until activity stops; throttle limits execution to at most once per interval. What is the difference between debounce and throttle? Implement both from scratch. Debounce Wait for things to go quiet, then run once the user stops. Throttle Run at most once per interval, however much the user does. Both reduce how often a piece of work runs, but their logic is opposite: Debounce: "As long as events keep coming, I'll wait. Once they stop , I'll run." Throttle: "I'll run once every X ms, no matter how many events arrive."

Deferring computation until the value is actually needed, using generators, Proxy, and on-demand patterns. What is lazy evaluation? How can generators enable lazy sequences in JS? Lazy Do the work only when the result is truly needed. Eager Do everything upfront, needed or not. Short-circuit Stop evaluating as soon as the result of && / || is known. Lazy means: don't compute anything until someone asks for it. JS already does this in several places: short-circuit && / || , generators, and dynamic import() .

Run JS on a background thread, separate from the main thread, so the UI doesn't block. What are Web Workers? What are their limitations? How do they communicate with the main thread? Web Worker A separate thread that runs JS without blocking the main thread. postMessage How Workers and the main thread communicate. Structured clone When you send a message, the data is copied; references are not passed along. The JS main thread can do only one thing at a time, so a heavy calculation can freeze the UI completely. A Worker gives you a separate thread . The calculation runs there while the UI keeps running. The two communicate through postMessage .

ESM uses import/export (static, tree-shakable); CJS uses require() (dynamic, synchronous). What is the difference between ES Modules and CommonJS? Why does it matter for bundlers? ESM ES Modules: import / export . Today's standard. CommonJS Node's older system: require / module.exports . Tree shaking A bundler removing unused code. Only possible with ESM. Both systems split code into files. The biggest difference: ESM is analyzed before it runs (static), while CommonJS is resolved while it runs (dynamic). That one difference drives everything else: tree shaking, top-level await, and how circular imports behave.

Ensures only one instance of an object exists — commonly used for config stores or DB connections. Implement the Singleton pattern in JavaScript. What are its downsides? Singleton A pattern where the whole app shares exactly one instance of something. Global state State that lives in a single place and can be read or changed from anywhere in the app. Sometimes there should be exactly one of something in the whole app, like a database connection, a config object, or a logger. The cleanest way in JS is to let the module itself be the singleton. A module runs only once and its exports are cached, so you just export a single object.

Objects subscribe to events; publisher notifies all subscribers — decouples sender from receivers. Implement a simple EventEmitter (on, emit, off) from scratch. Observer / PubSub A pattern where interested parties are notified whenever something happens. Subject The thing being observed, where the events happen. Subscriber The party that receives the notification. When something changes, everyone who cares is notified automatically, and the thing that changed doesn't need to know who is listening. You already use this: addEventListener is exactly this pattern.

A function or class that creates and returns objects without the caller knowing the exact type. What is the factory pattern? How does it differ from using the new keyword directly? Factory A function that creates objects so the caller doesn’t have to decide which kind. Factory function A common JavaScript way to create objects without a class. Keep the decision of which object to create in one place. The caller just says "I need one of these", and the factory decides which class to instantiate. In JavaScript this also shows up as a factory function : it creates objects without new and keeps data private through a closure.

Proxy intercepts object operations (get, set, delete); Reflect provides default behaviour for those ops. What can you do with Proxy that you cannot do otherwise? Give a real use case. Proxy A guard in front of an object that intercepts every read and write. Trap The function that intercepts an operation, such as get , set , or has . Reflect A clean way to run the default behavior, e.g. Reflect.get(...) . A Proxy stands in front of an object. Every read or write on that object now goes through your code first. That lets you add validation, logging, default values, or anything else you need.

Unique, non-string primitive used as private(-ish) object keys; well-known symbols customize language behaviour. What problem does Symbol solve? What is Symbol.iterator and how do you use it? Symbol An always-unique value. Two symbols are never equal. Well-known symbols JavaScript's built-in symbols that hook into language behavior. Symbol("id") returns a brand-new value every time, even if the description is the same. That means as an object key it never collides with anything. JavaScript also has built-in symbols (such as Symbol.iterator ) that let you customize language behavior.

Attaching a single listener to a parent instead of many children — exploits event bubbling. What is event delegation? Why is it a performance pattern? When does it fail? Bubbling An event starts at the child and travels up through its parents. Delegation Attaching one listener to a parent instead of one to each child. e.target The element that was actually clicked. Imagine 1000 rows, each with a delete button. Would you attach 1000 listeners? No. Attach one listener to the parent. The event bubbles up to it, and e.target tells you which element was actually clicked.

Changing the DOM triggers layout recalculation (reflow) and repainting, which gets expensive in bulk. What is the difference between repaint and reflow? How do you batch DOM changes to minimise cost? Reflow (layout) The browser recalculates the size and position of elements, which is expensive. Repaint Only colors and appearance change, which is cheaper than a reflow. Layout thrashing Repeated write-then-read cycles that force a reflow every time. Touching the DOM is one of the most expensive things you do in JS. Each change can force the browser to measure the layout again ( reflow ) or redraw the pixels (repaint). The classic bug is layout thrashing : writing, then reading, then writing ag

Four client-side storage mechanisms with different persistence, capacity, and security characteristics. Compare localStorage, sessionStorage, cookies, and IndexedDB. When do you use each? localStorage About 5 MB, persists indefinitely, synchronous (blocking). sessionStorage Same API, but the data is cleared when the tab is closed. IndexedDB A large, asynchronous database for structured data. Cookie About 4 KB, sent to the server with every request. The browser gives you four places to store data. Choose based on three questions: how big is it, how long must it last, and does the server need it ?

Fetch is a modern Promise-based HTTP API; XHR is the older callback/event approach. How does fetch work? What does it return? How is it different from axios? fetch The Promise-based network API and today’s standard. XHR The old XMLHttpRequest API, which is callback-based. AbortController A way to cancel an in-flight request. fetch returns a promise and reads cleanly. But one thing surprises almost everyone: fetch does not reject on a 404 or 500. It rejects only on a network failure (for example, no internet). You have to check the status yourself.

Background scripts that intercept network requests — enable offline-first PWAs and cache strategies. What is a Service Worker? What is its lifecycle? How does it enable offline support? Service Worker A script that sits between your page and the network. Cache API A store for requests and their responses. Offline-first Serve from the cache first and update in the background.
