A service worker is a proxy that runs inside the browser. Every network request passes through it, and you decide whether to answer from the cache or from the network. This is why PWAs can work offline.

Any object with [Symbol.iterator] is iterable; the iterator protocol defines how values are produced one by one. What is the iterator protocol? How do you make a custom object work with for...of? Iterable Something for...of can loop over, because it has Symbol.iterator . Iterator An object with a next() method that returns {value, done} . for...of , spread ( ... ), and destructuring all rely on the same thing: the iterable protocol . Any object with a [Symbol.iterator]() method works with all of them automatically.

Syntactic patterns to unpack values from arrays/objects and gather/spread elements. Explain destructuring with default values, renaming, and nested patterns. What about rest/spread? Destructuring Pulling values out of an object or array directly into variables. Rest (...) Collects the remaining elements into one variable. Spread (...) Expands an iterable or object into individual items. Destructuring lets you pull values straight out of an object or array, without writing obj.a , obj.b over and over. The ... syntax does two jobs: rest (collect the remaining items) and spread (expand items). The context tells you which one it is.

n: Regular Expressions — patterns, groups, lookaheads, common pitfalls
x: RegExp for pattern matching. Named groups (? ), lookaheads (?=...), lookbehinds (? ( ) that you can extract separately. Lookahead (?=...) means "this must come next", but it is not included in the match. Regex is a small language for describing text patterns. You can learn the basics in about 20 minutes and look up the rest as needed. Only a handful of features are useful day to day, and they are listed below.

n: JSON — parse, stringify, revivers, replacers, toJSON
x: JSON.parse with reviver function for custom deserialization. JSON.stringify with replacer for filtering/formatting. toJSON method on objects for custom serialization. JSON.stringify loses functions, undefined, Symbol, Infinity, Date (to string). What does JSON.stringify lose? How do you serialize a Date object properly? stringify Converts a JS value to a JSON string. parse Converts a JSON string to a JS value. replacer / reviver A function that transforms values during conversion. The methods are simple. The hidden rules are the real topic, because JSON doesn't support every JavaScript type.

n: Date/Time — Date, Intl.DateTimeFormat, Temporal API, timezone handling
x: Date is notoriously difficult (mutable, poor API). Intl.DateTimeFormat for locale-aware formatting. Temporal API (Stage 3) replaces Date with immutable, timezone-aware types. moment.js/date-fns/luxon are popular alternatives. What are the problems with JavaScript's Date object? How does the Temporal API improve on it? Date JS's old date object, full of gotchas. Intl The built-in way to format values for a locale. Temporal The new API that fixes the problems with Date. Date is widely considered one of JavaScript's worst designs: months start at 0, it is mutable, and its timezone behavior is odd. The modern approach is formatting with Intl , calculations with a library (date-fns or Day.js), an

try/catch/finally is JS error handling. A catch block receives the error object, and finally always runs (even after a return). Uncaught errors propagate up the call stack, and throw can re-throw an error or throw a new one. Explain try/catch/finally execution order. What happens if catch also throws? throw Raises an error. The code stops there and the error propagates upward. catch Handles a thrown error. finally Runs no matter what happens. Propagation The error travels up the call stack until someone catches it. When a throw happens, the function stops right there and the error climbs upward to the caller. If the caller has no catch , it keeps going up. If nothing catches it, the program

n: Error Types — TypeError, ReferenceError, SyntaxError, RangeError
x: TypeError: wrong type (e.g. calling non-function). ReferenceError: undefined variable. SyntaxError: invalid code. RangeError: value out of range. Each has distinct causes and debugging approaches. What is the difference between TypeError and ReferenceError? Give examples of each. TypeError The value has the wrong type, such as calling a method on undefined . ReferenceError The variable doesn't exist at all. SyntaxError A mistake in the code itself. It fails before execution. RangeError A value is outside the allowed range. JS has several built-in error types, and the error name is half the answer : it tells you right away what kind of mistake happened.

n: Custom Error Classes — extending Error, error codes
x: Extend Error to create domain-specific errors (ValidationError, NotFoundError). Set name, message, and custom properties (statusCode, code). Enables typed catch blocks and better API error responses. How do you create a custom error class in JavaScript? Why would you? Custom error Your own Error class, created with extends Error . Error code A machine-readable identifier such as "AUTH_EXPIRED" . cause Links the original error to the new one. throw new Error("something went wrong") gives the caller only a string , and code can't make reliable decisions from a string. Create your own Error class instead. The caller can then identify it with instanceof , and the error can carry data too.

n: Async Error Handling — unhandled rejections, .catch(), global handlers
x: Unhandled promise rejections crash Node.js (>=15). Always .catch() or use try/await. window.onunhandledrejection catches browser unhandled rejections. process.on("unhandledRejection") for Node. Error boundaries catch React render errors. What happens when a Promise rejects without a .catch()? How do you handle async errors globally? Unhandled rejection A rejected promise with no .catch attached. Global handler The last safety net. Errors that nothing else caught end up here. Async errors behave differently from sync errors, and they cause some of the nastiest bugs. Two rules to remember: (1) a throw inside a callback never reaches the outer try/catch . (2) A Promise with no .catch fails sile

n: Debugging — console methods, debugger statement, DevTools profiling
x: Use console.table/warn/error/group for structured logging. The debugger statement pauses execution. The DevTools Profiler shows CPU usage, the Network tab shows requests, and the Memory tab helps find leaks. Source maps let you debug minified code. What console methods do you use for debugging? When would you use console.table vs console.log? debugger A keyword that pauses execution when DevTools is open. Breakpoint The line where execution stops so you can inspect the state. Source map A file that maps minified code back to the original source. There is much more to debugging than console.log , and learning it can cut your debugging time in half.

n: Map & Set — when to use over objects, iteration, performance
x: Map preserves insertion order, accepts any key type, has size property. Set stores unique values. Both have O(1) lookup like objects but better for non-string keys. WeakMap/WeakSet allow garbage collection of keys. What is the difference between a Map and a plain object? When would you use a Set instead of an array? Map A key-value store where keys can be anything and insertion order is preserved. Set A collection of unique values. An object also stores key-value pairs, so why do we need Map ? Three reasons: a Map's keys can be anything (objects, functions), it keeps insertion order , and it gives you .size directly. It is also fast at adding and deleting entries in large collections.

WeakMap keys must be objects and are weakly held (GC can collect them). WeakSet holds objects weakly. Use WeakMap for private data, caching, and metadata without preventing garbage collection. What is a WeakMap? How does it differ from Map in terms of garbage collection? WeakMap Holds keys weakly, so the garbage collector can reclaim them. GC-friendly A collection that doesn't cause memory leaks. A normal Map holds strong references to its keys. If a key is a DOM node that gets removed from the page, it stays in memory anyway, because the Map is still holding it. WeakMap holds its keys weakly. Once nothing else can reach an object, both the object and its entry are garbage-collected.

TypeScript infers types automatically from values. The type system is structural. Const infers literal types; let infers widened types. What is the difference between type inference and explicit annotation? When does TypeScript infer the wrong type and you must annotate explicitly? Type inference TypeScript automatically understands the type of a value — you don’t have to write it. Widening With let the type widens — e.g., "hi" becomes string . Literal type A type that allows only a single value — e.g., "hi" . TypeScript mostly recognizes types on its own . When you write const x = 5 it knows this is a number — you don’t need to write : number . But there’s a small difference: with const the

Both describe object shapes. interface supports declaration merging and is open for extension. type is more flexible — supports unions, intersections, tuples, and mapped types. When would you use type over interface and vice versa? What is declaration merging and when is it useful or dangerous? interface Object blueprint. Merges when declared again. type alias Naming any type — union, primitive, function, object. Declaration merging Interfaces with the same name automatically combine. In 90% of cases they behave the same. There are two real differences: 1. type can be given any name — union, primitive, tuple. interface only describes an object shape. 2. When you write interface again with th

Union (A | B): the value can be either type. Intersection (A & B): the value must satisfy both types simultaneously. Explain union vs intersection with real examples. When does an intersection type produce never and why? Union (|) "Either this or that" — one of the two. Intersection (&) "Both this and that" — both together. Narrowing Reaching a single type from a Union by applying checks. | and & seem opposite, and that's the most common confusion. A | B = value can be A or B . Therefore you can only use what is present in both — fewer properties. A & B = value has fields of A and B . More properties.

Literal types narrow a type to an exact value (e.g. "GET"). as const freezes an object's inferred types to their literal values, preventing widening. What is a literal type? What does as const do that a regular type annotation cannot? Why is it crucial for arrays used as tuples? Literal type Type that allows only a single value — "up" , 42 , true . as const Lock the entire thing into literal types — objects and arrays as well. A type that allows only a single value . It seems useless on its own, but with a union it becomes TypeScript's most useful feature. "small" | "medium" | "large" — now a fourth value cannot be written, and the editor suggests all three.

TypeScript refines a union type to a narrower type inside conditional blocks using control-flow analysis — typeof, instanceof, in, equality checks, and type predicates. List all the ways to narrow a type in TypeScript. What is a type predicate (is) and when do you need one vs relying on built-in narrowing? Narrowing Reaching a specific type from a union by applying a check. Control flow analysis TypeScript infers the type by reading your if . Discriminant The common field whose value indicates which member it is. TypeScript reads your if . Inside if (typeof x === "string") it knows that x is a string — you can write x.toUpperCase() . This is called control flow analysis , and it is the smart

With strictNullChecks on, null and undefined are their own distinct types — you must explicitly handle them. The non-null assertion (!) removes them unsafely. What changes when you enable strictNullChecks? Explain the non-null assertion operator (!) and when it is a code smell vs genuinely necessary. strictNullChecks TS flag that treats null / undefined as separate types. Non-null assertion (!) "I swear this is not null" — the compiler stays silent. Optional (?) Field may exist or may not. Without strictNullChecks , null hides in every type — string means "string or null", and TypeScript can't protect you. With it, null and undefined become separate types , and you cannot move forward withou

n: Enums vs const enum vs Union Types
x: Regular enums generate a runtime JS object. const enums are erased at compile time (inlined). String literal unions are the modern, zero-runtime alternative. What is the difference between a regular enum, const enum, and a string literal union? Why do many teams prefer union types over enums? enum Group of named constants — creates a real object at runtime. const enum Same, but values are inlined at compile time. Union of literals "a" | "b" — often a better alternative to enums. enum seems like a natural feature of TypeScript — but it is one of the few things that generates real JavaScript code at runtime . The rest of the type system disappears after compilation; there is no enum. And in mo

TypeScript checks shape compatibility, not nominal identity. Excess property checking only applies to fresh object literals — not to variables already typed. What is structural typing and how does it differ from nominal typing? What is excess property checking and why does it only apply to object literals? Structural typing Type matches based on shape , not name. Nominal typing Type matches based on name — the Java/C# approach. Not in TS. Excess property check Error on extra fields when assigning an object literal directly. TypeScript does not look at the name of a type — it looks at whether its shape matches. If an object has the required fields, it will be considered that type, even if it

keyof T yields a union of known public property names of T. typeof gives you the type of a value at the type level — essential for extracting types from values. What does keyof T produce? How does typeof value differ from a type annotation? Show three real uses of combining keyof and typeof. keyof Extracts a union of all keys of a type. typeof Extracts the type of a value (in the type system). Two small operators that together form the most commonly used TypeScript pattern. keyof T = union of all keys of T. typeof x = type of the value x . Combined: "give the type of this object's keys".

T[K] accesses the type at key K within T. Supports nested access, union keys, and extends keyof constraints. Enables type-safe property lookups. How do you write an indexed access type in TypeScript? Show three examples: simple property, nested property, and union key access. Indexed access T[K] — extracting the type of a field from a type. T[number] Element type inside an array type. Just as you extract a value with user.name , you can extract a type with User["name"] . And for arrays, T[number] — “what’s inside this array.”

Functions with return type parameterName is Type act as type predicates. They tell TypeScript to narrow a type if the function returns true. What is a user-defined type guard? Implement isFish(pet: Fish | Bird): pet is Fish. What exactly does the is keyword do at the type level? Type guard A function that returns a boolean and also tells TypeScript the type. is x is Dog — special syntax that replaces the return type. Type predicate The x is Dog part. Normal function returns boolean — TypeScript doesn't know anything about it. In a type guard you write boolean instead of x is Dog , and now TS narrows the type inside the if .

Functions that throw if a condition fails, telling the compiler to narrow types (asserts x is T). Added in TypeScript 3.7. Cleaner than if !throw patterns. What is an assertion function? Write assertIsDefined (val: T | undefined): asserts val is T. How does it differ from a type guard? Assertion function A function that throws when the condition is false — and after that TS assumes the type. asserts asserts x is T — syntax that appears in place of a return type. A type guard returns true / false and you write an if . An assertion function throws when it's wrong — and after that line TypeScript accepts the type as correct. No if .

Type parameters that make code reusable across types. Constraints (extends) restrict what T can be. Defaults provide fallback types. Explain generics deeply. What is a generic constraint? What is a generic default? When does TypeScript fail to infer a generic and you must annotate? Generic Leaving a type as a placeholder , and filling it in when used. Type parameter That placeholder — usually T . Constraint T extends ... — a condition on the placeholder. A function that works with any type, without losing the type . any also works for every type — but the type gets lost there. With a generic, identity("hi") gives you a string , not any .

T extends U ? X : Y — evaluated at the type level. Distributes over union members by default. Enables type-level computation. How do conditional types work? What is distributive behaviour over unions and when does it produce surprising results? Conditional type The if-else of the type world — A extends B ? X : Y . extends (here) Not inheritance — "does it fit into that type?" At the type level, it’s an if . Read it like: " if A fits into B then X, otherwise Y". Here extends does not mean inheritance — it means "is it assignable".

Transform every property of an existing type: { [K in keyof T]: ... }. Used to build Partial, Readonly, Pick, and custom transformations. What are mapped types? Build Partial , Readonly , and Nullable from scratch using only mapped types and no built-in utilities. Mapped type Creating a new type by iterating over all keys of a type. Modifier readonly and ? — you can add or remove them with + / - . Just as array.map() iterates over each item, a mapped type iterates over each key and creates a new type. Partial , Required , Readonly , Record — these four are mapped types, and each is only 2-3 lines long.

Combine string literal types using template syntax: ${A}${B} . Enables type-safe event names, CSS properties, and path strings. What are template literal types? Show 3 real-world use cases where they catch bugs at compile time that would otherwise be silent runtime errors. Template literal type Creating a new string type by concatenating string types. Intrinsic types Uppercase , Lowercase , Capitalize — built-in string helpers. Just as you concatenate at the value level by writing ${name} in a backtick string, you can concatenate string types at the type level. When combined with a union, it generates all combinations — automatically.

Extract a type from within a conditional type. Used to pull out return types, promise values, array element types, and function parameters. What does infer do inside a conditional type? Implement ReturnType , Awaited , and UnpackArray using infer from scratch. infer In a conditional type, "capture whatever is here and give it a name". infer has only one job: extract a part from inside a type. Read it like: "if T looks like Promise<something> , give that something the name U and return it."

Types that reference themselves — for trees, nested JSON, deeply nested objects. TypeScript supports recursive types with some depth limits. How do you define a recursive type in TypeScript? Implement DeepPartial and DeepReadonly . Recursive type A type that uses itself. Depth limit TypeScript goes up to about 50 levels, then gives up. A type can reference itself — like a recursive function. JSON, tree, nested config — all are modeled with it. And by combining with mapped types you can create utilities like DeepPartial .

Tuple types can spread other tuples using ...T syntax — enables typed rest parameters, Concat, Zip, and function argument manipulation. What are variadic tuple types? How do they enable building typed Concat or typed function composition with exact argument types? Tuple Fixed-length and fixed-order array — [string, number] . Variadic Within a tuple, ...T — "whatever else follows". Using spread ( ... ) inside tuple types. This lets you write types like "first argument is this, and whatever else follows". Honestly: this isn’t needed daily. It’s required when you are writing utilities that transform functions such as bind , curry or pipe .

When a conditional type acts on a generic type T that is a union, it distributes over each member. This enables type-level operations like Exclude, Extract, and custom filters. What is distribution in conditional types? Why does T extends U ? X : Y distribute over unions of T? Show how Exclude leverages this. Distributive Conditional type operating on each member of a union separately . Naked type parameter T extends X — where T is written alone, without brackets. When the input of a conditional type is a union and T is written alone, TypeScript applies the type to each member of the union separately and then recombines the results into a union again. This is often desired — and sometimes no

Mapped types support key remapping with as: { [K in keyof T as NewKey]: T[K] }. Enables prefixing, suffixing, filtering, and transforming object keys at the type level. What is key remapping in TypeScript mapped types? Show how to: prefix all keys with "_", filter out functions from an object type, and make all keys optional. Key remapping Renaming keys inside a mapped type using as . never se filter Make a key never to remove it completely. In a mapped type, by using as you can rename a key — or turn it into never to remove it.

TypeScript 4.1+ provides Uppercase, Lowercase, Capitalize, Uncapitalize as intrinsic types — handled by the compiler, not expressible in userland. Used in template literal type transformations. What are intrinsic string types in TypeScript? Show how Capitalize, Uncapitalize, Uppercase, and Lowercase work. Why are they "intrinsic" and not implementable by users? Intrinsic Built inside the compiler — cannot be written in TypeScript. Four built-in string types: Uppercase , Lowercase , Capitalize , Uncapitalize . These are intrinsic — meaning they are written inside the compiler in C++, not in TypeScript. Therefore you cannot create them yourself.

n: Abstract Classes — abstract methods, constructor access, vs interfaces
x: Abstract classes can't be instantiated directly. Abstract methods have no body — subclasses must implement them. Unlike interfaces, abstract classes can have constructors, state, and concrete methods. Use when you need shared implementation across related classes. What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface in TypeScript? When would you use each? abstract class Incomplete class — cannot be instantiated directly. abstract method Only the name, no body — the child must implement it. A class that is incomplete . It has some methods that are complete (the same for everyone) and some abstract — which each child must implement themselves. new AbstractClass() does not work — y

n: Variance Annotations — in, out, invariant on type parameters
x: TypeScript 4.7+ supports variance annotations: out T (covariant), in T (contravariant), in out T (invariant). Controls how type parameter subtyping works. Methods are contravariant in parameters, covariant in return types by default with strictFunctionTypes. What are variance annotations in TypeScript? What does in and out mean on a type parameter? Covariant (out) Type parameter only goes out (return position). Contravariant (in) Type parameter only goes in (parameter position). Invariant Both places — so you can’t make it wider or narrower. TypeScript automatically determines how a generic type parameter behaves. in / out you can specify it by writing. Honestly: this is not needed in 99% of

Partial makes all props optional. Required makes all required. Readonly prevents reassignment. None are deep — they only affect the top level. Implement Partial , Required , Readonly from scratch using mapped types. What are their limitations (shallow only)? Partial Make all fields optional. Required Make all fields required. Readonly Prevent all fields from being changed. Three mapped types that produce different shapes of the same type — without rewriting the whole interface. Each contains just 2 lines of code, and all three are shallow .

Pick/Omit work on object keys. Extract/Exclude work on union members. They are often confused because the names are symmetrical. What is the difference between Omit and Exclude ? What is the difference between Pick and Extract ? Give concrete examples. Pick Keep only these keys. Omit Remove these keys. Extract / Exclude Work on unions, not on objects. Four utilities, two pairs — and these pairs work on different things , which is the most common confusion. Pick / Omit → on object keys. Extract / Exclude → on union members.

Creates an object type with keys of type K and values of type V. Stronger than { [key: string]: V } because it enforces all union keys are present. When is Record better than { [key: string]: V }? How does Record with a union key enforce exhaustive key handling? Record An object whose all keys are of type K and whose values are of type V. Record<K, V> = "an object whose keys are of type K and whose values are of type V". Internally it is a one-line mapped type: { [P in K]: V } .

Extract types from function signatures without repeating them — essential for wrappers, decorators, and middleware. What does ReturnType do internally (hint: infer)? Show 3 real use cases for Parameters and ReturnType in production code. ReturnType Extract the function's return type. Parameters Extract a tuple of the function's arguments. typeof fn Extract its type from the function value . Utilities that extract a type from a function. All three are built with infer . And their most useful pattern is just one: ReturnType<typeof fn> .

Recursively unwraps Promise to get T. Handles nested Promises and thenables. Added in TS 4.5 to replace the broken ReturnType pattern. Why was Awaited added in TypeScript 4.5? What was broken about using ReturnType to type async functions before it? Awaited The type of the value inside a Promise — no matter how many layers. Awaited<Promise<string>> = string . And if a promise contains another promise, it also unwraps it — just like await does itself.

Combine generics, conditional types, mapped types, and infer to create domain-specific utility types. Build these from scratch: DeepPartial , Mutable (reverse of Readonly), FunctionKeys (only keys whose values are functions). Custom utility A reusable type helper you build yourself. Built-in utilities are often insufficient. Some helpers are needed in every project and TypeScript doesn't provide them. Here are the five that are most useful.

NonNullable removes null and undefined from T. Useful after filter(Boolean) or in combination with Partial. Not deep — only removes top-level nullability. What does NonNullable do? Implement it from scratch. Why does Array .filter(Boolean) not automatically narrow the type to NonNullable ? NonNullable null and undefined removed. A one-line utility: NonNullable<string | null> = string . Internally: T extends null | undefined ? never : T .

NoInfer (TS 5.4+) prevents TypeScript from using that position for generic inference. Forces callers to provide a type explicitly while still constraining it. What does NoInfer do? Show a use case where it prevents TypeScript from inferring a too-wide type from one parameter versus another. NoInfer Tell TypeScript: "don't infer the type from this place". When a generic type appears in two places, TypeScript infers from both and merges them — and the result often becomes wide. With NoInfer<T> you exclude one place from inference.

ThisType defines the this context inside an object literal (used in Vue options API, Svelte, and chain builders). ThisParameterType and OmitThisParameter extract/remove the this parameter from a function. What does ThisType do? How is it used in framework types like Vue's Options API? What happens without it? ThisType Set the type of this inside an object literal. ThisParameterType Extract the type of a function's this parameter. Very few utilities that work with this . Honestly: ThisType is hardly needed today — it was for Vue 2-style this -based APIs. But it shows up in interviews.

Uppercase, Lowercase, Capitalize, Uncapitalize are built-in intrinsic types. Frequently used with template literal types for key transformation and naming convention enforcement. List all 4 intrinsic string utilities. Show how to build a type that converts camelCase to kebab-case and back using these utilities. Intrinsic Built into the compiler — cannot be written in TypeScript. Four string utilities: Uppercase , Lowercase , Capitalize , Uncapitalize . They are covered in the full lesson "Intrinsic String Manipulation Types" — just remember that they are part of the utility types family and are separate from other utilities: the rest are written in TypeScript, these are ins

Controls strict checks, compilation target, module output format, path aliases, and project references. Getting tsconfig wrong causes silent runtime bugs. Explain these 10 tsconfig options: strict, target, module, moduleResolution, esModuleInterop, paths, baseUrl, isolatedModules, noUncheckedIndexedAccess, exactOptionalPropertyTypes. tsconfig.json TypeScript settings file — the root of the project. include / exclude Which files should be checked. extends Borrow settings from another config. A file that determines how strict TypeScript will be, which files it will check, and what the output will look like. It contains over 100 options. Only 8-10 truly matter — the rest default are fine.

strict enables: strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes, strictPropertyInitialization, strictBindCallApply, strictBuiltinIteratorReturn, useUnknownInCatchVariables, noImplicitThis. What are all the flags that strict enables? Which ones cause the most pain when enabling on a legacy JavaScript codebase? strict A switch that turns on 8 different flags. strictNullChecks The one that provides the most benefit. "strict": true is a shortcut — it turns on 8 different flags. Each catches its own kind of mistake. Among them, strictNullChecks alone provides half of TypeScript's benefit.

Type definitions without implementation. Libraries ship them or you install via @types/*. Declaration merging adds to existing types. What is a .d.ts file? When do you write one vs install @types/*? What is the difference between declare module and declare global? .d.ts A file that contains only types — no executable code. DefinitelyTyped The repository of @types/* packages. declare "This thing exists elsewhere, and this is its type." A file that contains only types , no executable code. It is used to attach types to JavaScript libraries. You will find them in three places: inside the library, in a @types/* package, or in your own project.

TS compiles to CJS, ESM, or others. Module resolution (how imports are found) is separate from module format (what is emitted). Mixing them causes import errors. What is the difference between CommonJS and ESM output from TypeScript? What breaks when a CJS consumer requires an ESM package? ESM import / export — standard. CommonJS require / module.exports — Node's legacy. moduleResolution How TypeScript determines where an import originates. In TypeScript, the module hassle is a mixed result of three settings: module , moduleResolution , and the package.json field in "type" . Most "Cannot find module" errors arise because these three do not align.

Split a large monorepo into sub-projects with their own tsconfig. TypeScript builds only what changed using .tsbuildinfo files. What are TypeScript project references? How do they speed up large monorepo builds? What is composite: true and why is it required? Project references A TS project depends on another — they are built separately. Incremental Only the changed part is recompiled. composite The flag that makes a project referenceable. Compiling everything at once in large repos is slow. Project references let you split it into pieces, and TypeScript only rebuilds the changed pieces.

TypeScript exposes its compiler as a public API. Used by ESLint, ts-morph, and custom build tools to analyse and transform code. What is the TypeScript Compiler API? What can you do with it that you cannot do with regular type checking alone? Compiler API Using TypeScript as a library. AST Abstract Syntax Tree — the tree representation of code. ts-morph An easy wrapper around the Compiler API. TypeScript is not just a compiler — it's also a library . You can import it, parse code, walk its tree, and write new code. The raw API is heavyweight; ts-morph is its easy wrapper and should be used for most work.

Source maps map compiled JS back to TS for debugging. Declaration maps map .d.ts back to .ts source for IDE go-to-definition. Essential for library authors. What is the difference between sourceMap and declarationMap? Why should library authors ship declaration maps? How does "go to source" work in node_modules? Source map File that links compiled code back to the original code. Declaration map .d.ts file that links to the original source. The browser runs your compiled JS, but you need to debug your TypeScript. Source map is the link that connects the two. Declaration map is a separate thing: it makes the editor’s "Go to Definition" take you to the original source instead of the .d.ts .

jsx controls JSX emission: react (React.createElement), react-jsx (_jsx runtime, TS 4.1+), preserve (keep for Babel), react-native. jsxFactory, jsxFragmentFactory for custom runtimes. What are the TS jsx options and when should you use each? What changed with the automatic JSX runtime (react-jsx) and why is it preferred? jsx: react-jsx New transform — no need for import React . .tsx The file extension where JSX can be written. A setting that determines how JSX will be compiled. The correct answer today is "react-jsx" .

target sets the JS language level (ES2015, ES2020, ESNext). lib specifies which ambient declarations to include. module sets the output module system. These three interact. What is the interaction between target, lib, and module in tsconfig? Why would you set target: ES2015 but lib: ES2023? What does "lib" actually control? target Which version of JavaScript the output will be. lib Which built-in types will be available. DOM lib Types of the browser APIs. Settings that are interrelated and often cause confusion: target = "which JS version the output will be in". lib = "which built-in types will be visible to me". When you set target , lib is set automatically — but you can override it.

paths and baseUrl enable import aliases like @/components/Button instead of ../../../components/Button. Requires matching bundler config (vite, webpack, tsconfig-paths at runtime). How do you configure path aliases in TypeScript? What is the relationship between baseUrl and paths? Why do path aliases need separate runtime configuration? paths Shortcut for import paths — @/utils . baseUrl The folder from which relative paths start. Write ../../../utils/format instead of @/utils/format . But an important point: TypeScript only understands this for type-checking . At runtime you need to inform your bundler separately.

React.FC adds implicit children and restricts generics. Explicit typed functions give more control. PropsWithChildren adds children explicitly. What is the difference between React.FC and a plain typed function? Why do many teams avoid React.FC? What problems does it cause? Props Data passed to a component — a normal object. ReactNode Anything that can be rendered — JSX, string, number, array, null. React.FC Old way of typing props. Not recommended today. A React component is a normal function that takes an object. So typing it is just like typing a normal function — no special React magic. You don't even need to write the return type — TypeScript works it out from the JSX itself.

useState infers from initial value. useRef has two overloads: DOM ref (HTMLElement | null) and mutable ref (MutableRefObject ). useReducer needs explicit action types. When does TypeScript infer useState correctly vs when must you annotate? Show 3 common useState typing mistakes in real code. Inference TypeScript infers the type itself — this is what happens in most hooks. Type argument useState<T>() — when inference is not sufficient. Most hooks don't need to be typed — no need at all — TypeScript understands everything from the initial value. The type only needs to be written in three places: when the initial value is null , when it is an empty array, and when at the start you don't

React wraps native events in SyntheticEvent. Each element type has specific event types: React.ChangeEvent , React.MouseEvent . What is the difference between React.ChangeEvent, React.FormEvent, and React.MouseEvent? How do you type a generic onChange handler that works across input types? SyntheticEvent React's own event wrapper — like a native event but cross-browser. ChangeEvent When an input/select/textarea changes. React events are not native events — they are React's own wrappers. Therefore their types also come from React, not from the DOM. And a small trick: if the handler is written directly in JSX , you don't need to write a type — React infers it automatically.

Components that accept type parameters — for typed lists, tables, selects. Arrow function generics in .tsx files clash with JSX angle brackets. How do you write a generic React component? Implement a typed List component with a typed renderItem prop and keyExtractor. Generic component A component that works with data of any type without losing the type. A List component that can take User[] as well as Product[] — and can provide the correct type in the render function . Using any makes this work, but then autocomplete inside renderItem disappears.

createContext requires a default. Using undefined as default with a custom assertion hook avoids casting everywhere while keeping TypeScript happy. What is the best pattern for typing React Context with TypeScript? Why is createContext (undefined) + a custom hook better than createContext (staleDefault)? Context Passing data down without prop drilling. Default value Fallback provided to createContext . Typing Context is easy — but everyone gets stuck at one place: what default value should you give? There are two approaches, and the second one is much better.

forwardRef needs explicit type params. useImperativeHandle constrains what the parent can access via the ref handle. What is the exact type signature of React.forwardRef? Why do you need to annotate both the ref type and the props type explicitly? forwardRef Parent's ref reaching the child's inner DOM element. useImperativeHandle Exposing custom methods through the ref. Normally the ref is not received by the component — it is a reserved prop in React. With forwardRef you can pass it down. Additionally, useImperativeHandle lets you expose your methods instead of the DOM node.

Redux requires typing actions (discriminated unions), reducers, and selectors. Zustand uses infer and generic stores. Both benefit from typed middleware. How do you type a Redux reducer with discriminated union actions? What is the pattern for typing createSlice (RTK) to get typed actions and state? Store The entire app’s state in one place. Slice A portion of the store (Redux Toolkit). Selector A function that extracts a piece from the store. Both Redux Toolkit and Zustand are inference-first — you don’t write types, they are inferred . The shape of the state comes from the store, and it never becomes outdated.

Custom hooks often need generics for flexibility — useFetch , useLocalStorage , useDebounce . Generic hooks propagate types from input to output seamlessly. Design a typed useFetch hook that takes a URL, returns { data: T | null, loading: boolean, error: Error | null }. How does the generic flow from caller to return type? Custom hook A function that starts with use and uses hooks internally. as const Locking a tuple return — so that destructuring provides the correct type. Custom hook is a normal function. Typing it is also normal — except one thing : if you are returning a tuple (array), you need to use as const .

A component that renders as different HTML elements (as prop — ). Requires complex generic props merging with proper type narrowing. What is a polymorphic component in React + TypeScript? Implement Button with an as prop that correctly types the additional props based on the chosen element. Polymorphic component A component that can become any HTML element via the as prop. as prop <Text as="h1" /> — which tag will be rendered. A <Text> component that can become as="h1" or as="a" or as={Link} — and in each case it should accept the correct props for that element. This is the tricky part: when as="a" it should have href , but not when as="button" .

Union types with a shared literal discriminant. TypeScript narrows each branch in a switch. Assigning to never at the end enforces exhaustiveness. What is a discriminated union? Build an exhaustive check pattern using never that causes a compile error when a new union member is added. Discriminant The common literal field whose value identifies which member it is. Exhaustive check Ensuring via the compiler that no case is omitted. never A type that can never have a value. A union where each member has a common field with a distinct value — status , kind , type . When that field is checked, TypeScript infers the full shape of the remaining properties.

Add a phantom brand property to make structurally identical types incompatible — prevents accidentally passing a UserId where an OrderId is expected. What is a branded type? Implement UserId and OrderId that are both strings but not assignable to each other without an explicit cast. Branded / Nominal type A trick to make two things with the same shape distinct. Brand A fake field that exists only in types, not at runtime. TypeScript structural is — UserId and PostId are both string , so it treats them as the same. Passing the wrong id is not caught. Branding is a trick that lets you differentiate them — by adding a fake field that doesn’t exist at runtime.

Method chaining where TypeScript tracks which methods have been called via phantom type parameters — build() is only allowed after required setters. How do you use TypeScript generics to enforce that a Builder has had all required methods called before .build() is allowed? Builder Creating an object step by step. Type tracking Changing the type at each step so the compiler remembers what has been set. Normal builder works but there is a problem: .build() can still be called when required fields have not been set. Type tracking changes the return type of each .set() — and .build() is only available when all required items have been set.

Extend third-party type definitions without modifying node_modules — add a user property to Express Request, or custom methods to String.prototype. What is module augmentation? How do you add a user: User property to Express's Request interface so TypeScript knows it everywhere? Module augmentation Adding something to the types of another library. Declaration merging Two interfaces with the same name automatically combine. You can add your own fields to the types of a third-party library — without modifying the library. This is done via the merging behavior of interface — the same thing that is a bug in your own code, here it is a feature.

satisfies (TS 4.9) checks that an expression matches a type WITHOUT widening it — you keep literal types AND get shape validation simultaneously. What does the satisfies operator do that a type annotation or as cast cannot? Give a concrete example where it gives better autocomplete AND type safety. satisfies Perform a type check but do not lose the original (narrow) type. A new feature (TS 4.9) that fixes an old annoyance. Adding : Type performs a check but the type becomes wide . as Type doesn't perform a check at all. satisfies provides both — a check and the original narrow type.

n: Template Literal Types for API Safety
x: Combine template literals with mapped types to create type-safe event names, CSS-in-TS, path routers, and API method generators. Build a type-safe EventEmitter where event names must match "on${Capitalize }" and each event name has a specific typed handler signature. Template literal type Creating a new string type by concatenating string types. Path params Parts of a URL like :id . Template literal types' real use — making API routes and event names type-safe. The most impressive: extracting its parameters from a route string.

Use phantom types and method chaining to enforce compile-time constraints on builder calls. A build() method is only callable after required setters. Design a type-safe URL builder where setProtocol() and setHost() must be called before build() compiles. Use phantom type parameters to track state. Fluent API Method chaining — each method returns itself. Phantom type A type parameter that only tracks state and holds no value. The fluent form of the builder pattern — db.from("users").where(...).select(...) . And with type tracking the return type changes at each step, so autocomplete shows only the next valid step .

Generic Event Emitter where each event name has a typed payload. Uses mapped types + template literals to enforce event name → payload mapping. Design a typed EventEmitter where T is a map of event names to payloads. Implement on(event, handler) and emit(event, payload) with full type safety. Event map A type that specifies what payload each event has. In a normal event emitter the event name is a string and the payload is any — so typos and wrong payloads both silently slip through. An event map type catches both.

Functions that throw to narrow types. Used at runtime to assert invariants and let TypeScript narrow from the caller's perspective. Cleaner than if (!x) throw. Design assertDefined, assertInstanceOf, and assertShape functions with proper asserts return types. How do they compose with other type guards? Assertion function Throws a throw on error, and thereafter the type is assumed. Invariant A statement that must be definitely true at this point. Syntax (in the "Assertion Functions" lesson) after learning, the real question is: where to use it . There are three places where this is clearer than if and safer than ! .

n: Mixins — class composition patterns in TypeScript
x: Mixins compose class behavior from multiple sources. TypeScript pattern: create a type with constructor signature, write a function returning a class extending the base. Different from interfaces (can have state) and abstract classes (composable). How do you implement mixins in TypeScript? How do they differ from multiple inheritance? Mixin A piece of behavior that is mixed into many classes. Constructor type new (...args: any[]) => T — the type of a class. In TypeScript, a class can have only one parent . A mixin is a workaround: a function that takes a class and returns a new class by extending it. Then you can chain them.

Jest needs ts-jest or @swc/jest for transformation. Vitest has built-in TypeScript support via esbuild. Both require tsconfig matching for path aliases. What is the difference between configuring Jest with ts-jest vs @swc/jest? Why does Vitest not need a separate TypeScript compilation step? Transpile Convert TS to JS so the test runner can execute it ts-jest / SWC / esbuild tools that perform transpilation — SWC/esbuild are fast, ts-jest is slower but does type-checking Definition: Jest and Vitest are JavaScript test runners. To run TypeScript they first need to transpile TS → JS, either with ts-jest or with SWC/esbuild. Remember — the test runner does not type-check . It just removes types

TypeScript lacks built-in type tests. tsd and vitest's expectTypeOf provide assertion-based type testing. Catch type regressions during CI without running a compiler. What tools exist for testing TypeScript types? How does expectTypeOf work under the hood? Write tests for: Equal, NotEqual, and Extends type assertions. Type-level test a test that runs nothing at runtime — it only checks whether the type is correct or not Expect-error deliberately writing incorrect code and checking that TypeScript reports an error Definition: Type-level testing meaning writing tests for your types. A normal test checks that the value is correct; a type test checks that the type is correct. Tools: expectTypeOf

jest.mock and vi.mock create typed mocks. jest.Mocked and vi.Mocked wrap the original type with mock functions. Partial mocks require explicit type alignment. How does jest.Mocked work? What is the difference between jest.mock('module') auto-mocking and manual __mocks__ with type assertions? Mock a fake function that replaces the real function and that you control Fixture sample data object created for a test Partial mock making only a part of the whole object fake Definition: Mock = actual dependency (API call, DB, timer) replaced in a test with a fake version. In TypeScript the challenge is that the fake version's type must match the real one , otherwise type safety is lost. Two tools: vi.

Organizing tests alongside source (co-located), testing type exports, snapshot testing for complex types, and integration testing with tsx/ts-node. What are best practices for organizing TypeScript tests? Should you co-locate test files? How do you test that a library exports the correct public types? AAA Arrange-Act-Assert — the standard 3-step test framework Test double mock/stub/spy — any fake thing that replaces the real thing Definition: In TypeScript projects, the ways of writing tests that leverage types — typed factories, exhaustive case testing ( satisfies ), and type-safe it.each tables.

Incremental migration strategies: allowJs + checkJs, @ts-check in JSDoc, max tsconfig strictness gradually, module-by-module conversion using allowJs. The "biting the apple" vs "strangler fig" approaches. What is the recommended incremental migration strategy from JS to TypeScript? How does @ts-check + JSDoc annotations help in the intermediate phase? allowJs tsconfig flag that lets .js and .ts files coexist checkJs type-checks JS files as well — reads JSDoc comments Strangler pattern replace the old code gradually with new code, not in one go Definition: Moving a JS project to TS — file-by-file, not all at once. Apply allowJs: true , let both .js and .ts files coexist, and start with leaf f

Enabling all strict flags on an existing codebase requires systematic fixes: strictNullChecks is the hardest. Use noUncheckedIndexedAccess, exactOptionalPropertyTypes incrementally. How do you migrate a large codebase to strict mode? What is the correct order to enable the 8 strict flags? Which flag typically causes the most errors? strict a flag that turns on 8 separate safety flags together strictNullChecks treat null/undefined as a separate type — the biggest and most essential flag Ratchet error count can only decrease, not increase — enforce in CI Definition: Instead of turning on strict mode all at once, enable its sub-flags one by one. strict: true = 8 flags. Turn on each flag separat

Library authors must ship .d.ts files alongside JS. Dual CJS/ESM packages need package.json exports with types conditions. The "declaration strategy" affects consumer experience. How should a TypeScript library author set up their package.json exports to support both CJS and ESM consumers with correct types? .d.ts declaration file — only types, no code DefinitelyTyped community repo for @types/* packages Public API surface the types of the library that are visible to the user Definition: When building a library, how to ship types. Three ways: (1) Write in TS and generate .d.ts with declaration: true — best; (2) Write in JS and manually write .d.ts; (3) Publish on @types/your-lib on Definitel

ts-node, tsx, esbuild, swc, tsup, ts-morph, TypeScript ESLint, typescript-json-schema. Each tool has different TypeScript compatibility and use cases. Compare ts-node, tsx, esbuild, and swc for running TypeScript files. When would you use each? What are their TypeScript fidelity differences? Type-aware linting lint rules that read types to decide (slow but powerful) Bundler esbuild/swc/rollup — builds but does not type-check Definition: Tools around TS — typescript-eslint (linting), tsx / ts-node (to run directly), tsup / esbuild (build), zod (runtime validation), attw (published types check). Most important point: bundler does not type-check . A passing build does not mean type safety.

n: TC39 Decorators — stage 3 proposal, decorator factories
x: Decorators are functions that modify classes, methods, properties, or parameters. TC39 Stage 3 decorators (TS 5.0+) replace the legacy experimental decorators. A decorator receives (target, context) and returns a modified value. What is a TypeScript decorator? How do TC39 decorators differ from legacy experimental decorators? Decorator a function that, when placed with @ above a class/method, changes its behavior Decorator factory a function that returns a decorator — so you can pass arguments Stage 3 the TC39 proposal level where the syntax is finalized — native in TS 5.0+ Definition: A decorator is a function that, when you write @name above a declaration (class, method, field, getter), wr

Class decorators receive the class constructor and can modify, replace, or wrap it. Common uses: sealed classes, dependency injection, auto-registration, mixin support. How do you write a class decorator that prevents a class from being extended? Class decorator decorator that applies to the entire class ClassDecoratorContext the second argument in stage-3 — class name, kind, addInitializer Definition: A class decorator is a function that takes the class constructor and either (a) returns nothing — only a side effect (registering), or (b) returns a new class that replaces the original.

n: Method & Property Decorators — logging, memoization, validation
x: Method decorators intercept method calls for logging, timing, caching, or validation. Property decorators track property access. Common in frameworks like NestJS, TypeORM, and Angular. How do you create a method decorator that logs execution time? How do you create a property decorator that validates values? Method decorator wraps a method — signature stays the same, behavior is added Field decorator applies to a property; can change the initializer's value addInitializer function on the context — to run something when an instance is created Definition: Method decorator takes the original method and returns a new function that wraps it. Field/getter decorators work similarly but have a diffe

n: Decorator Composition — ordering, combining multiple decorators
x: Multiple decorators compose bottom-to-top (inner decorator runs first). Decorator factories return functions, enabling parameterization. NestJS uses this heavily for @Controller, @Injectable, @Get. How do decorators compose? What is the execution order when you apply multiple decorators to a single method? Composition applying multiple decorators to the same thing Bottom-up the lowest decorator is applied first Outermost the topmost — runs first at call time Definition: Applying multiple decorators to a method/class. There are two different orders and this is a favorite interview question: Apply order — bottom-up (bottom-up). The lowest one wraps first. Execution order — at call time top-dow

Using the right element for meaning: header, nav, main, article, section, aside, footer. Why does semantic HTML matter? What do you lose by building everything with divs? Semantic element A tag whose name itself describes its purpose — <nav> , <main> , <article> . Landmark A large section of the page that a screen reader user can jump to directly. div soup Putting everything inside <div> — browsers and assistive technologies cannot understand anything. Definition: Semantic HTML means selecting tags according to the content's meaning , not based on appearance. Use <nav> for navigation, <main> for primary content, and <article> for a standalone post. S

doctype, html lang, head vs body, meta charset, viewport, title, link/script placement. Walk me through the essential contents of a . Why does the viewport meta tag matter? doctype <!doctype html> — tells the browser to render in standards mode, not quirks mode. viewport meta Informs mobile browsers to display the page at device width, not a zoomed-out desktop layout. charset Specifies the text encoding — always utf-8 . Definition: The skeleton of every HTML page: doctype , <html lang> , <head> (metadata, not visible) and <body> (visible). <head> contains charset, viewport, title, stylesheet links, and description.

form, label association, input types (email, number, date, etc.), name/value, method/action. How do you correctly associate a label with an input, and why does it matter? label association <label for=id> or a label wrapping the input — clicking focuses the input and the screen reader reads the name. name attribute The field’s key in a form submission is this; without a name the value is never sent. input type email , number , date — appropriate keyboard on mobile and free validation. Definition: <form> collects user input and sends it to the server ( action + method ). Each field should have a name and a <label> . Choosing the correct type opens the appropriate keyboard on

required, pattern, min/max, type-based validation, :valid/:invalid, Constraint Validation API. How does native HTML form validation work? When would you override it with JS? Constraint validation Browser's built-in validation — required , pattern , min , max , type-based. setCustomValidity API to set a custom error message from JavaScript; an empty string clears the error. :user-invalid Pseudo-class that shows the invalid state only after the user interacts (not on page load). Definition: Validation can be done using only HTML attributes: required , minlength , pattern , min/max , type=email . The browser prevents submission and shows an error bubble. For JavaScript, you have form.checkValid

alt text, responsive images via srcset/sizes, art direction, lazy loading, video/audio. How do srcset and sizes work? How would you serve different images to mobile vs desktop? alt text Text substitute for the image — shown to screen readers and when the image fails. Use alt="" for decorative images. srcset / sizes Providing multiple image sizes to the browser so it can choose the appropriate one based on screen size and DPR. <picture> Art direction — to show different crops or formats (AVIF/WebP) on different screens. Definition: Always provide <img> , alt , and width/height with loading="lazy" . Use srcset + sizes for responsiveness; use <picture> for different crops/form

Semantic-first accessibility, ARIA roles/states/properties, when ARIA is needed vs harmful, focus management. What is the first rule of ARIA? When should you reach for aria-* attributes? ARIA Accessibility attributes (role, aria-*) that give assistive technology extra meaning. First rule of ARIA If a native element is available, do not use ARIA — <button> > div role=button . Focus management When a modal/menu opens, move focus inside; when it closes, return focus. Definition: The first path to accessibility is semantic HTML. ARIA is needed only when a native element cannot do the job — such as custom tabs, comboboxes, live updates ( aria-live ). ARIA only changes meaning; you still hav

Render-blocking scripts, async (load+run ASAP), defer (run after parse, in order), module scripts. What is the difference between async and defer? Which would you use for a third-party analytics script? Render-blocking The parser stops until the script is downloaded and executed, halting page rendering. defer Parallel download, execute in order after HTML parsing. async Parallel download, execute as soon as download finishes — no order guarantee. Definition: Normal <script> parsing stops. defer downloads in parallel and runs after the document is parsed, in order. async runs as soon as the download finishes, with no order guarantee. type="module" scripts behave like defer by default.

Custom data-* attributes, dataset API, when to use them vs classes or JS state. What are data-* attributes for? How do you read them in JavaScript? data-* attribute Custom attribute that starts with data- — for storing small extra data in HTML. dataset JS API: el.dataset.userId (the 'data-user-id' attribute in camelCase). Hook A stable way to capture an element for JavaScript or testing, separate from styling. Definition: data-* attributes store small custom data on an element that JavaScript reads via dataset and can be used with CSS attribute selectors ( [data-state="open"] ). Values are always strings.

t: CSS Core — Selectors, Cascade, Box Model
x: Type, class, id, attribute selectors; descendant, child (>), sibling (+, ~) combinators; :is()/:where(). Explain the different CSS combinators with examples. What does :where() add over :is()? Combinator The relationship between selectors: space (descendant), > (child), + (next sibling), ~ (later siblings). Attribute selector [type="email"] — selects based on an attribute. :is() / :where() They shorten selector lists; :where() has zero specificity. Definition: A selector indicates which elements the rule will apply to. Type ( p ), class ( .card ), id ( #nav ), attribute ( [href^="https"] ) and with combinators you can target precisely. :is() and :where() compress repeated selectors.

t: CSS Core — Selectors, Cascade, Box Model
x: How the browser resolves conflicting rules: specificity (id > class > type), source order, importance. How is CSS specificity calculated? How would you resolve two rules fighting over the same element? Specificity Selector weight — inline > id > class/attr/pseudo-class > type/pseudo-element. Cascade order Origin/importance → specificity → source order (the later one wins). !important Overrides the normal cascade; using it without a war is hard to justify. Definition: When two rules conflict on the same property, the browser first checks importance, then specificity (the count of IDs, classes, and types), and if there is a tie, the rule written later wins. Think of specificity as a triple of

t: CSS Core — Selectors, Cascade, Box Model
x: Which properties inherit (color, font) vs not (margin, border); inherit, initial, unset, revert keywords. Which CSS properties inherit by default and which do not? How do you force inheritance? Inherited property Goes from parent to child: color , font-* , line-height , visibility . Non-inherited Layout/box: margin , padding , border , background . unset / revert unset = if inherited then inherit, otherwise initial; revert = back to browser default. Definition: Some properties (related to text) are automatically received by child elements. Box-related properties are not received. Keywords: inherit (take the parent’s value), initial (spec default), unset , revert .

t: CSS Core — Selectors, Cascade, Box Model
x: Content, padding, border, margin; content-box vs border-box; why border-box is the sane default. Explain the CSS box model. What does box-sizing: border-box change and why do people set it globally? Box model Every element is a 4-layer box: content → padding → border → margin. content-box Default: width applies only to the content; padding and border are added on top. border-box width includes padding and border — predictable sizing. Definition: Every element is a rectangle: content, padding around it, then border, then margin (the outer space). box-sizing: border-box means width: 200px represents the whole box at 200px, including padding and border.

t: CSS Core — Selectors, Cascade, Box Model
x: How elements flow: block (full width), inline (no box dimensions), inline-block (box + inline flow). What is the difference between block, inline, and inline-block? Give a use case for each. block Takes the full width, starts on a new line; width/height/margin all work. inline Flows within text; width/height are ignored, vertical margins have no layout effect. inline-block Flows like inline but takes width/height like block. Definition: display decides how an element will flow. div , p are block; span , a are inline; inline-block is a mix of both; none removes the element (also from the layout). Today, for layout, most often flex and grid are used.

t: CSS Core — Selectors, Cascade, Box Model
x: Adjacent vertical margins collapse to the larger value; when it happens and how to prevent it. What is margin collapsing? Show a case where it surprises developers. Margin collapsing Adjacent vertical margins do not add — the larger one remains. BFC Block Formatting Context — margins inside it do not collapse with outside margins. Parent-child collapse The child's top margin escapes the parent if there is no padding or border in between. Definition: When the vertical margins of block elements touch, they do not add; instead the larger one applies ( 20px + 30px = 30px ). This happens only in the vertical direction in normal block flow. Margins of flex/grid items do not collapse.

n: Units — px, em, rem, %, vw/vh, ch
t: CSS Core — Selectors, Cascade, Box Model
x: Absolute vs relative units; em (relative to parent font-size) vs rem (root); viewport and content units. What is the difference between em and rem? When would you choose each? rem Relative to the root (html) font-size — predictable, best for accessibility. em Relative to the current element’s font-size (in padding/margin) or the parent’s (in font-size) — nesting causes compounding. vw / vh / ch 1% of the viewport width/height and the width of the '0' character. Definition: Absolute: px . Relative: % (parent), em , rem , viewport units ( vw , vh , dvh ) and content units ( ch , ex ). For font-size rem , for component-internal spacing em , for borders px is common.

t: CSS Core — Selectors, Cascade, Box Model
x: --var declarations, var() with fallbacks, scoping/cascade, runtime theming, contrast with Sass variables. How do CSS custom properties differ from Sass variables? Why are they powerful for theming? Custom property --brand: #0a84ff; — your variable, changeable at runtime. var() Read the value with var(--brand, fallback) , with a fallback. Scope The variable cascades/inherits — overriding it on an element affects its children. Definition: CSS custom properties --name are declared and used with var(--name) . They are normal cascading properties, so they can be changed at runtime via selectors, media queries, or JavaScript. Sass variables are replaced at compile time, so they cannot be used for

flex container vs items, main/cross axis, justify-content, align-items, align-content, flex-direction. Explain the flexbox axes. How do justify-content and align-items differ? Main axis The line of the flex direction (horizontal in a row). justify-content works on this. Cross axis Perpendicular to the main axis. align-items works on this. Flex container display:flex parent; its direct children become flex items. Definition: Flexbox is a layout system that aligns and spaces items in a single dimension (row or column). Apply display:flex to the container; flex-direction determines the main axis. justify-content = main axis, align-items = cross axis, gap = spacing between items, flex-wrap = wra

The flex shorthand; how items distribute free space; flex-basis vs width; flex:1 meaning. What does flex: 1 expand to and what does it actually do? flex-grow How much of the free space to take (ratio). flex-shrink How much to shrink when space is reduced. flex-basis Item's starting size before grow/shrink (higher priority than width). Definition: flex: grow shrink basis is a shorthand. flex: 1 = 1 1 0 — equal share. flex: none = no grow, no shrink. flex: 0 0 200px = fixed 200 px. First the flex-basis sets the starting size, then any remaining (or deficit) space is divided according to the grow/shrink ratios.

grid-template-columns/rows, fr unit, repeat(), gap, minmax(), auto-fit vs auto-fill. When would you choose Grid over Flexbox? Explain fr and minmax(). fr unit Fraction of free space — 1fr 2fr = 1:2 ratio. minmax() Minimum and maximum size of a track — minmax(200px, 1fr) . auto-fit / auto-fill With repeat() , create as many tracks as fit; auto-fit collapses empty tracks. Definition: CSS Grid is a 2D layout: rows and columns. Apply display:grid to the container and define tracks with grid-template-columns/rows ; items automatically occupy cells. gap is the spacing between tracks.

Named grid-template-areas, grid-column/row line placement, spanning, implicit vs explicit grid. How do grid-template-areas work? When are they clearer than line-based placement? grid-template-areas Naming layout regions like ASCII art—easy to read. Line placement grid-column: 1 / 3 — span an item using line numbers. Implicit grid Tracks that were not defined but are created because of content. Definition: grid-template-areas assigns names to layout regions, and items use grid-area: name . Alternatively, placement can use line numbers/ span : grid-column: 1 / span 2 . An explicit grid is the one defined in the template; extra items go into implicit tracks.

Normal flow vs positioned; containing block; offsets; sticky = relative until threshold then fixed. Explain each position value. What is the containing block for an absolutely positioned element? Containing block Reference for an absolute element — the nearest positioned ancestor (relative/absolute/fixed/sticky). sticky Behaves like relative until the scroll threshold is reached, then sticks like fixed. Offset top/right/bottom/left — works only on positioned elements. Definition: static (default, normal flow), relative (offset from its original position, space is still reserved), absolute (out of flow, positioned according to the nearest positioned ancestor), fixed (relative to the viewport)

What creates a stacking context (position+z-index, opacity, transform), why z-index:9999 can fail. Why can a z-index: 9999 element still appear behind another? Explain stacking contexts. Stacking context An isolated layer group — the z-index of its children matters only within it. z-index Layer order of positioned/flex/grid items; compared only within its own stacking context. Isolation isolation: isolate creates a new stacking context without side effects. Definition: A new stacking context is created when: the root element, position + z-index (not auto), opacity < 1 , transform , filter , isolation:isolate , and many other cases. Elements in different contexts are compared using the z-i

Flex/grid centering, margin auto, absolute + transform, when each applies. Give me three ways to center a box both horizontally and vertically. Trade-offs of each? Flex centering display:flex; justify-content:center; align-items:center . Grid centering display:grid; place-items:center — the smallest. margin auto Centers a block horizontally when its width is set. Definition: Centering depends on context: for text use text-align:center ; for a fixed-width block use margin-inline:auto ; for both axes use flex or grid; for overlays use position:absolute + inset:0; margin:auto .

Historical layout with floats, clearfix hack, why floats caused collapsing parents. What were floats originally for and why did they get abused for layout? float Move the element to the left/right side so that text wraps around it. clearfix A hack that stretches the parent to the height of its floated children. flow-root Modern, clean clearfix: display: flow-root . Definition: The original use of float was to wrap text around an image. In the 2000s it was hijacked for layout (columns), which required clear/clearfix hacks. Today, flex/grid are used for layout; float remains only for image-text wrapping.

@container queries size components by their container, not the viewport — true component responsiveness. How do container queries differ from media queries? Why are they a big deal for design systems? Container query @container (min-width: 400px) — the component changes style based on its container’s width. container-type Make the parent a 'container': container-type: inline-size . cqw / cqi Container query units — 1% of the container width. Definition: Media queries look at the viewport; container queries look at the component’s own parent. Apply container-type: inline-size on the parent and write @container in the child.

min-width/max-width breakpoints, feature queries, orientation, prefers-color-scheme / reduced-motion. How do media queries work? What does prefers-reduced-motion let you do? Breakpoint Viewport width at which the layout changes — let the content decide, not the device. Feature query @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) , (prefers-reduced-motion) , (hover: hover) . @supports Browser support check — not a media query, a feature query. Definition: @media is conditional CSS that applies rules based on viewport width (min-width/max-width), orientation, and user preferences (dark mode, reduced motion, contrast). Modern syntax: min-width .

Base styles for small screens, layer up with min-width; why it produces simpler, faster CSS. What does mobile-first mean in practice? Why is it preferred over desktop-first? Mobile-first Base CSS for the small screen, then layer on larger screens with min-width . Progressive enhancement Basic experience for everyone, better features for capable devices. Desktop-first Base for large screens, override for smaller with max-width — more overrides. Definition: First write the layout for the smallest screen (default CSS, without media queries), then add complexity with @media (min-width) as the space grows.

clamp(min, preferred, max) for fluid font sizes and spacing without breakpoints. How does clamp() work? Write a fluid font-size that scales between 16px and 24px. clamp(min, val, max) Keeps the value between min and max; val grows with the viewport. Fluid scale Font/spacing continuously scale, without jumps at breakpoints. Accessibility Using only vw for font size breaks zoom — mix with rem . Definition: The clamp(1rem, 0.8rem + 1vw, 1.5rem) scales the font smoothly with the viewport, but never smaller than 1rem or larger than 1.5rem.

Serving right-sized images per viewport/DPR, sizes attribute, for art direction, aspect-ratio. How do you avoid shipping a 2000px image to a phone? Explain srcset + sizes. srcset w-descriptor The actual width of each candidate: img-800.jpg 800w . sizes Tells the browser how wide the image will appear in the layout, so it selects the correct candidate. aspect-ratio Reserves space before the image loads with aspect-ratio: 16/9 (prevents CLS). Definition: srcset + sizes lets the browser choose the best image based on viewport and DPR; <picture> provides a different crop or format; CSS max-width:100%; height:auto and aspect-ratio keep the image fluid.

vw/vh/vmin/vmax, the mobile 100vh address-bar problem, dvh/svh/lvh dynamic units. Why does 100vh behave badly on mobile browsers, and how do dvh/svh fix it? vh / vw 1% of the viewport height/width. svh / lvh / dvh Small / large / dynamic viewport height — based on the mobile address bar. vmin / vmax 1% of the smaller or larger dimension. Definition: vw/vh are viewport-relative. On mobile the address bar hides and shows on scroll, so 100vh assumes a fixed (large) viewport and content can hide under the bar. Fix: dvh (dynamic, changes with the bar), svh (always safe, small), lvh (with the bar removed).

font shorthand, line-height, letter-spacing, font stacks/fallbacks, web-safe fonts, text-wrap: balance. What makes body text readable? Talk about line-height, measure, and font fallbacks. font stack Fallback list: font-family: Inter, system-ui, sans-serif . line-height Unitless value (1.5) is best — it scales with font-size. text-wrap: balance Balances heading lines evenly (reduces widows). Definition: Levers for readable typography: font-family stack, font-size , line-height (body text ~1.5), letter-spacing , max-width in ch (45–75 characters), and text-wrap ( balance for headings, pretty for paragraphs).

overflow visible/hidden/scroll/auto, single-line ellipsis, multi-line line-clamp. How do you truncate a single line of text with an ellipsis? What about multi-line? overflow visible (default), hidden , scroll , auto , clip . text-overflow: ellipsis Truncated text with '…'; requires nowrap + overflow:hidden . line-clamp Multi-line truncation: -webkit-line-clamp: 3 + display:-webkit-box . Definition: For a single-line ellipsis, use three properties together: white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis . For multi-line, use line-clamp .

State selectors, structural pseudo-classes, :focus-visible vs :focus, :not(), functional pseudo-classes. What is the difference between :focus and :focus-visible? Why does it matter for accessibility? :focus-visible Focus ring appears only on keyboard navigation — not on mouse click. :nth-child() Based on position: :nth-child(2n) , :first-child . :not() / :has() Exclude elements; :has() works like a parent selector. Definition: Pseudo-classes select an element's state or position: :hover , :focus-visible , :checked , :disabled , :nth-child() , :not() , :has() .

Generated content, the content property, decorative shapes, icons, and layout tricks. What is the difference between a pseudo-class and a pseudo-element? ::before / ::after Generated content inside the element; content property is required. ::placeholder / ::selection Styles input placeholders and selected text. content: "" Give an empty string to create a decorative shape box. Definition: ::before / ::after create a virtual child before/after an element's content. They require a content value (use "" for empty). Used for decorative icons, underline effects, clearfix, overlays.

background shorthand, multiple backgrounds, linear/radial/conic gradients, background-size/position. How do you layer multiple backgrounds? What is the difference between cover and contain? background-size cover (fills the area, may crop) vs contain (fits entirely). linear/radial/conic-gradient CSS-generated gradients instead of images. Multiple backgrounds Multiple layers separated by commas: background: url(a), linear-gradient(...) . Definition: The background shorthand includes color, image, position, size, repeat. Gradients are background-image . Multiple backgrounds stack from top to bottom (the first is on top).

border-radius, box-shadow (inset, spread), drop-shadow filter vs box-shadow, outline vs border. What is the difference between box-shadow and filter: drop-shadow? When does each matter? box-shadow x y blur spread color ; inset for inner shadow. filter: drop-shadow Shadow based on the element's actual shape (transparent PNG/SVG). outline vs border Outline does not take layout space and is for focus rings. Definition: border-radius rounds corners ( 50% = circle). box-shadow creates a shadow behind the element's box; multiple shadows are comma-separated. outline is like a border but does not affect layout.

transition-property/duration/timing-function/delay, which properties are animatable, easing curves. How does a CSS transition work? Which properties are cheap to animate and which are expensive? transition Smooth interpolation when a property’s value changes: transition: opacity .2s ease . timing-function Easing curve: ease , ease-out , cubic-bezier() , linear() . Animatable property A property whose value is continuous (color, transform, opacity). display normally is not.
