Definition: Transition property’s value automatically creates the intermediate frames when moving from one state to another. It occurs on a trigger state change (hover, class toggle). Syntax: property duration timing-funct

@keyframes, animation shorthand, iteration, direction, fill-mode, play-state. How do @keyframes differ from transitions? When would you reach for each? @keyframes Defines the animation steps: from / to or percentages. animation-fill-mode forwards = the end state is retained; backwards = the start state during delay. animation-iteration-count How many times: a number or infinite . Definition: @keyframes name { 0% {...} 100% {...} } creates a multi-step animation; we apply it to an element with animation: name 1s ease-in-out infinite alternate . It can run on its own without a trigger.

2D/3D transforms, transform-origin, why transforms do not trigger layout, will-change. Why is animating transform smoother than animating top/left? translate / scale / rotate 2D transforms; now there are individual properties as well: translate: 10px . transform-origin The point around which rotate/scale occurs (default center). will-change Hints to the browser that this property will change — the layer may be promoted. Definition: transform visually moves/scales/rotates/skews an element without changing layout (it stays in the same place relative to other elements). Order matters: translate() rotate() and rotate() translate() produce different results.

Animate only transform & opacity to stay on the compositor; avoid layout/paint thrash; will-change budget. Which two properties can you animate without triggering layout or paint, and why? Compositor-only transform and opacity animate on the GPU without the main thread. Layout / paint thrash Animating width , top , box-shadow forces layout/paint on every frame. will-change budget Only where needed; many layers consume memory. Definition: For smooth animation, animate only transform and opacity . These properties skip layout and paint and run on the compositor, whereas width/height/top/left trigger layout, and background/box-shadow trigger paint.

DOM + CSSOM → render tree → layout → paint → composite; render-blocking CSS/JS; how the browser paints. Walk me through how the browser turns HTML and CSS into pixels on screen. Render tree Combined DOM + CSSOM; only visible nodes. Render-blocking CSS (and sync JS) prevent the page's first paint. Layout → Paint → Composite Extract geometry, fill pixels, combine layers on the GPU. Definition: Browser creates DOM from HTML, CSSOM from CSS, combines both into render tree, then layout (positions/sizes), paint (pixels), composite (layers). CSS is render-blocking; synchronous JS is parser-blocking and also waits on CSSOM.

Layout (reflow) recalculates geometry; paint fills pixels; composite layers GPU-blend. Which props trigger which. What is the difference between reflow, repaint, and composite? Which is most expensive? Reflow (layout) Recalculates element geometry — expensive. Repaint Refills pixels (color/shadow changed, geometry unchanged). Composite Combines layers on the GPU — cheapest. Definition: When a property changes, the browser does work: layout ( width , margin , font-size , top ) → paint → composite. Paint-only : color , background , box-shadow . Composite-only : transform , opacity . If layout changes, paint and composite also occur.

Forced synchronous layout from read-after-write in JS; batching reads then writes; requestAnimationFrame. What is layout thrashing? How do you avoid forced synchronous layout in a loop? Forced synchronous layout Reading a layout property immediately after changing style forces the browser to perform layout immediately. Batching Do all reads first, then all writes. requestAnimationFrame Schedule visual updates before the next frame. Definition: Layout thrashing occurs when a loop alternates reads ( offsetHeight ) and writes ( style.height = ... ) — each read forces the browser to recompute layout.

Largest Contentful Paint, Cumulative Layout Shift, Interaction to Next Paint; targets and common fixes. What are the Core Web Vitals and what causes a poor score in each? LCP Largest Contentful Paint — when the largest content is shown (target ≤ 2.5 s). CLS Cumulative Layout Shift — how much the layout moves (target ≤ 0.1). INP Interaction to Next Paint — how quickly the screen updates after a click/tap (target ≤ 200 ms). Definition: Core Web Vitals are three real-user experience metrics: LCP (loading), CLS (visual stability), INP (responsiveness; replaces FID). Fixes: preload/optimize LCP images, provide width/height and font fallback for CLS, break up long tasks for INP.

font-display swap/optional, preloading fonts, fallback metrics, layout shift from font swaps. What is the difference between FOUT and FOIT? How does font-display control it? FOUT Flash of Unstyled Text — fallback font appears, then swaps. FOIT Flash of Invisible Text — text is hidden until the font arrives. font-display swap , optional , fallback — controls loading behavior. Definition: Until the web font finishes loading, the browser either hides the text (FOIT) or displays it with a fallback font (FOUT). font-display: swap shows the fallback immediately and swaps when the font arrives; optional uses the font only if it is already in cache (no shift).

contain property, content-visibility: auto to skip offscreen rendering, performance isolation. What does content-visibility: auto do for a long page? contain Tell the browser that changes in the subtree do not affect the outside: layout , paint , size , style . content-visibility: auto Skip rendering of off-screen content, render on scroll. contain-intrinsic-size Placeholder size for skipped content (to prevent scrollbar jump). Definition: The contain property gives the browser a hint that changes inside the element will not affect outside layout/paint, allowing it to isolate the work. content-visibility: auto skips layout/paint for off-screen sections.

BEM block__element--modifier, why naming conventions fight specificity and scale in large codebases. What problem does BEM solve? How does it keep specificity flat? Block Independent component: .card . Element Part of the block: .card__title (double underscore). Modifier Variant/state: .card--featured (double hyphen). Definition: BEM (Block__Element--Modifier) is a naming convention: .block__element--modifier . The class name itself indicates which component it belongs to.

Locally scoped class names, hashing, composition; solving the global namespace problem. How do CSS Modules prevent class-name collisions? What does the build step do? Local scope Class names are local to the file; the build tool generates a unique hash. composes Reuse another class’s styles within a class. Global escape :global(.x) when a global class is needed. Definition: When a *.module.css file is imported, each class name becomes a unique generated name ( card_3xK9a ), so collisions are impossible. You use them via styles.card .

Runtime vs zero-runtime CSS-in-JS, dynamic styling from props, SSR concerns, performance trade-offs. What are the pros and cons of CSS-in-JS? What is the runtime cost? Runtime CSS-in-JS styled-components/emotion: styles in JS, CSS is injected at runtime. Zero-runtime Linaria/vanilla-extract/Panda: static CSS generated at build time. Props-based style Dynamic styles derived from component props. Definition: CSS-in-JS writes styles in JavaScript together with the component (using template literals or objects). Runtime libraries inject CSS during rendering; zero-runtime tools extract static CSS at build time.

Utility classes, design tokens via config, purge/JIT, when utility-first helps or hurts maintainability. What is the case for and against Tailwind / utility-first CSS? Utility class A single-purpose class: p-4 , flex , text-center . Design tokens Defined in spacing/color config; utilities are generated from them. JIT / purge CSS is generated only for the classes that are used. Definition: In utility-first (Tailwind), you style HTML by applying small single-purpose classes instead of writing custom CSS. Configuration (theme tokens) provides consistent spacing and colors.

Token layers, CSS variables for theming, prefers-color-scheme, per-component theming without JS. How would you architect a themeable design system that supports light/dark and brand themes? Design token A named design decision: --color-bg , --space-4 . Semantic token Purpose-based name ( --color-surface ) versus raw value ( --gray-900 ). prefers-color-scheme User's OS-level dark/light preference. Definition: Keep tokens in two layers: primitive ( --blue-600 ) and semantic ( --color-primary: var(--blue-600) ). Changing a theme means remapping semantic tokens; components use only semantic tokens.

Sass nesting/mixins/functions, native CSS nesting, cascade layers (@layer) for predictable ordering. What do preprocessors still offer now that CSS has variables and nesting? Sass Variables, nesting, mixins, functions — compiled into CSS. Native CSS nesting .card { &:hover {...} } — now built-in to browsers. @layer Cascade layers: the order of layers declared first takes precedence over specificity. Definition: Preprocessors like Sass gave CSS features that were not native (variables, nesting, mixins). Today CSS variables, nesting, @layer , color-mix() are native, so the need for a preprocessor is reduced. Using @layer reset, base, components, utilities; determines ordering by layer order in

Props interface, naming conventions, required vs optional, TypeScript generics for component APIs API surface all the props of a component that external users use Escape hatch a prop that lets the user step outside the default behavior (className, render) Prop explosion adding a new prop for every new requirement — a component with 20 props Definition: Component API design means defining the component’s public contract : which props, what names, which are required, which have defaults, and what not to provide. In the design round the interviewer asks first — "What will its API be?" Your answer should not be a list of props, but a thoug

When each fits, forwardRef, useImperativeHandle, ref forwarding patterns Controlled value comes from the parent’s state Uncontrolled the component maintains its own value Hybrid supports both — if a value is provided it’s controlled, otherwise internal Definition: In a design interview, just mentioning "controlled vs uncontrolled" is not enough — support both. The production component standard is: if the value prop is provided, it is controlled; if not, the component keeps its own state (starting from defaultValue ). This pattern exists in every g

Implicit state sharing via Context, flexible composition, dot notation API (Tabs.Panel etc.) Compound multiple components that together form a widget Implicit state parent state that children automatically receive via Context Slot the place where the user can insert their content Definition: It holds a parent state and provides it to its children via Context. The user writes it like HTML — <Tabs><Tabs.List><Tabs.Tab/></Tabs.List><Tabs.Panel/></Tabs> . In a design round this is the answer to flexibility — when the interviewer asks "what if

children pattern, render props, slot pattern — avoiding prop explosion Composition building a larger component by combining small pieces Configuration describing everything about a component via props Slot pattern named prop that receives JSX — header, footer, actions Definition: There are two ways to provide flexibility: Configuration — <Card title icon actions showBorder /> . Simple, but each new case needs a new prop. Composition — <Card><Card.Header/><Card.Body/></Card> . More code to write, but unlimited flexibility. The middle

Keep state as close to usage as possible — lifting vs drilling vs context vs global store Colocation keeping state next to where it is used Lifting state up moving state up to the common parent Prop drilling passing props down 4-5 levels Definition: Keep the state only as high as necessary — no more than one level. Default is at the bottom; lift it up only when both siblings need it. In the design round this is the first answer for performance — before memo.

ARIA roles/states/properties, keyboard navigation, focus management, screen reader testing ARIA Accessible Rich Internet Applications — extra information for screen readers Roving tabindex only one element in a group is tab-focusable, the rest are reachable via arrow keys Focus trap keep focus confined inside a modal Definition: Accessibility is not added later — it is built into the component's design. Four things are required in every widget: Semantic HTML — <button> , <nav> , <dialog> (not onClick on a div) Keyboard — Tab, Enter/Space, Arrow, Escape, Home/End ARIA — role, state ( aria-expand

To prevent deadlock, which one would you eliminate? Mutual exclusion Resource has a single holder. Hold & wait Holding one resource while requesting another. No preemption Resources cannot be forcibly taken. Circular wait A→B→A cycle. Definition: A deadlock occurs when all four Coffman conditions hold simultaneously. Breaking any one prevents a deadlock. Classic example: Thread 1 holds lock A and requests B; Thread 2 holds B and requests A.

Prevention: eliminate one Coffman condition. Avoidance: Banker's algorithm. Detection: find cycles in RAG. Compare deadlock prevention, avoidance (Banker's algorithm), and detection. What does each cost? Prevention Break one Coffman condition. Avoidance Banker's algorithm — allocate only in a safe state. Detection Find a cycle in the wait-for graph, then recover. Definition: Prevention: lock ordering (circular wait), acquire all locks at once (hold & wait), tryLock+timeout (no preemption). Avoidance decides by looking at the system state. Detection+recovery: if a cycle is found, abort a victim.

Livelock: threads keep responding to each other but make no progress. Starvation: a thread never gets CPU time. What is the difference between deadlock, livelock, and starvation? Give a real-world analogy for each. Livelock Threads are active but progress is zero. Starvation A thread never gets the resource. Backoff Breaking symmetry with a random wait. Definition: In a deadlock, threads are blocked; in a livelock they keep running but make no progress. In starvation, a thread is always left behind because of the scheduler/lock policy.

Acquire locks in a consistent global order across all threads — the most practical deadlock prevention technique. How does consistent lock ordering prevent deadlock? What is tryLock with timeout? Global order A fixed rank for all locks. Ordered acquire Always acquire from lower rank to higher. Identity hash Use id/address for ordering. Definition: If every thread acquires locks in the same order (e.g., ascending account ID), circular wait is impossible, so no deadlock.

Pre-created pool of threads that pick up tasks from a queue. Avoids thread creation overhead, controls resource usage. Why use a thread pool instead of creating a new thread per task? How do you size a thread pool? Worker threads Pre-created, reused. Task queue Buffer of pending tasks. Rejection policy What to do when the queue is full. Definition: Thread pool keeps a fixed/bounded set of threads that take tasks from a queue. It saves thread-creation cost and provides a concurrency limit. Sizing: CPU-bound ≈ cores; I/O-bound ≈ cores × (1 + wait/compute).

Hardware-supported instruction: atomically compare memory location to expected value and swap if equal. No lock needed. How does CAS work? Implement an atomic counter using CAS. What is the ABA problem? CAS compareAndSwap(addr, expected, new) atomically. Retry loop If CAS fails, read again and retry. ABA problem Value changed from A to B and back to A, which CAS cannot detect. Definition: CAS is a CPU instruction: if the value in memory equals the expected value, write the new value; otherwise fail. Lock-free counters and stacks are built on it.

Lock-free: system-wide progress guaranteed (at least one thread progresses). Wait-free: every thread progresses. What is a lock-free data structure? Why is it hard to implement? When would you use one? Lock-free At least one thread always makes progress. Wait-free Each thread finishes in a bounded number of steps. Obstruction-free Finishes if it runs in isolation. Definition: Lock-free algorithms use CAS instead of mutexes, so a stalled or suspended thread does not block the others. Wait-free provides the strongest guarantee but is very hard to implement.

A Future represents a value not yet computed. Promise resolves it later. Async/await is syntactic sugar over Futures. What is the difference between a Future and a Promise? How does CompletableFuture in Java work? Future Placeholder for a value that has not yet arrived. Promise Writable side that sets the value. async/await Sequential-looking syntax built on Futures. Definition: A Future is a pending result that is resolved or rejected later. async/await creates a compiler/runtime state machine that releases the thread at await (does not block).

Concurrency without shared state — actors communicate via message passing only. Used in Erlang, Akka, Go channels. Explain the Actor model. How does it avoid race conditions without locks? Actor Private state + mailbox; one message at a time. Message passing No shared memory, only messages. Supervision The parent actor restarts the child on failure (Erlang). Definition: In the Actor model each actor exclusively owns its state; other actors can only send messages. Messages in a mailbox are processed one at a time, so locks are not needed. Go’s mantra: “share memory by communicating”.

n: Memory Ordering — sequential consistency, acquire-release, relaxed
x: Memory ordering defines the order in which memory operations become visible to other threads. Sequential consistency: all threads see the same order. Acquire-release: release on write, acquire on read (synchronizes). Relaxed: no ordering guarantees (fastest). x86 is mostly TSO (Total Store Order). ARM/POWER are weakly ordered. What is the difference between sequential consistency and relaxed memory ordering? Sequential consistency All threads see the same global order. Acquire/release Writes before a release become visible to the acquiring thread. Relaxed Only atomicity, no ordering. Definition: CPU/compiler instructions reorder. The memory model determines which orderings are guaranteed. SC

n: volatile keyword — Java, C++, JavaScript differences
x: Java volatile: visibility guarantee (no caching) + happens-before ordering. C++ volatile: prevents compiler optimization (NOT thread-safe, use std::atomic). JavaScript: no volatile (single-threaded). Common misconception: volatile does NOT provide atomicity in Java. What does volatile guarantee in Java? Why is it NOT sufficient for thread safety? Java volatile Visibility + happens-before; not atomic. C++ volatile Prevents compiler optimizations; not thread-safe. JS No volatile; use Atomics. Definition: In Java, a volatile variable's write is seen immediately by all threads and prevents reordering. But volatile int x; x++ is not atomic. In C++, volatile is not for threading (use std::atomic).

n: Thread Interruption — cooperative cancellation, InterruptedException, flags
x: Thread interruption is cooperative: interrupt sets a flag, the thread must check and respond. Java: Thread.interrupt() + InterruptedException. Python: threading.Event. Go: context.Context with cancel. Never ignore InterruptedException — either rethrow or restore interrupt flag. How does cooperative thread cancellation work? Why is it preferred over forceful termination? Cooperative The thread must check itself to stop. InterruptedException A blocking call throws this when interrupted. Cancellation token The equivalent in JS/C#/Go (context). Definition: Forcefully killing a thread is unsafe (locks leak). Therefore interrupt only sets a flag; the thread checks isInterrupted() on blocking calls

n: Green Threads vs OS Threads — fibers, coroutines, M:N scheduling
x: Green threads (goroutines, Kotlin coroutines, Python asyncio tasks) are multiplexed onto OS threads by a runtime. M:N model: M green threads on N OS threads. Lightweight (~2KB stack for goroutines vs ~1MB for OS threads). Scheduled by runtime, not OS. Blocked green thread yields OS thread. What is the difference between green threads and OS threads? How does M:N scheduling work? Goroutine Go's lightweight thread (~2KB stack). M:N scheduling M green threads on N OS threads. Virtual threads Java 21 lightweight threads. Definition: Green threads run on the runtime scheduler, not the OS. On blocking I/O the runtime parks the green thread and gives the OS thread to another green thread. Hence hun

JS is single-threaded but non-blocking via event loop: call stack + task queue + microtask queue + libuv. Explain the JS event loop in detail. What is the difference between microtasks and macrotasks? Call stack Currently executing synchronous code. Microtask queue Promise.then, queueMicrotask — runs first. Macrotask setTimeout, I/O callbacks. Definition: Loop: when the stack is empty → all microtasks are drained → one macrotask → repeat. Node has libuv phases (timers, poll, check) and process.nextTick runs before microtasks.

Node.js Worker Threads enable true parallelism for CPU-bound work. Each worker has its own V8 and event loop. When would you use Worker Threads in Node.js? How do you communicate between them? Worker Separate V8 isolate + event loop. postMessage Data is copied via structured clone. SharedArrayBuffer Zero-copy shared memory + Atomics. Definition: worker_threads remove CPU-heavy work from the main loop. Workers do not share memory (by default) — messages are copied; you can share memory with SharedArrayBuffer.

Promises implement the microtask queue. Unhandled promise rejections can crash Node.js in newer versions. How do Promises work internally? What is Promise chaining vs async/await? What are the error propagation rules? States pending → fulfilled / rejected (settled, immutable). then chain Each then returns a new promise. unhandledRejection Node 15+ default: process crash. Definition: Promise callbacks run in the microtask queue. The return value of then resolves the next promise; throwing converts it to a rejection.

Node Cluster forks multiple worker processes (one per CPU core) sharing the same port — achieves parallelism. How does Node.js Cluster module work? How does the master process distribute connections to workers? Primary/worker Master forks, workers share the port. Round-robin Default distribution on Linux. PM2 Cluster manager. Definition: The cluster module runs a Node process on each CPU core, all sharing the same port. Memory is not shared, so in-memory sessions/caches are not consistent across workers.

Producers add items to a bounded buffer; consumers remove items. Synchronize to avoid overflow and underflow. Implement the Producer-Consumer problem using semaphores. Then solve it with a BlockingQueue. Bounded buffer Fixed-size queue — provides backpressure. empty/full Consumer waits when empty, producer waits when full. BlockingQueue Built-in thread-safe implementation. Definition: Producers add items to the queue, consumers remove them. A bounded buffer slows producers when consumers fall behind (backpressure).

Multiple readers can read simultaneously. Writers need exclusive access. Variants: reader-first vs writer-first. Solve the Readers-Writers problem. Which variant prevents starvation and how? Reader-preference Readers have priority — writer may starve. Writer-preference When the writer is waiting, new readers are blocked. Fair Arrival order. Definition: Multiple readers can access shared data simultaneously, writer has exclusive access. Variants determine fairness. Solution: ReadWriteLock or semaphores + reader count.

N philosophers alternate eating/thinking, sharing N forks. Demonstrates deadlock and starvation challenges. Explain the Dining Philosophers problem. Give two different solutions to avoid deadlock. Forks Shared resources (N). Circular wait All picked up the left fork → deadlock. Resource hierarchy Number the forks and acquire the lower-numbered one first. Definition: Each of the N philosophers needs two forks to eat. If everyone picks up the left fork simultaneously, deadlock occurs. Fixes: fork ordering, a semaphore allowing at most N-1 philosophers at the table, or alternating odd/even ordering.

Creating a singleton in a multi-threaded environment — naive lazy initialization is not thread-safe. What is wrong with double-checked locking for Singleton? How do you implement it correctly? Double-checked locking First check without lock, then check inside lock. Holder idiom Static inner class lazy + thread-safe. Enum singleton The simplest safe approach in Java. Definition: Naive if (inst==null) inst=new X() can create two instances in different threads. Safe options: eager static initialization, holder class, enum, or volatile with double-checked locking.

Token bucket or leaky bucket algorithm implemented with atomic operations or locks for concurrent requests. Design a thread-safe rate limiter that allows 100 req/sec. Implement it in code. Token bucket Tokens refill, allowing bursts. Leaky bucket Output at a fixed rate. Sliding window Count within a time window. Definition: Token bucket: capacity C, refill rate r. Each request takes a token. To make it thread-safe, update (tokens, lastRefill) in a single unit using a lock or CAS.

LRU cache with concurrent reads/writes — naive locking kills throughput. Segmented locking is the solution. Implement a thread-safe LRU cache. How do you handle concurrent reads without a write lock? LRU HashMap + doubly linked list. Lock striping Separate locks per segment. Read-through Load and store on a miss. Definition: A global lock kills throughput. Options: segmented/striped locks, or a library like Caffeine; get also reorders the list, so a read lock is not enough.

Race conditions and deadlocks are non-deterministic — hardest bugs to reproduce and fix. How do you debug a deadlock in production? What tools and techniques do you use? Thread dump Stack snapshot of all threads. Race detector Go -race, ThreadSanitizer. Stress test Many threads, repeated runs. Definition: Approach: logs with thread-id + timestamp, thread dump (jstack) to find deadlock cycles, TSan/ go test -race , stress with randomized delays, and a minimal reproducible case.

Thread-per-request vs thread pool vs async event-driven. Each has different performance characteristics. Compare multi-threaded vs event-driven concurrency models for a web server. When does each excel? Thread-per-request Simple, blocking, memory heavy. Thread pool Bounded threads + queue. Event-driven Few threads, non-blocking (nginx, Node). Definition: Thread-per-request (Apache prefork) is simple but fails at 10k connections (C10K). A pool is resource-bound. Event loop is best for I/O-bound work but blocks CPU-intensive tasks. Hybrid: event loop + worker pool.

n: Python GIL — what it is, why it exists, when it matters
x: The Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) is a mutex in CPython that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. It exists because CPython's reference counting is not thread-safe. It affects CPU-bound code but not I/O-bound code. Removed in Python 3.13+ (free-threaded mode, opt-in). What is the Python GIL? Why does it exist and when does it matter? GIL In CPython, one thread executes bytecode at a time. CPU-bound Threads provide no benefit. I/O-bound The GIL is released during I/O, so threads can work. Definition: GIL keeps CPython's reference counting safe. CPU-bound threads do not run in parallel; I/O (sockets, files) or C extensions (NumPy) release the GIL. In Python 3.13+ the fr

n: Threading in Python — threading module, daemon threads, Thread(target=)
x: Python's threading module creates OS threads. Due to the GIL, threads don't help CPU-bound tasks but do help I/O-bound tasks (network, file I/O). Daemon threads die when the main thread exits. join() waits for thread completion. When would you use Python threading? Why doesn't it help with CPU-bound work? threading.Thread OS thread wrapper. daemon Stops when the main program exits, without waiting. Lock / Event Sync primitives. Definition: threading is for I/O-bound concurrency. Thread(target=fn, args=...) , start() , join() . Daemon threads do not prevent program exit.

n: asyncio — event loop, coroutines, await, asyncio.gather()
x: asyncio provides single-threaded concurrency via an event loop. async/await defines coroutines. asyncio.gather() runs multiple coroutines concurrently. asyncio creates tasks that interleave during I/O waits. No GIL contention because single-threaded. How does asyncio work? What is the difference between asyncio.gather() and asyncio.create_task()? Coroutine async def function. await Returns control to the event loop. gather Run multiple coroutines together. Definition: asyncio performs cooperative multitasking on a single thread. When a task reaches await , it suspends and the loop runs another task. A blocking call (time.sleep, requests) stops the entire loop.

n: multiprocessing — bypassing the GIL, shared memory, Process(target=)
x: multiprocessing spawns separate processes, each with its own Python interpreter and GIL. Bypasses the GIL for CPU-bound work. Communicate via Queue, Pipe, or shared memory (Value, Array, Manager). Overhead of process creation and IPC. How does multiprocessing bypass the GIL? What are the tradeoffs vs threading? Process Separate interpreter + GIL. Pool Pool of worker processes. Pickling Arguments/results are serialized. Definition: multiprocessing runs separate processes, so CPU-bound work is truly parallel. Data is transferred via pickling (overhead); shared_memory enables zero-copy sharing.

n: Encapsulation — bundling data + methods, access modifiers
x: Encapsulation binds data and methods that operate on that data together, restricting direct access to internal state. Access modifiers (private, protected, public) enforce boundaries. Why does encapsulation protect object invariants and reduce coupling? How do access modifiers enforce boundaries? State Object's own internal data or variables Behavior Object's methods or functions that work with that state Access Modifiers keywords like private, public, protected that decide who can view/change the data Encapsulation simply means data (variables) and behavior (methods) encapsulated in a single container (class), and preventing that container from being directly modified from outside. It works

n: Inheritance — IS-A relationships, super/sub classes, method overriding
x: Inheritance creates an IS-A hierarchy where a subclass inherits fields and methods from a parent class. Method overriding allows subclasses to provide specialized behavior. Why does inheritance create tight coupling and when should you prefer composition over inheritance? Superclass (Parent) The class whose features are being inherited Subclass (Child) The new class that takes the parent's features IS-A Relationship This relationship indicates that the child is actually a type of the parent (e.g., Car IS-A Vehicle) Inheritance means creating a new class that automatically takes the properties (state) and methods (behavior) of an existing class. It establishes an "IS-A" relationship.

Polymorphism means "many forms". Compile-time polymorphism (method overloading) vs runtime polymorphism (method overriding, virtual dispatch). How does polymorphism enable treating objects of different types uniformly through a common interface? Poly Many Morph Forms Method Overloading Multiple methods with the same name in a single class but different parameters (compile-time) Method Overriding Child class replaces its parent's method (run-time) Polymorphism simply means "many forms". A single function or method can behave differently for different objects.

n: Abstraction — abstract classes vs interfaces, hiding complexity
x: Abstraction hides implementation details and exposes only essential features. Achieved via abstract classes (partial impl + abstract methods) and interfaces (pure contracts). How does abstraction reduce complexity for the caller and isolate change? What is the difference between abstract classes and interfaces? Abstract Class A partially implemented class that cannot be instantiated Interface A contract (set of rules) with no implementation Abstraction means showing the necessary details and hiding the rest of the complexity (background mess).

n: Association, Aggregation, Composition — has-a vs owns-a differences
x: Association (uses-a), Aggregation (has-a, independent lifecycle), Composition (owns-a, dependent lifecycle). These define relationships with different ownership semantics. What is the difference between association, aggregation, and composition? How does ownership affect lifecycle management? These three HAS-A relationships are different levels (strength).

n: SRP — Single Responsibility: one class, one reason to change
x: A class should have one, and only one, reason to change. Every class should be responsible for a single part of the system functionality. Why do SRP classes lead to more cohesive, focused, and testable code? What is the God Object anti-pattern? Responsibility Reason why the class changes (Reason to change) God Object The stubborn class that does a large portion of the system's work alone Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) states that a class should have only one reason to change. In other words, a class should handle only a single part of the system.

n: OCP — Open/Closed: open for extension, closed for modification
x: Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. Add new behavior through new code, not by changing existing code. How does the Strategy pattern exemplify the Open/Closed Principle? Why prevents modifying tested code? Open for Extension New features can be added easily Closed for Modification Existing tested code does not need to be touched Open/Closed Principle (OCP) states that code should be designed so that adding new functionality is easy (Open), but the existing code does not need to be changed (Closed).

n: LSP — Liskov Substitution: subtypes must replace base types
x: Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of a subclass without affecting correctness. Subtypes must satisfy the base type contract. Why is the Square-Rectangle problem the classic example of violating LSP? How do preconditions and postconditions relate? Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) states that if Class B inherits from Class A, then wherever Class A is used in a program, substituting Class B should not cause the program to fail.

n: ISP — Interface Segregation: small focused interfaces
x: Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. Large interfaces should be split into smaller, more specific ones. How does Interface Segregation reduce coupling and prevent dummy method implementations? Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) says that clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. It is better to create many small specific interfaces rather than one large (fat) interface.

n: DIP — Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions, not concretions
x: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions. Abstractions should not depend on details. How does Dependency Injection implement the Dependency Inversion Principle? What problem does it solve? High-level modules Your main business logic (e.g. OrderProcessing) Low-level modules Small utilities or tools (e.g. MySQLDatabase, SmtpEmail) Abstraction Interface or base class Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) says that high-level classes should not directly depend on low-level classes. Both should depend on abstractions (interfaces).

n: Composition over Inheritance — prefer has-a over is-a when possible
x: Favor has-a relationships over is-a relationships. Achieve reuse by composing objects, not by inheriting from a base class. Why does composition provide more flexibility than inheritance at runtime? How does the Decorator pattern demonstrate this? Inheritance (IS-A) Creating a new class by extending an existing class Composition (HAS-A) Combining small parts (objects) to build a larger object Composition over Inheritance is a rule of thumb that says reusing code by linking (composing) objects together is better than inheriting from a base class.

n: Law of Demeter (Principle of Least Knowledge) — talk only to immediate friends
x: A method should only call methods on: itself, its parameters, objects it creates, its own fields. Dont talk to strangers (method chaining like a.getB().getC().do()). Why does the Law of Demeter reduce coupling? What is the trade-off of following it too strictly? Law of Demeter (Principle of Least Knowledge) says that an object should know as little as possible about the surrounding world (the internals of other objects).

n: DRY, KISS, YAGNI — dont repeat, keep simple, avoid over-engineering
x: DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself), KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid), YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It). Three principles guiding pragmatic software design. How can over-applying DRY lead to premature abstraction? When does YAGNI apply to design patterns? Three basic rules that every developer should know: DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself): Don't copy-paste code. If the same logic appears in two places, put it into a single function. KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid): Don't over-engineer the code. Write simple code that you can read tomorrow. YAGNI (You Aren't

n: Coupling & Cohesion — low coupling, high cohesion
x: Coupling measures how dependent one module is on another. Cohesion measures how focused the responsibilities within a module are. Aim for low coupling, high cohesion. Why is low coupling and high cohesion the sweet spot for software maintainability and testability? Coupling: How much classes depend on each other. (Aim: Low Coupling – classes should be independent). Cohesion: How closely a class's methods and variables relate to each other. (Aim: High Cohesion – the class should have a single focus, like SRP).

n: Tell-Dont-Ask — command objects what to do, dont query state
x: Tell objects what to do rather than asking about their state and then deciding. Encapsulate behavior with data. How does Tell-Dont-Ask preserve encapsulation and eliminate anemic domain models? Give a code example. Tell-Don't-Ask principle states that instead of asking an object for data and making decisions yourself, you tell the object to perform its own work.

n: Singleton — ensure one instance, global access point. Thread-safety considerations.
x: Singleton ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access. Thread-safety through eager initialization, synchronized getInstance, or Bill Pugh inner class. How do you implement a thread-safe Singleton in Java? Why is enum Singleton considered the most robust approach? Instance An object of the class Global Access Point A way to access that object from anywhere Singleton Pattern ensures that a class has only one instance (object) throughout the entire application, and provides a global way to access it.

n: Factory Method — define interface for creating objects, subclasses decide instantiation
x: Factory Method defines an interface for creating an object, but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate. The Creator class defers instantiation to subclasses. How does Factory Method decouple clients from concrete types and enable the Open/Closed Principle? Creator The class that contains the factory method Product The object that the factory method creates Factory Method is a creational pattern that moves the logic for creating an object into a separate method. Subclasses can override that method to decide which type of object to create.

n: Abstract Factory — create families of related objects without concrete classes
x: Abstract Factory provides an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes. A "factory of factories". When would you use Abstract Factory over Factory Method? How does it ensure product compatibility? Abstract Factory is a level up from regular factories. It is a factory of factories. It lets you create an entire "Family" of related objects (theme) without specifying their concrete classes.

n: Builder — separate construction of complex objects from representation
x: Builder separates the construction of a complex object from its representation. The same construction process can create different representations via a director + builder interface. How does Builder solve the telescoping constructor problem? What makes it different from Factory? Builder Pattern helps construct complex objects step-by-step. Instead of passing 10 parameters to a constructor (telescoping constructor anti-pattern), we use a Builder object.

n: Prototype — clone existing objects instead of creating new from scratch
x: Prototype creates new objects by cloning/copying an existing instance (the prototype). Avoids costly creation from scratch, especially when object initialization is expensive. What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy in the Prototype pattern? When is it useful?

n: Object Pool — reuse objects that are expensive to create (connections, threads)
x: Object Pool manages a reusable set of initialized objects. Clients borrow from the pool and return objects instead of creating/destroying them. What problems does Object Pool solve beyond performance? How do you handle stale/broken objects in the pool?

n: Adapter — convert interface of a class to another interface clients expect
x: Adapter converts the interface of a class into another interface that clients expect. Lets classes work together that couldn't otherwise due to incompatible interfaces. What is the difference between class adapter and object adapter? Why is composition preferred? Adapter Pattern is a structural design pattern that allows two classes to work together when their interfaces do not match (incompatible interfaces).

n: Bridge — decouple abstraction from implementation so they vary independently
x: Bridge decouples an abstraction from its implementation so the two can vary independently. Avoids permanent binding between abstraction and implementation at compile time. How does Bridge prevent the Cartesian product explosion of subclasses? Give a real-world example.

n: Composite — compose objects into tree structures, treat individuals uniformly
x: Composite composes objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies. Clients treat individual objects and compositions uniformly via a common interface. How does Composite simplify client code when dealing with tree structures like file systems or UI components?

n: Decorator — attach responsibilities to objects dynamically (wrapper)
x: Decorator attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically. Provides a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending functionality. How is Decorator more flexible than inheritance for adding behavior? How do decorators stack? Decorator Pattern is a structural pattern that allows adding new behaviors (features) to objects at runtime, without modifying their class or creating a subclass.

n: Facade — provide a simplified interface to a complex subsystem
x: Facade provides a unified, simplified interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem. Defines a higher-level interface that makes the subsystem easier to use. How does Facade differ from Mediator? Does Facade hide the subsystem or just simplify access? Facade Pattern (pronounced: Fa-saad) provides a very simplified interface (or front face) for accessing a library, framework, or complex system.

n: Flyweight — share fine-grained objects to support large numbers efficiently
x: Flyweight minimizes memory usage by sharing as much data as possible with similar objects. Intrinsic state (shared) vs extrinsic state (passed in context). How do you decide what goes into intrinsic vs extrinsic state in the Flyweight pattern? Give an example.

n: Proxy — provide a surrogate or placeholder to control access
x: Proxy provides a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access. Variants: virtual proxy (lazy load), protection proxy (access control), remote proxy. What are the four variants of Proxy and what problem does each solve? How does Proxy differ from Decorator? Proxy Pattern provides a surrogate (or substitute) for another object so that access to that object can be controlled.

n: Chain of Responsibility — pass requests along a chain of handlers
x: Chain of Responsibility passes a request along a chain of handlers. Each handler decides to process the request or pass it to the next handler. How does Chain of Responsibility decouple the sender from the receiver? What happens if no handler processes the request?

n: Command — encapsulate a request as an object (undo/redo, queue, log)
x: Command encapsulates a request as an object, allowing parameterization, queuing, logging, undo/redo. Contains all info needed to perform an action. How does Command enable undo/redo functionality? What is the relationship between Command and Memento?

n: Interpreter — define grammar + interpreter for language sentences
x: Interpreter defines a grammar for a language and an interpreter that uses the representation to interpret sentences in the language. When is Interpreter appropriate vs using a parser generator? What are the trade-offs?

n: Iterator — provide sequential access to elements without exposing internals
x: Iterator provides a way to access elements of a collection sequentially without exposing the underlying representation. How does Iterator separate traversal logic from the collection? Why is it useful for different collection types?

n: Mediator — reduce chaotic coupling by centralizing communication
x: Mediator reduces chaotic communication between multiple objects by introducing a mediator object that centralizes interactions. What is the trade-off of Mediator? How does it risk becoming a God Object and how do you prevent that?

n: Memento — capture and restore object state without violating encapsulation
x: Memento captures and externalizes an object's internal state so it can be restored later without violating encapsulation. How does Memento preserve encapsulation while enabling undo/checkpoint functionality? What are the three roles?

n: Observer — define one-to-many dependency; when one changes, all dependents notified
x: Observer defines a one-to-many dependency between objects. When the subject changes state, all its dependents (observers) are notified and updated automatically. What is the difference between push model and pull model in Observer? When would you use each?

n: State — alter behavior when internal state changes (state machine)
x: State allows an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes. The object appears to change its class. Each state is a separate class. How does State eliminate complex if/else switch statements? How does it differ from Strategy?

n: Strategy — define family of algorithms, make them interchangeable
x: Strategy defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable. The algorithm can vary independently from clients that use it. How does Strategy enable selecting algorithms at runtime? Give an example where it replaces complex conditional logic.

n: Template Method — define skeleton of algorithm, subclasses override steps
x: Template Method defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a method, deferring some steps to subclasses. Subclasses redefine certain steps without changing the algorithm's structure. What is the Hollywood Principle and how does Template Method embody it? What are hook methods?

n: Visitor — separate algorithm from object structure (Double Dispatch)
x: Visitor lets you define a new operation without changing the classes of the elements on which it operates. Separates algorithm from object structure via Double Dispatch. What is Double Dispatch and how does Visitor achieve it? When is Visitor appropriate vs when does it become a maintenance burden?

n: Active Object — decouple method execution from invocation (async + scheduler)
x: Active Object decouples method execution from method invocation. Each object has its own thread of control and a scheduler that queues invocation requests. How does Active Object enable asynchronous processing without explicit thread management? How does it relate to the Actor model?

n: Balking — only execute action if object is in appropriate state
x: Balking Pattern prevents an action if the object is in an inappropriate state. If the guard condition fails, the method returns immediately (bails out). How does Balking provide a simple alternative to blocking for handling race conditions? Give a real-world example.

n: Barrier — synchronize a group of threads at a common point
x: Barrier synchronizes multiple threads at a common point. All threads must arrive at the barrier before any can proceed past it. How does CyclicBarrier differ from CountDownLatch? When would you use a barrier for parallel algorithms?

n: Double-Checked Locking — reduce lock overhead by checking before acquiring
x: Double-Checked Locking reduces the overhead of acquiring a lock by first testing the locking criterion without acquiring the lock. Why does Double-Checked Locking require the volatile keyword in Java? What problem occurs without it?

n: Future / Promise — placeholder for async result (CompletableFuture)
x: Future/Promise represents a placeholder for a result that hasn't been computed yet. The future is returned immediately; the caller can check, block, or attach callbacks. How does CompletableFuture enable non-blocking asynchronous composition without callback nesting?

n: Producer-Consumer — decouple producers from consumers via a buffer
x: Producer-Consumer decouples producers (create data) from consumers (process data) using a shared buffer/queue. How does BlockingQueue simplify Producer-Consumer? What happens if the buffer is full or empty?

n: Read-Write Lock — allow concurrent reads, exclusive writes
x: Read-Write Lock allows multiple threads to read simultaneously but requires exclusive access for writes. Improves concurrency for read-heavy workloads. Why is Read-Write Lock better than a regular mutex for read-heavy workloads? What is the risk of writer starvation?

n: Thread Pool — manage reusable threads for executing tasks
x: Thread Pool manages a reusable pool of worker threads. Tasks are submitted to a queue, and idle workers pick up tasks. What are the different types of thread pools (fixed, cached, scheduled)? What is a rejection policy?

n: Thread-Local Storage — isolate data per thread (no synchronization needed)
x: Thread-Local Storage provides each thread with its own copy of a variable. No synchronization needed because each thread has exclusive access to its own copy. How does ThreadLocal eliminate contention for per-thread data? What is the memory leak risk in thread pools?

n: MVC — Model-View-Controller: separate data, UI, and input handling
x: MVC separates an application into three components: Model (data + business logic), View (UI presentation), Controller (handles input and updates Model/View). How does MVC enable multiple views of the same model and testable business logic independent of UI?

n: MVP / MVVM — presentation patterns for testable UIs
x: MVP/MVVM are presentation patterns for testable UIs. MVP: View is passive, Presenter contains logic. MVVM: View binds to ViewModel via data binding. Compare MVP and MVVM. When would you choose one over the other for testability and boilerplate?

n: Layered Architecture — horizontal layers (presentation, business, persistence)
x: Layered Architecture organizes code into horizontal layers (presentation, business, persistence). Each layer has a specific responsibility and communicates only with adjacent layers. What is the sinkhole anti-pattern in Layered Architecture? When does layered architecture become a monolithic problem?

n: Microservices — decompose by business capability, independently deployable
x: Microservices decomposes an application into small, independently deployable services organized around business capabilities. What are the trade-offs of microservices vs monoliths? How do you handle distributed transactions?

n: Event-Driven Architecture — components communicate via events (pub/sub)
x: Event-Driven Architecture components communicate through events. Producers emit events, consumers react. Can use message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ). What are the challenges of event-driven architecture in terms of tracing and debugging? Compare pub/sub to point-to-point.

n: CQRS — separate command (write) and query (read) models
x: CQRS separates read operations (queries) from write operations (commands). They may use different models and even different data stores. How does CQRS optimize reads and writes independently? Why is it often paired with Event Sourcing?

n: Event Sourcing — store state changes as sequence of events
x: Event Sourcing stores state changes as a sequence of events. Current state is derived by replaying all events. Events are the single source of truth. How does Event Sourcing provide a complete audit trail? What is the snapshot optimization for large event streams?

n: Hexagonal / Ports & Adapters — core logic isolated from external systems
x: Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters) isolates core business logic from external systems. Core defines ports (interfaces); adapters implement them. How does Hexagonal Architecture make core logic testable without infrastructure? What are driving vs driven adapters?

n: Domain-Driven Design — ubiquitous language, bounded contexts, aggregates
x: Domain-Driven Design focuses on modeling the domain first. Uses ubiquitous language, bounded contexts, aggregates, entities, value objects. What is a bounded context and an aggregate in DDD? How does ubiquitous language bridge domain experts and developers?

n: Repository Pattern — mediate between domain and data mapping layers
x: Repository Pattern mediates between the domain and data mapping layers. Acts like an in-memory collection of domain objects. How does Repository abstract persistence details away from domain code? How does it simplify unit testing?

n: Unit of Work — maintain list of changed objects, commit as transaction
x: Unit of Work maintains a list of objects affected by a business transaction. Coordinates writing changes and resolves concurrency problems. How does Unit of Work ensure transactional consistency? What is the relationship with Repository?

Design a multi-level parking lot handling vehicle entry/exit, spot assignment, fee calculation. Patterns: Singleton, Factory, Strategy. LLD Problem: Design a parking lot system. Model different vehicle types, spot assignment, and fee calculation.

Design elevator logic with request handling, direction strategy, door operations. Patterns: State, Command, Observer. LLD Problem: Design an elevator control system. Handle concurrent requests from multiple floors.

Design product selection, payment processing, change calculation, and inventory management. Patterns: State, Factory. LLD Problem: Design a vending machine with product selection, payment, and change calculation.

Model pieces with movement rules, board state, player turns, check/checkmate detection. Patterns: Composite, Command, Strategy, Memento. LLD Problem: Design a chess game system with move validation, undo/redo, and AI opponents.

Design books, members, borrowing/returning, fines management. Patterns: Repository, Singleton, Factory. LLD Problem: Design a library management system with borrowing, returns, reservations, and fine calculation.

Design a flexible logging system with multiple appenders, log levels, formatting. Patterns: Singleton, Chain of Resp, Factory. LLD Problem: Design a logging framework with configurable log levels, appenders, and formatting.
Design a topic-based publish/subscribe system. Patterns: Observer, Singleton, Thread Pool. LLD Problem: Design a pub-sub message queue with topics, subscribers, and async delivery.

Model card authentication, account types, transactions. Patterns: State, Command, Chain of Resp. LLD Problem: Design an ATM system with card authentication, PIN verification, and transaction processing.
Design the board, players, win condition checking. Patterns: Strategy, Factory. LLD Problem: Design a Tic Tac Toe game supporting human vs human and human vs computer modes.

Create stories/tasks, assign, transition through workflow states. Patterns: State, Command, Observer, Composite. LLD Problem: Design a task management system with workflow states, assignments, and notifications.
Limit API requests per client within time windows. Patterns: Strategy, Proxy, Factory. LLD Problem: Design a rate limiter supporting multiple algorithms (Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Sliding Window).

Design real-time messaging with rooms, private messages, user status. Patterns: Observer, Mediator, Command, Singleton. LLD Problem: Design a real-time chat system with rooms, private messaging, and presence tracking.

n: God Object — one class knows/does too much (violates SRP)
x: God Object — a single class that knows too much or does too much. It has too many responsibilities and becomes extremely hard to maintain. How does the God Object violate SRP? What refactoring steps would you take to fix one?

n: Spaghetti Code — no clear structure, GOTO-like logic
x: Spaghetti Code — code with no clear structure, characterized by excessive nesting, and unpredictable control flow. How does deep nesting and scattered state mutations create spaghetti code? How do design patterns help?

n: Golden Hammer — applying a favorite pattern everywhere
x: Golden Hammer — treating every problem as a nail because you have a favorite pattern. Over-applying a pattern that worked well elsewhere. When does using a design pattern become over-engineering? How does YAGNI relate to the Golden Hammer?

n: Callback Hell — deeply nested callbacks, use Promises/async patterns
x: Callback Hell (Pyramid of Doom) — deeply nested callbacks that make code hard to read, reason about, and debug. How do Promises and async/await solve Callback Hell? What design pattern can help organize callback chains?

n: Singleton Abuse — overusing global state, testing difficulties
x: Singleton Abuse — overusing the Singleton pattern leads to global state that is hard to test, reason about, and maintain. Why are Singletons considered an anti-pattern in many contexts? What is the preferred alternative?

n: Yo-Yo Problem — deep inheritance hierarchies making code hard to follow
x: Yo-Yo Problem — deep inheritance hierarchies where understanding behavior requires jumping up and down the hierarchy repeatedly. How does deep inheritance create the fragile base class problem? How does composition over inheritance solve this?

n: Premature Optimization — optimizing before understanding the real bottleneck
x: Premature Optimization — optimizing code before understanding the actual bottleneck. Knuth: "Premature optimization is the root of all evil." Why is premature optimization problematic even when the optimization seems obvious? What is the correct approach?

n: "Design a system to support multiple notification channels" (Strategy + Observer)
x: Design a system that sends notifications via email, SMS, push, and in-app. Strategy (channel algorithms), Observer (trigger events), Factory (channel creation). Design a notification system that supports email, SMS, push, and in-app notifications. How do you add a new channel?

n: "Design a document editor with undo/redo" (Command + Memento)
x: Design text operations as Command objects. Each command stores state for undo (Memento). Command history stack enables undo/redo navigation. Design a document editor with full undo/redo capability. How do you handle large document memory for undo history?

n: "Design a cache with eviction policies" (Strategy + Proxy)
x: Design a cache with pluggable eviction algorithms. Strategy (LRU, LFU, FIFO), Proxy (wrap data source), Singleton (cache manager). Design a thread-safe cache with pluggable eviction policies. How would you implement LRU efficiently?

n: "Design a workflow engine" (Chain of Resp + Command + State)
x: Design a system that executes a series of steps with branching, parallel execution, and state persistence. Design a workflow engine that supports sequential steps, branching, parallel execution, and state persistence.

Architecture for loading third-party extensions at runtime. Strategy (plugin interface), Factory (discovery/instantiation), Proxy (sandboxed wrapper). Design a plugin system that loads third-party extensions at runtime with security isolation.

n: "Design a UI component library" (Composite + Decorator + Strategy)
x: Design a reusable component system. Composite (component tree), Decorator (add styling/behavior), Strategy (rendering for themes). Design a UI component library that supports theming and composable component trees.

n: Strategy vs State — same structure, different intent (algorithm vs state machine)
x: Strategy vs State — both have identical class structures (Context + interface + concrete classes). Difference is intent: Strategy selects algorithm, State manages behavior transitions. Strategy and State have identical UML. How do you distinguish them by intent and usage?

n: Decorator vs Proxy — both wrap, but intent differs (add features vs control access)
x: Decorator vs Proxy — both wrap an object and forward calls. Intent differs: Decorator adds new behavior, Proxy controls access. How is the intent different between Decorator and Proxy when they both wrap objects? Give examples.

n: Factory vs Builder — Factory creates in one step, Builder in multiple steps
x: Factory vs Builder — Factory creates in one step (single method call). Builder creates in multiple steps, allowing different configurations. When would you choose Builder over Factory? What problem does each solve?

n: Observer vs Mediator — Observer is distributed, Mediator is centralized
x: Observer vs Mediator — both handle communication. Observer distributes (one-to-many notification). Mediator centralizes (many-to-many through coordinator). When does Observer's distributed communication become a problem, and how does Mediator solve it?

n: Adapter vs Facade — Adapter changes interface, Facade simplifies
x: Adapter vs Facade — both wrap something existing. Adapter converts one interface to another (interface transformation). Facade provides simplified interface (simplification). What is the key difference in motivation between Adapter and Facade? Compare their level of abstraction.

n: Command vs Strategy — Command has undo/redo, Strategy is interchangeable algorithms
x: Command vs Strategy — both encapsulate behavior in objects. Command represents a request (action + parameters) with undo support. Strategy represents interchangeable algorithms. How does Command's undo/redo capability distinguish it from Strategy which also encapsulates behavior?

A Null Object implements the interface with no-op behavior. Client code works with real and null objects identically — no null checks needed. Common in UI trees (no-op component), logging (null logger), and caching (null cache that just doesn't cache). How does the Null Object pattern eliminate null checks and where is it commonly used?

Specification pattern encapsulates business rules as composable objects. Each specification tests an object against a rule. Compose with AND, OR, NOT to build complex queries. Separates business logic from data access. How does the Specification pattern encapsulate and compose business rules? How does it fit with the Repository pattern?

A monolith is a single application where ALL the code runs in one process and deploys as one unit. Login, ordering, payments, emails — one codebase, one server, one deploy command. What is a monolith? Why is it the correct starting architecture for most products? Monolith One codebase, one process, one deploy. In-process call Function call, no network. Single DB A shared database. Definition: All functionality (login, orders, payments, emails) is deployed in a single application, in a single process. Modules communicate with each other via function calls.

Monoliths are simpler in every dimension: function calls instead of network calls (microseconds vs milliseconds), one database transaction covers everything, you can read all code in one place. Why are monoliths simpler than microservices? What advantages do they have in the early stages? Modular monolith A single deployment, with clear module boundaries inside. Local transaction A single DB transaction. Low ops Low infrastructure complexity. Definition: A monolith is simple in every dimension: function calls instead of network calls, a single debugger, a single deployment, easy refactoring and transactions.

Monoliths break at scale in four concrete ways: independent scaling becomes impossible, deployments become risky, teams block each other, and one crash takes down everything. What are the four concrete ways a monolith breaks at scale? Independent scaling Scaling only the hot module. Deploy coupling One change = full redeploy. Team contention Conflicts in the same codebase. Definition: The four pain points of a monolith at scale: (1) no independent scaling, (2) a single bug can bring everything down, (3) deploys are slow and risky, (4) merge conflicts and unclear ownership in large teams.

A microservice is a small, independently deployable process that owns one business domain. Each service has its OWN codebase, database, and deployment pipeline. What is a microservice? How does it differ from a monolith architecturally? Independently deployable Deploy independently without affecting others. Owns its data Its own database. Single business capability A single function done well. Definition: A microservice is a small, independent process that owns a business capability — its own code, its own data, its own deployment. It communicates with other services over the network (HTTP/gRPC/events).

Microservices require Docker, Kubernetes, a service registry, distributed tracing, a message broker, and engineers who know all of it. A 3-person team using microservices spends more time on infrastructure than on product. When should you NOT use microservices? What is the team size test? Distributed monolith Cost of microservices, coupling of monolith. Operational overhead K8s, tracing, discovery, CI per service. Premature split Incorrectly guessed boundaries. Definition: Small team, unclear domain, early product, or without strong ops skills, do not adopt microservices. Changing wrong boundaries later is more expensive than a monolith.

Organizations design systems that mirror their own communication structure. A company with 5 engineering teams will inevitably build 5 services. Amazon applied this deliberately with the two-pizza team rule. What is Conway's Law and how does it influence service boundary decisions? Conway's Law Mirrors the system's organization's communication structure. Inverse Conway Design the team structure first. Team Topologies Stream-aligned teams. Definition: 'The organization that designs a system creates a design that copies its communication structure.' Three teams = three modules.

Architectural style where app is a collection of loosely coupled, independently deployable services. Each owns its domain, data, and lifecycle. What are the core characteristics of microservices? What tradeoffs do they introduce? Loose coupling A change in one does not break the other. High cohesion Related things together. Polyglot Each service uses a different technology. Definition: Application a collection of small independent services, each focused on a business capability, with its own data and lifecycle, lightweight communication.

Domain-driven design defines bounded contexts — each service owns a subdomain. Strangler Fig pattern for incremental migration. Vertical slicing over horizontal. How do you decide where to draw service boundaries? What is a Bounded Context? Bounded context DDD boundary where the model is consistent. By business capability Orders, Payments, Shipping. Strangler Fig Gradually extract from the monolith. Definition: Decompose services by business capability or bounded context, not by technical layers. For an existing monolith, Strangler Fig: new features go into a new service, old ones migrate gradually.

Synchronous (HTTP/gRPC) for request-response. Asynchronous (messages/events) for decoupling. gRPC uses protobuf, HTTP/2, streaming — preferred for internal service-to-service. Compare synchronous and asynchronous inter-service communication. When would you use each? Sync HTTP/gRPC request-response. Async Events/messages. Coupling Temporal coupling is higher in sync. Definition: Sync is simple but depends on the caller and callee's availability. Async decouples but introduces eventual consistency and complexity. Mix: queries sync, workflows async.

Single entry point for all clients — routes, aggregates, transforms. BFF (Backend For Frontend): separate gateway per client type (mobile, web, IoT). What is an API Gateway and why is it necessary in a microservices architecture? API Gateway Single entry, routing, auth, rate limit. BFF Backend-for-frontend per client type. Aggregation Multiple calls in a single response. Definition: Gateway protects clients from the internal structure of services. BFF provides separate tailored APIs for web/mobile.

How services find each other's network locations. Client-side: service registry + client load balancing. Server-side: load balancer in front (K8s Service, AWS ALB). How do services discover each other in a dynamic environment like Kubernetes? Registry List of service instances. Client-side Client chooses from the registry. Server-side LB/Kubernetes DNS. Definition: Instances dynamically come and go, IPs change. Discovery: Kubernetes DNS/Services, Consul, Eureka. Unhealthy instances are removed via health checks.

Each service owns its data exclusively — no direct DB sharing. Polyglot persistence: choose the right DB per service (SQL for orders, document for catalog, graph for recommendations). Why must each microservice own its own database? What happens when services share a DB? Database per service Each service's private data store. Polyglot persistence DB based on the use case. No shared tables The other service's DB is not accessed directly. Definition: The service's data is accessed only through its API. This makes schema changes independent. Cross-service queries are done via API composition or CQRS views.

Sequence of local transactions with compensating rollbacks. Choreography: each service listens for events and acts. Orchestration: central coordinator tells each service what to do. How do you handle a transaction that spans multiple services? Explain the Saga pattern. Saga Sequence of local transactions + compensation. Choreography Driven by events, no central controller. Orchestration Central orchestrator executes the steps. Definition: Instead of a distributed transaction, each service performs a local transaction; if it fails, compensating actions (refund, release stock) are executed.

CQRS separates read models (queries) from write models (commands). Event sourcing stores all state changes as an append-only event log — current state is derived by replaying events. What is CQRS and when does it make sense in a microservices architecture? CQRS Read and write models are separate. Event sourcing State = sequence of events. Projection Read model derived from events. Definition: CQRS commands (writes) and queries (reads) in separate models. Event sourcing stores events instead of state — full history, replay possible.

Services communicate through events — producers emit facts, consumers react. Message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ) provide durability, ordering, and routing. What is event-driven architecture? How does it decouple services? Event A fact that has already happened (past tense). Producer/Consumer Emit / react. Event vs command Event notification; command instruction. Definition: Services emit facts (OrderPlaced); interested services subscribe. The producer doesn't know the consumers — loose coupling.

No distributed transactions across services. Embrace eventual consistency. CAP theorem in practice: partition tolerance is non-negotiable, choose consistency (CP) or availability (AP). What is eventual consistency and how does it differ from strong consistency? Eventual consistency Everything syncs after a short delay. Idempotency Duplicate processing safe. Outbox Event saved within the DB transaction. Definition: There is no strong consistency between services; accept eventual consistency. Tools: sagas, outbox, idempotency keys, reconciliation jobs.

Request-response over HTTP/REST or gRPC. Client waits for response. Simple, familiar, but couples availability — if downstream is down, caller is down too. Compare REST and gRPC for inter-service communication. What are the tradeoffs? REST Resource HTTP/JSON. gRPC HTTP/2 + protobuf, fast, typed. Timeout On every call. Definition: Sync request-response is simple. REST is public/compatible; gRPC is internal low-latency. Resilience: timeout, retry, circuit breaker.

Producer sends message to broker → consumer processes later. Decouples sender and receiver in time and space. Message vs event: message has a specific consumer, event is a fact anyone can react to. How does asynchronous messaging decouple services? What guarantees do brokers provide? Broker Kafka/RabbitMQ/SQS. At-least-once Duplicates possible. DLQ Failed messages. Definition: Producer sends a message to the broker, consumer processes it later. Temporal decoupling, buffering, retry, fan-out.

How services agree on data format. Protobuf (compact, typed, schema evolution), Avro (Hadoop-native, schema on read), JSON (human-readable, no schema). Why is schema management important in event-driven systems? Compare JSON, Protobuf, and Avro. Protobuf/Avro Compact typed schemas. Schema registry Central schema versions. Compatibility Backward/forward. Definition: Agreement on data format between services. The schema registry enforces compatibility so that changes by the producer do not break consumers. JSON is flexible but untyped.

When a single operation spans multiple services. Two-phase commit (2PC) for short-lived ACID. Outbox pattern for reliable publishing. Saga for long-lived transactions. How does the Outbox Pattern ensure reliable event publishing alongside database writes? 2PC Prepare + commit, blocking. Saga Compensation based. TCC Try-Confirm-Cancel. Definition: If an operation spans multiple services, then 2PC (strong consistency, coordinator single point of failure, lock holding) or Saga/TCC (eventual) can be used. In microservices, saga is preferred.

Federated GraphQL: multiple services (subgraphs) each own a piece of a unified graph. Gateway (router) composes schemas and routes queries to correct subgraph. What is GraphQL Federation and how does it differ from a monolithic GraphQL API? Subgraph Part of the service's GraphQL schema. Supergraph/Router Combined schema. Entity Shared type between services defined with @key. Definition: In Federation, each service owns its subgraph; the router connects them into a unified graph. Clients fetch data from multiple services with a single query.

Wraps remote call with state machine: CLOSED (normal) → OPEN (failing, fast-fail) → HALF-OPEN (test recovery). Prevents cascading failures and lets downstream recover. Explain the Circuit Breaker pattern. What are its three states and when does it trip? Closed Normal, calls pass. Open Fail fast, calls are not sent. Half-open Check recovery with some trial calls. Definition: The circuit breaker counts failures; when the threshold is crossed it goes OPEN — calls fail immediately (or fallback). After the timeout it moves to HALF-OPEN for test requests; on success it becomes CLOSED.

Retry transient failures with exponential backoff + jitter. Timeouts prevent waiting forever. Never retry on the critical path without circuit breaker. How should you implement retries safely? What is exponential backoff with jitter? Backoff Retry delay increases. Jitter Random delay — prevents thundering herd. Timeout On every call. Definition: Retry on transient failures (exponential backoff + jitter, max attempts). Retry only idempotent operations. Maintain a retry budget.

Isolate resources into pools so failure in one pool doesn't drain shared resources. Thread pool isolation (each service gets its own thread pool) or semaphore isolation (limit concurrent calls). What is the Bulkhead pattern? How does it prevent one slow service from affecting others? Bulkhead Separate resource pools. Thread/connection pool Per-dependency limit. Isolation A slow dependency should not consume the rest. Definition: Like compartments of a ship — each dependency has its own pool/semaphore. A slow service will only fill its own pool, not the entire app.

Control how many requests a client can make in a window. Protects services from abuse, misconfiguration, or traffic spikes. Token bucket, leaky bucket, sliding window. What are the main rate limiting algorithms? Compare token bucket and sliding window. Rate limit Max requests / window. Throttling Slow down or reject excess. 429 Too Many Requests + Retry-After. Definition: Per-client limits prevent the service from being overloaded. Algorithms: token bucket, sliding window. At the gateway or service level; if distributed, use Redis.

When a dependency fails, degrade the feature instead of breaking the user. Show cached data, hide the widget, serve a fallback response. Fail-open vs fail-closed. What is graceful degradation? How do you decide between fail-open and fail-closed? Graceful degradation Feature kam, system up. Fallback Cache/default response. Load shedding Non-critical requests drop. Definition: If the recommendation service is down, show popular items, not an error. Classify features as critical vs non-critical.

Trace a single request across multiple services. Each request gets a traceId propagated in headers. Spans represent units of work. OpenTelemetry is the standard. How does distributed tracing work? What is the role of traceId and spans? Trace Complete request journey. Span A step of a service. Context propagation Forward the Trace ID in headers. Definition: Each request receives a trace ID that propagates between services (W3C traceparent). Backends: Jaeger, Tempo; instrumentation: OpenTelemetry.

All services send logs to a central platform (ELK, Loki, CloudWatch). Correlation IDs tie logs across services. Structured logging (JSON) for machine parsing. Why is centralized logging essential in microservices? What is a correlation ID? Structured logs JSON with fields. Correlation ID Link the request in logs. ELK/Loki Central search. Definition: Each service writes JSON logs to stdout; an agent sends them to a central system. Fields: timestamp, level, service, traceId, userId (no PII/secrets).

RED method: Rate (requests/sec), Errors (failed requests/sec), Duration (latency percentiles). Four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation. What is the RED method?
