How do you use it to monitor microservice health? RED Rate, Errors, Duration. USE Utilization, Saturation, Errors. Percentiles p95/p99 latency. Definition: RED for services, USE for resources. Prometheus + Grafana. SLO-based alerts (burn rate) on symptoms, not on causes.

Consumer-driven contract tests: consumer defines expectations, provider validates them against its API. Pact framework. Ensures compatibility without full integration tests. What is contract testing and why is it preferred over full integration tests in microservices? Consumer-driven contract Defined by consumer expectations. Pact Popular tool. Provider verification Provider verifies the contract. Definition: The consumer writes its expectations (request/response) in a contract; the provider verifies it in CI. Breaking changes are caught before deployment — instead of full E2E.

Test services together with real dependencies. Testcontainers for DB/message broker in tests. WireMock for external API stubs. Focus on critical paths. How do you test microservices with real dependencies? What is Testcontainers? Testcontainers Real DB/broker tests with Docker. Test pyramid Unit > integration > E2E. Test data Isolated, repeatable. Definition: Test the service with real dependencies (DB, Kafka) — better confidence than mocks. Testcontainers provides disposable containers for each test run.

Monorepo (single repo, many services) vs polyrepo (repo per service). Monorepo: unified tooling, atomic cross-service changes, but harder to scale CI. Compare monorepo and polyrepo strategies for microservices. What are the tradeoffs? Monorepo One repo, many services. Polyrepo One repo per service. Path filters Only build the changed service. Definition: Each service has its own independent pipeline: build → test → image → deploy. In a monorepo, path-based triggers; in a polyrepo, shared-libs versioning.

Kubernetes: declarative deployment, auto-scaling, self-healing, service discovery, load balancing, secrets, and config management. What are the core Kubernetes objects for running microservices? How does K8s enable self-healing? Orchestrator Kubernetes. Self-healing Restart/reschedule. Declarative Desired state. Definition: Kubernetes containers schedule, scale, heal, and handle service discovery. Rolling updates, resource limits, probes.

Blue/Green: two identical environments, switch traffic at once. Canary: gradually shift traffic (1% → 5% → 50% → 100%) — monitor metrics, rollback if needed. Compare blue/green and canary deployment strategies. When would you choose each? Blue/Green Instant switch. Canary Gradual %. Rollback Previous version. Definition: Blue/Green fast rollback with double capacity. Canary rollout by observing metrics on a small portion of real traffic. Mesh/ingress traffic split.

Externalize config from code — environment-specific values, feature flags, and secrets. Tools: K8s ConfigMaps/Secrets, HashiCorp Vault, AWS Parameter Store. How should you manage configuration and secrets in a microservices deployment? 12-factor config Config in the environment. Secrets manager Vault/AWS Secrets Manager. Dynamic config Change at runtime. Definition: Config separate from code (environment-specific), secrets from encrypted store, rotation, per-environment values. Feature flags for runtime behavior.

n: Why Microservices — monolith first, when to split, Conway's Law
x: Start with monolith, split when team size or deployment frequency demands it. Conway's Law: system design mirrors org structure. Microservices add operational complexity (networking, data consistency, deployment). Split by business domain, not technical layer. When should you move from a monolith to microservices? What are the hidden costs? Monolith first First monolith, then split. Split triggers Team size, deploy frequency, scale needs. Conway Team boundaries. Definition: Microservices when the team size, independent scaling, or release cadence demand it. Martin Fowler: 'MonolithFirst'. Splits should be data-driven, not trend-driven.

n: Domain-Driven Design — bounded contexts, aggregates, ubiquitous language
x: DDD aligns software with business domains. Bounded Context: autonomous domain with its own model. Aggregate: cluster of entities with a root (consistency boundary). Ubiquitous Language: shared vocabulary between devs and domain experts. Context Maps define inter-domain relationships. What is a Bounded Context in DDD? How do you identify service boundaries? Bounded context The boundary of the model. Aggregate Consistency boundary. Ubiquitous language Dev + business shared vocabulary. Definition: DDD models the business domain. An Aggregate (Order + OrderLines) is a transaction boundary; other aggregates are referenced by IDs. A context map shows the relationships between contexts.

n: Kafka — event sourcing, CQRS, exactly-once semantics, consumer groups
x: Kafka: distributed append-only log. Topics partitioned for parallelism. Consumer groups for load balancing. Exactly-once requires idempotent producers + transactional consumers. Event sourcing: store events, derive state. CQRS: separate read/write models. How does Kafka achieve exactly-once delivery? What is the difference between at-least-once and exactly-once? Partition Parallelism + ordering unit. Consumer group Partitions are shared. Offset Log position. Definition: Kafka distributed append-only log. Key to partition → order for the same key is guaranteed. Consumer group scale-out. Exactly-once (idempotent producer + transactions) in a limited scope.

n: Service Mesh — Istio, Envoy sidecar, mTLS, traffic management
x: Service mesh handles cross-cutting concerns (observability, security, traffic) via sidecar proxies. Istio uses Envoy sidecars. mTLS between services automatically. Traffic management: canary deployments, circuit breaking, retries. Adds latency (~1-2ms per hop). What is a service mesh? When does the overhead justify the benefits? Sidecar Proxy (Envoy) with each pod. mTLS Service-to-service encryption. Traffic management Retries, splits, timeouts. Definition: Mesh cross-cutting concerns (mTLS, retries, observability, traffic shifting) are moved from application code into proxies. Istio/Linkerd.

n: Chaos Engineering — game days, fault injection, Netflix Chaos Monkey
x: Chaos Engineering: deliberately inject failures to find weaknesses before they cause outages. Chaos Monkey kills random instances. Game days: coordinated failure scenarios. Steady state hypothesis: define expected behavior, then break things. Tools: Chaos Monkey, Litmus, Gremlin. What is Chaos Engineering? How do you run a chaos experiment safely? Hypothesis Steady state expectation. Blast radius Limit scope. Chaos Monkey Random instance kill. Definition: Verify resilience by injecting failures into a production-like environment. Latency, pod kill, dependency down, AZ failure. GameDays give teams practice.

n: Event Storming — collaborative design, domain events, aggregates
x: Event Storming is a workshop format for exploring complex domains. Participants map domain events (orange stickies) on a timeline. Commands (yellow), aggregates (blue), policies (purple), read models (green). Big Picture → Process Modeling → Software Design. What is Event Storming and how do you facilitate one? What are the different types of stickies? Domain event Orange sticky: OrderPlaced. Command / Aggregate Blue / yellow stickies. Bounded context They are formed by clusters. Definition: Workshop where developers and domain experts create an events timeline on the wall. Then they suggest commands, aggregates, policies, hotspots; clusters of bounded contexts.

n: What is DevOps — Culture, Principles, CALMS Framework
x: DevOps is a cultural and technical movement that breaks down silos between development and operations. CALMS: Culture, Automation, Lean, Measurement, Sharing. Explain the CALMS framework and how it applies to DevOps adoption. CALMS Culture, Automation, Lean, Measurement, Sharing. You build it, you run it The dev team takes ownership of production. Silo A wall between Dev and Ops. Definition: DevOps is a set of culture and practices that connects development and operations so that software is delivered quickly, safely, and repeatedly. The CALMS framework is a way to assess adoption. In the old model, developers would “throw the code over the wall” and operations had to handle

n: DevOps vs SRE vs Platform Engineering
x: DevOps is the philosophy. SRE applies software engineering to operations. Platform Engineering builds internal developer platforms (IDPs) for self-service. What is the difference between DevOps, SRE, and Platform Engineering? DevOps Philosophy/culture. SRE Ops using software engineering; SLOs, error budgets. Platform Engineering Internal developer platform (self-service). Definition: DevOps 'what and why', SRE 'how to make reliability measurable' (SLI/SLO/error budget), Platform Engineering 'golden paths/portal for developers'.

The software delivery lifecycle: plan → code → build → test → release → deploy → operate → monitor. Automation at every stage reduces lead time and errors. Walk through the SDLC pipeline from commit to production. What metrics define elite performance? Pipeline Automated build→test→release stages. Shift left Testing/security first. Fast feedback Fail early. Definition: Plan → code → build → test → release → deploy → operate. Automate every stage; fast tests first, slow tests later.

Trunk-based development: short-lived branches merged to main frequently. Feature flags decouple deployment from release — merge dark code, turn on later. What is trunk-based development and how do feature flags enable it? Trunk-based Short-lived branches, frequent merges into main. Feature flag Code is deployed, feature hidden. Long-lived branch Merge hell. Definition: Developers often merge into main during the day; incomplete features are hidden behind feature flags. Release = flag on, deploy = code shipping — they are separate.

DORA identifies four key metrics: Deployment Frequency, Lead Time for Changes, Change Failure Rate, Time to Restore Service. What are the four DORA metrics and what benchmarks define elite performance? Deployment Frequency How often production is deployed. Lead Time Time from commit to production. Change Failure Rate / MTTR How many deployments fail; how long recovery takes. Definition: The four DORA metrics: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, time to restore. Elite teams perform well in both speed and stability.

n: CI/CD Pipeline Design — Stages, Gates, Artifact Promotion
x: CI (Continuous Integration): merge frequently, build and test every change. CD (Continuous Delivery): every change is deployable but release is manual. Design a CI/CD pipeline from scratch. What are the key stages and gates? CI Frequent merge + automated build/test. Continuous Delivery Always deployable; manual approval. Continuous Deployment Auto prod deploy. Definition: Build once, promote same artifact across environments (dev→staging→prod). Gates: tests, scans, approvals. Artifact immutable.

n: GitHub Actions — Workflows, Runners, Matrix Builds
x: GitHub Actions is CI/CD natively integrated with GitHub. Workflows are YAML with triggers, jobs, steps. Runners can be GitHub-hosted or self-hosted. How do you design an efficient GitHub Actions workflow? Explain matrix builds and caching. Workflow YAML in .github/workflows. Runner Machine that runs the job. Matrix Multiple versions/OS parallel. Definition: Jobs/steps run on events (push, PR). Matrix builds, caching, secrets, reusable workflows, environments with approvals.

n: Deployment Strategies — Blue/Green, Canary, Rolling, A/B
x: Blue/green: two identical environments, switch traffic. Canary: percentage of traffic to new version. Rolling: gradually replace instances. Compare blue/green, canary, and rolling deployment strategies. When would you choose each? Blue/Green Two environments, traffic switch. Canary Small percentage first. Rolling Instances replace gradually. Definition: Blue/green provides instant rollback but requires double capacity. Canary reduces risk on real traffic. Rolling is the default K8s strategy. For A/B experiments.

Artifacts are versioned, signed, and stored in registries. Immutability: once tagged/pushed, artifact never changes. Why is artifact immutability critical for reproducible deployments? How do you enforce it? Registry Artifacts store (ECR, Nexus, npm). Immutability Tag cannot be overwritten. Semver / SHA Version identifier. Definition: Each build is a versioned artifact (image digest/SHA). Immutable tags, signed, retention policy, vulnerability scan in the registry.

n: Pipeline Security — SAST, DAST, SBOM, Supply Chain
x: SAST scans source code. DAST scans running app. SBOM catalogs dependencies. Supply chain security ensures trusted artifacts. How do you build security into a CI/CD pipeline? Explain SAST, DAST, and SCA. SAST Source scan. DAST Running app scan. SBOM Components inventory. Definition: In the pipeline, secrets scan, SAST, SCA, container scan, DAST, signing and provenance (SLSA). The pipeline itself is also an attack target — least privilege tokens.

n: Docker Architecture — Images, Layers, Union FS, Overlay2
x: Docker images are read-only layers built from a Dockerfile. Each instruction creates a layer. Union filesystem (overlay2) merges layers. Explain Docker image layers and how the overlay2 filesystem works. Image Read-only layered template. Layer Each Dockerfile instruction creates a layer. Overlay2 Union filesystem — layers stack + writable top layer. Definition: Image layers are a stack, container = image + writable layer. Layers are cached and shared. Containers use namespaces (isolation) and cgroups (resource limits).

n: Dockerfile Best Practices — Multi-stage, Cache, Minimal Images
x: Multi-stage builds: use one image to build and a separate minimal image to run. Result: tiny production images without build tools. How do you write an optimized Dockerfile? Explain multi-stage builds and layer caching. Multi-stage Separate build stage, smaller runtime stage. Layer cache Things that change less are on top. Minimal base alpine/distroless. Definition: Dependencies first copy+install, then source — more cache hits. Multi-stage means compilers are not in the final image. .dockerignore, non-root user, pinned versions.

n: Container Networking — Bridge, Host, Overlay, CNI
x: Bridge: default network. Host: shares host network stack. Overlay: multi-host networking via VXLAN. CNI: standard interface for container networking. Compare bridge, host, and overlay networking in Docker. When would you use each? Bridge Default private network on host. Host Shares the host network with the container. Overlay Multi-host networking. Definition: On a bridge network, containers communicate with each other by name (user-defined bridge). Ports are published to the outside. In K8s, CNI plugins provide pod networking.

n: Container Security — Non-root, Read-only FS, Seccomp, AppArmor
x: Run containers as non-root user. Mount filesystem read-only where possible. Seccomp restricts syscalls. AppArmor/SELinux Mandatory Access Control. List the key container security hardening techniques and why each matters. Non-root USER directive. Seccomp Syscalls filter. AppArmor MAC profile. Definition: Root user, privileged mode, docker.sock mount avoid. Read-only rootfs, capabilities drop, seccomp default profile, resource limits.

Docker Compose defines multi-container applications in YAML. Services, networks, volumes, environment variables configured in docker-compose.yml. How do you set up a reproducible local development environment with Docker Compose? Service Container definition. depends_on Start order (no readiness). Volumes Persistent data. Definition: In docker-compose.yml, you can run the app, DB, and cache with a single command. Perfect for local development and integration tests; not for production orchestration.

n: K8s Architecture — Control Plane, Nodes, etcd, Scheduler
x: Control plane: API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager. Workers: kubelet, kube-proxy, container runtime (containerd). Explain the Kubernetes control plane components and their responsibilities. API server Cluster's front door. etcd Cluster state store. Scheduler/Controllers Pod placement / desired state reconcile. Definition: Control plane: API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager. Nodes: kubelet, container runtime, kube-proxy. Declarative model: write the desired state, and controllers match the actual state.

Pod: smallest deployable unit. Deployment: declarative updates for Pods. Service: stable network endpoint for a set of Pods. Explain the relationship between Pods, Deployments, and Services in Kubernetes. Pod Smallest unit; containers share network. Deployment Replicas + rolling updates. Service Stable virtual IP/DNS for pods. Definition: Deployment manages pods through a ReplicaSet. Service load-balances pods using a label selector. ConfigMap provides configuration, Secret holds sensitive data (base64, not encrypted by default).

n: K8s Networking — Ingress, CNI, Service Mesh
x: Ingress: L7 load balancing with path/host-based routing. CNI: pod networking and network policies. Service mesh: mTLS, traffic management. How does Kubernetes handle networking? Compare Ingress, CNI, and service mesh. Ingress L7 routing host/path. CNI Pod network plugin (Calico, Cilium). Service mesh Sidecar proxies. Definition: Service types: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer. Ingress controller (nginx) provides HTTP routing. Each pod has its own IP; CNI provides pod-to-pod connectivity.

Helm: Kubernetes package manager — Charts bundle templates + values. CRD: extends K8s API. Operator: controller that watches CRDs and reconciles state. What are Helm Charts, CRDs, and Operators? How do they work together? Helm chart Templates + values package. CRD Custom resource definition. Operator CRD + controller automation. Definition: Helm templating creates the same manifests for different environments; Operators (e.g., Postgres operator) use domain knowledge (backup, failover) to automate.

n: K8s Security — RBAC, Pod Security, Network Policies
x: RBAC: Role-based access control for API operations. Pod Security Standards: privileged, baseline, restricted. NetworkPolicies: pod-level firewall. How do you secure a Kubernetes cluster? Explain RBAC, Pod Security, and NetworkPolicies. RBAC Roles + bindings. NetworkPolicy Pod traffic firewall. Pod Security Restricted/baseline standards. Definition: Least-privilege RBAC, default-deny NetworkPolicy, Pod Security Admission, secrets encryption/external secrets, image policies, audit logs.

Terraform declares infrastructure in HCL. State file maps config to real resources. Modules encapsulate reusable infrastructure. Workspaces isolate environments. Explain Terraform state management, modules, and workspaces. State Mapping of configuration to real resources. Module Reusable infra block. Provider AWS/GCP plugin. Definition: Terraform HCL declares the desired infrastructure. plan shows the diff, apply makes the change, and the state file tracks it.

n: Terraform Advanced — Remote State, Locking, Drift Detection
x: Remote state stores terraform.tfstate in S3/GCS with DynamoDB locking. Plan detects drift between declared state and real infrastructure. What is infrastructure drift and how does Terraform detect and handle it? Remote state S3/GCS backend. Locking DynamoDB lock — prevents concurrent apply. Drift Different from the real infrastructure configuration. Definition: Remote, locked, and encrypted state for the team. Drift detection scheduled from terraform plan . State split per environment/component.

n: Configuration Management — Ansible vs Chef vs Puppet
x: Ansible: agentless, push-based, YAML playbooks. Chef: agent-based, Ruby DSL, pull-based. Puppet: agent-based, declarative DSL, pull-based. Compare Ansible, Chef, and Puppet. When would you choose each? Ansible Agentless, push, YAML. Chef/Puppet Agent-based, pull. Idempotent Same result when run repeatedly. Definition: Config management servers manage software/configuration inside them. Ansible via SSH; for provisioning with Terraform, for configuration with Ansible.

n: Immutable Infrastructure — Packer, AMIs, Golden Images
x: Immutable infrastructure: never modify running servers — replace them. Packer builds machine images with everything baked in. Golden images are versioned templates. What is immutable infrastructure and how does it eliminate configuration drift? Immutable Server replace, no patch. Packer Machine images build. Golden AMI Pre-baked image. Definition: Change = new image build → new instances launch → old terminate. Snowflake servers and drift eliminated.

n: GitOps — ArgoCD, Flux, Declarative Continuous Delivery
x: GitOps: Git repo is the single source of truth. ArgoCD/Flux reconciles cluster state with what's in the Git repo. Syncs automatically on commit. What is GitOps and how does ArgoCD implement it for Kubernetes deployments? GitOps Git = source of truth. ArgoCD/Flux Cluster reconciles with Git. Pull-based Cluster pulls from Git. Definition: Deploy = Git commit/PR. Controller continuously compares the desired state with the live state and syncs. Audit trail, rollback = git revert.

n: Capacity Planning & Auto-scaling — HPA, VPA, Cluster Autoscaler
x: HPA: scales pods based on CPU/memory or custom metrics. VPA: adjusts pod resource requests. Cluster autoscaler: adds/removes nodes. Explain HPA, VPA, and cluster autoscaler. How do they work together? HPA Increase/decrease the pod count. VPA Pod resources adjust. Cluster Autoscaler Nodes add/remove. Definition: HPA scales pods based on CPU/custom metrics (RPS, queue depth). For nodes, use Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter. Set the baseline using a load test.

n: Disaster Recovery & Backup — RPO, RTO, Multi-region
x: RPO: max acceptable data loss. RTO: max acceptable downtime. Multi-region: active-active vs active-passive. Define RPO and RTO. How do you design a disaster recovery strategy for a cloud application? RPO Max data loss window. RTO Max downtime. Strategies Backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby, active-active. Definition: RPO/RTO define the business; strategy follows that (cost increases). Testing the restore of backups is essential.

Chaos engineering: proactively inject failures to build confidence in system resilience. Principles: steady state hypothesis, run experiment in production. What is chaos engineering? How do you run a safe GameDay in production? Steady state Normal behaviour hypothesis. Blast radius Scope of the experiment. GameDay Planned failure drill. Definition: Find weaknesses in production-like conditions using controlled failures (pod kill, latency inject, AZ outage). Hypothesis → experiment → learn → fix.

n: Compliance & Audit — SOC2, HIPAA, Policy-as-Code (OPA, Kyverno)
x: SOC2: security controls for service providers. HIPAA: healthcare data protection. Policy-as-code: OPA and Kyverno enforce rules as code. How do you implement policy-as-code in a Kubernetes environment using OPA or Kyverno? Policy as code OPA/Kyverno rules. SOC2 Controls audit. Admission control Check before entering the cluster. Definition: Policies in code: 'no privileged pod', 'images only from trusted registry', 'S3 not public'. Enforced on both CI and admission controller; audit evidence automatically.

n: EC2 — instances, AMIs, security groups, key pairs
x: EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) provides virtual servers in the cloud. An AMI is a template for an instance (OS + software). Security groups act as virtual firewalls controlling inbound/outbound traffic. Key pairs provide SSH access. What is an EC2 instance? How do security groups differ from network ACLs? AMI Machine image. Security Group Stateful firewall. Instance types General/compute/memory optimized. Definition: EC2 virtual servers. Purchasing: On-Demand, Reserved/Savings Plans, Spot. Key pair for SSH (or SSM Session Manager is better). ASG scaling.

n: S3 — buckets, lifecycle policies, presigned URLs, versioning
x: S3 (Simple Storage Service) stores objects (files) in buckets. Lifecycle policies auto-move objects between storage classes (Standard, IA, Glacier). Presigned URLs grant temporary access to private objects. Versioning keeps object history. What is S3? How do lifecycle policies reduce storage costs? Bucket/object Flat key-value storage. Lifecycle Tier/expire rules. Presigned URL Temporary access link. Definition: S3 11 9's durability. Versioning, lifecycle (IA/Glacier), SSE-KMS, Block Public Access, presigned URLs for direct upload/download.

n: RDS — managed databases, Multi-AZ, read replicas, backups
x: RDS (Relational Database Service) manages PostgreSQL, MySQL, etc. Multi-AZ provides automatic failover for high availability. Read replicas scale read traffic. Automated backups enable point-in-time recovery. What is RDS? How does Multi-AZ differ from Read Replicas? Multi-AZ Standby failover (HA). Read replica Read scaling (async). PITR Point-in-time restore. Definition: RDS managed backups, patching, failover. For Multi-AZ availability, for read replica performance — both are separate things.

n: Lambda — serverless functions, cold starts, event sources
x: Lambda runs code without managing servers. Triggered by events (API Gateway, S3, SQS, DynamoDB streams). Cold start = first invocation delay. Provisioned concurrency eliminates cold starts at extra cost. What is AWS Lambda? What causes cold starts and how do you mitigate them? Cold start Startup delay of a new execution environment. Event source API GW, S3, SQS, EventBridge. Concurrency Parallel executions limit. Definition: When a Lambda event arrives, it runs the code, with per-invocation billing. Limits: 15 minutes, 10 GB memory. Provisioned concurrency reduces cold starts.

n: VPC — subnets, route tables, NAT gateway, internet gateway
x: VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) is your isolated network in AWS. Public subnets have internet access via Internet Gateway. Private subnets use NAT Gateway for outbound-only internet. Route tables control traffic flow between subnets. What is a VPC? How do public and private subnets differ? Public subnet IGW route. Private subnet Egress via NAT. Route table Traffic rules. Definition: In a VPC, CIDR, subnets (multi-AZ), route tables, IGW (internet), NAT GW (outbound from private), VPC endpoints (AWS services without internet).

n: IAM — users, roles, policies, least privilege
x: IAM (Identity and Access Management) controls who can do what. Users have long-term credentials. Roles provide temporary credentials (for EC2, Lambda, etc.). Policies are JSON documents granting/denying permissions. Least privilege = only grant what is needed. What is IAM? What is the difference between an IAM user and an IAM role? Role Assume temporary credentials. Policy JSON permissions. Least privilege Only necessary actions. Definition: SSO/MFA for users, roles for workloads (instance profile, IRSA), avoid long-lived access keys. Explicit Deny > Allow. Access Analyzer shows unused permissions.

CloudWatch collects metrics (CPU, memory, request count), logs (Lambda, EC2, RDS), and alarms (notify when threshold breached). Dashboards visualize metrics. CloudWatch Events/EventBridge route events between services. How do you set up an alarm for high CPU on an EC2 instance using CloudWatch? Metrics Time series (CPU, requests). Logs Insights Log query. Alarm Threshold → SNS/action. Definition: CloudWatch metrics, logs, alarms, dashboards. Custom metrics, composite alarms. Memory/disk requires an agent.

n: ALB & ELB — load balancing, health checks, target groups
x: ALB (Application Load Balancer) routes HTTP/HTTPS traffic to targets (EC2, Lambda, IP). ELB is the umbrella name. Health checks ensure traffic only goes to healthy targets. Target groups define which instances receive traffic. What is the difference between ALB and NLB? When would you use each? ALB L7 HTTP routing. NLB L4, high performance. Target group + health check Healthy targets. Definition: ALB path/host routing, WebSocket, WAF integration. Health checks remove unhealthy targets. Connection draining during deployments.

n: Serverless — Lambda, API Gateway, event-driven architecture
x: Serverless = no server management. AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, GCP Cloud Run. API Gateway routes HTTP to Lambda. Event-driven: S3, SQS, DynamoDB streams trigger functions. Cold starts, execution limits (15min Lambda), vendor lock-in. What are the limitations of serverless? When should you NOT use serverless? FaaS Function as a service. Event-driven Execution on triggers. Pay-per-use Zero cost when idle. Definition: In serverless, the provider handles infrastructure management; auto-scale, per-ms billing. Patterns: API GW+Lambda, S3→Lambda, queue workers, step functions.

n: Cloud Networking — VPC, subnets, security groups, load balancers
x: VPC isolates your cloud network. Public subnets have internet access. Private subnets are internal only. Security groups are stateful firewalls. NACLs are stateless. ALB for HTTP routing. NLB for TCP/UDP. NAT Gateway for private subnet internet access. What is the difference between a security group and a NACL? Subnet/VPC Isolated network. Security group Stateful instance-level. Load balancer Traffic distribute. Definition: Public/private subnets, SG vs NACL, LB layers (L4/L7), DNS (Route53), CDN, VPN/peering/Transit Gateway.

n: Cloud Cost Optimization — Reserved Instances, Spot, right-sizing
x: Reserved Instances: 1-3 year commitments for 30-60% discount. Spot Instances: up to 90% discount but can be terminated. Right-sizing: match instance type to workload. Savings Plans: flexible commitment. Cost allocation tags for per-team billing. How do you reduce AWS costs by 50%? What is the difference between Reserved Instances and Savings Plans? Right-sizing Based on instance size usage. Savings Plans/RI Commitment discount. Spot Interruptible cheap capacity. Definition: First get visibility (tags, Cost Explorer), then right-size, delete idle resources, apply commitment discounts for steady load, use Spot for fault-tolerant workloads, tier storage, and reduce data transfer.

n: Feature Flags — progressive delivery, A/B testing, kill switches
x: Feature flags control feature visibility without deployment. Progressive delivery: gradual rollout (1% → 10% → 100%). A/B testing: split traffic between variants. Kill switches: instantly disable broken features. Tools: LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagsmith. How do feature flags enable progressive delivery? What is the difference between release flags and experiment flags? Progressive delivery Percentage rollout. Kill switch Turn a feature off instantly. Targeting User/segment rules. Definition: Flags change behavior at runtime without deployment. Use: gradual rollout, A/B, kill switch, ops toggles. Flag lifecycle: create → rollout → cleanup.

Confidentiality, integrity, availability — the three pillars every security control maps back to. Includes defense in depth, least privilege, and fail secure. Explain the CIA triad. How does each principle apply to a real-world system you have designed? Confidentiality Only authorized people can view the data (encryption, access control). Integrity Data cannot be changed without authorization (hash, signature, checksums). Availability Service runs when needed (redundancy, DDoS protection). Definition: The CIA triad consists of three security pillars. Each control protects one of them. Along with: defense in depth (multiple layers), least privilege (minimum access), fail secure (denies access

Authentication verifies identity ("who you are"). Authorization determines access ("what you can do"). Factors: something you know, have, are. Common failure: checking AuthN but forgetting AuthZ. What is the difference between authentication and authorization? Why do engineers confuse them? Authentication (AuthN) Who you are — identity verification. Authorization (AuthZ) What you can do — permissions. 401 vs 403 401 = identity unknown; 403 = known but not allowed. Definition: AuthN first (password, MFA, token), AuthZ after that on every request (RBAC, ABAC, ownership check). Both are implemented on separate layers.

Symmetric (AES-256-GCM), asymmetric (ECDSA, Ed25519), hashing (SHA-256, bcrypt), and digital signatures. AEAD encrypts and verifies integrity together. Compare symmetric and asymmetric cryptography. When would you use AES-256-GCM vs RSA? Symmetric Single key: AES-256-GCM (fast, bulk data). Asymmetric Public/private key: RSA, ECDSA, Ed25519. Hash vs encrypt Hash one-way; encryption reversible. Definition: Encrypts symmetric data; for asymmetric key exchange and signatures; for hash integrity. Use a slow hash (bcrypt/argon2) with salt for passwords, not SHA-256.

Hierarchy of Certificate Authorities (CAs) that trust each other up to a root CA. TLS certificate chain validation, CRL, OCSP, Let's Encrypt, and Certificate Transparency. Explain how the TLS certificate chain works. What happens when a certificate is revoked? CA Trusted authority that signs certificates. Chain of trust Leaf → intermediate → root. Revocation Certificate revocation via CRL / OCSP. Definition: In PKI, the browser trusts root CAs; the server sends the leaf certificate and intermediates. The certificate includes the domain, public key, expiration, and the CA’s signature.

STRIDE (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Info disclosure, DoS, Elevation of privilege) maps threats to components. Attack trees model multi-step paths. Risk = likelihood × impact. How do you perform threat modeling on a new system? Walk through the STRIDE framework. STRIDE Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Info disclosure, DoS, Elevation of privilege. Trust boundary Where data moves from one trust level to another. DFD Data flow diagram — the basis of the threat model. Definition: Threat modeling at the design stage asks: What are we building? What could go wrong? What will we do? Did we do it right? Create a DFD, mark trust boundaries, apply STRIDE to each element.

The most critical web application security risks: Broken Access Control, Cryptographic Failures, Injection, Insecure Design, Security Misconfiguration, and more. Name the current OWASP Top 10. Which three are most common in modern web applications? Broken Access Control #1 — authZ checks missing. Injection SQL/NoSQL/OS command. Security misconfiguration Default creds, debug on. Definition: The OWASP Top 10 is the list of the most common risks for web applications (Broken Access Control, Cryptographic Failures, Injection, Insecure Design, Misconfiguration, Vulnerable Components, Auth Failures, Integrity Failures, Logging Failures, SSRF).

Stored XSS (saved on server), Reflected (in URL), DOM-based (client-side). CSP (Content Security Policy) prevents all three. Output encoding must be context-aware. Explain the three types of XSS. How does Content Security Policy prevent each? Stored XSS Payload saved in DB, triggers for everyone. Reflected XSS URL parameter reflected immediately on the page. CSP Informs the browser which scripts are allowed. Definition: In XSS, the attacker’s JavaScript runs in the victim’s browser on your site’s origin — it can steal cookies/tokens. Fix: output encoding, framework auto-escape, CSP, HttpOnly cookies.

CSRF tricks a victim into performing actions on another site. Anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookie attribute (Lax, Strict, None) provide browser-level protection. How does a CSRF attack work? What defenses would you implement in a modern web app? CSRF Attacker triggers an authenticated request from the victim’s browser. SameSite Cookie does not go on cross-site requests (Lax/Strict). CSRF token Unpredictable per-session token. Definition: Browser cookies are sent automatically, so a POST from evil.com to bank.com can occur. Defense: SameSite=Lax/Strict, anti-CSRF tokens, Origin/Referer check, custom header for APIs.

SQLi injects malicious SQL through input fields — UNION-based, error-based, blind. NoSQLi targets MongoDB/Couchbase with $where and $regex. Parameterized queries are the fix. Explain blind SQL injection. How do you detect and prevent it? SQLi The query structure changes from input. Parameterized query Data and code are separate. NoSQLi {"$ne": null} operators are injected. Definition: When a query is built by string concatenation, an attacker can insert ' OR 1=1 -- to change the logic. Fix: prepared statements/ORM parameters, least-privilege DB user, input validation.

SSRF makes the server fetch internal resources (cloud metadata endpoints). IDOR lets attackers access resources by changing IDs. Both require server-side validation and authorization checks. How would you exploit SSRF to steal AWS IAM credentials? How do you defend against it? SSRF Having the server make a request to the URL supplied by the attacker. Metadata endpoint 169.254.169.254 — cloud credentials. IDOR Changing the ID to access someone else’s data. Definition: In SSRF, the server sends a request to internal services/metadata (AWS IMDS). Fix: URL allowlist, block private IPs, IMDSv2, egress filtering. IDOR: ownership check missing.

n: XXE — XML External Entity injection, XXE mitigation
x: XXE attacks exploit XML parsers that process external entities. Attacker injects XML entities to read local files, SSRF, or cause DoS. Mitigation: disable DTD processing, disable external entities. JSON APIs are not vulnerable. Only affects XML-based systems (SOAP, SAML, SVG, DOCX). What is XXE and which systems are vulnerable? How do you prevent it? External entity In XML <!ENTITY x SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd"> . DTD Document Type Definition where entities are defined. Mitigation Disable DTD/external entities in the parser. Definition: XXE occurs when the XML parser resolves external entities. An attacker can read local files, perform SSRF, or cause DoS (billion laughs).

n: SSTI — Server-Side Template Injection, auto-escaping, sandboxing
x: SSTI occurs when user input is embedded in a template without escaping. Attacker injects template syntax to execute code server-side. Jinja2, Twig, Handlebars, FreeMarker all vulnerable. Mitigation: auto-escaping, sandbox mode, never render user input directly. What is SSTI and how do you detect it? What is the impact of SSTI in Jinja2? Template injection User input becomes template code. Auto-escape Output HTML-encode. Sandbox Template engine in a restricted environment. Definition: If you concatenate user input into a template string and render it ( render_template_string("Hello " + name) ), the attacker can send {{7*7}} and achieve code execution.

n: Directory Traversal — path traversal, null bytes, URL encoding
x: Directory traversal uses ../ sequences to access files outside the web root. Bypasses: URL encoding (%2e%2e%2f), null bytes (%00), double encoding. Mitigation: validate paths against whitelist, use chroot/jail, never use user input in file paths directly. What is directory traversal and what are common bypass techniques? ../ Parent directory sequence. Encoding bypass %2e%2e%2f, double encoding, null byte. Canonicalize Resolve the path and check that it stays within the base. Definition: /download?file=../../etc/passwd so the attacker can read files outside the web root. Fix: map the filename to an ID, or resolve it and verify the base directory prefix.

n: Open Redirect — parameter manipulation, SSO bypass, phishing
x: Open redirect: application redirects user to attacker-controlled URL via manipulated parameter. Used in phishing (legitimate domain → malicious site), OAuth/SSO bypass, token theft. Mitigation: validate redirect URLs against whitelist, use callback URLs. What is an open redirect vulnerability? How is it used in phishing attacks? Open redirect ?next=https://evil.com redirect. Phishing Trusted domain link, evil destination. Allowlist Only known paths/hosts. Definition: After login, blindly redirecting on ?returnTo= lets the attacker create a phishing link from a trusted domain and provides a path for token leakage in OAuth/SSO flows.

n: Insecure Deserialization — object injection, remote code execution
x: Insecure deserialization: untrusted data is deserialized into objects without validation. Can lead to remote code execution (Java RCE, PHP object injection). Mitigation: avoid deserializing untrusted data, use signed/encrypted serialization, integrity checks. What is insecure deserialization and how does it lead to RCE? Deserialization Bytes → object. Gadget chain Existing classes combined to achieve code execution. Safe format JSON + schema validation. Definition: Loading untrusted data with a native deserializer (Java ObjectInputStream, Python pickle, PHP unserialize) allows an attacker to create objects or invoke methods — often resulting in RCE.

n: Clickjacking — UI redressing, X-Frame-Options, CSP frame-ancestors
x: Clickjacking: attacker iframes victim site transparently, tricks user into clicking. Mitigation: X-Frame-Options: DENY or SAMEORIGIN. CSP frame-ancestors directive (preferred). Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'. JavaScript frame-busting is bypassable. What is clickjacking and how do you prevent it? UI redressing Getting the user to click on an invisible iframe. X-Frame-Options DENY / SAMEORIGIN. frame-ancestors CSP's modern replacement. Definition: Attacker loads your site in a transparent iframe and places it over a button on their page; the user clicks "free gift" but actually presses "delete account".

Sessions: server stores state, client gets cookie. Tokens (JWT): client stores claims, server validates signature. Access tokens (short-lived) vs refresh tokens (long-lived, rotated). Compare session-based and token-based authentication. What are the trade-offs for scalability and security? Session Server state + session ID in cookie. Stateless token JWT: claims reside on the client. Revocation Session easy; JWT difficult. Definition: Sessions store state server-side (Redis), allowing immediate logout/revoke. JWT is stateless, scales easily but revocation is difficult — requires short expiry + refresh token.

Three base64url segments: header, payload, signature. Common attacks: alg=none, algorithm confusion, weak HMAC secret. Always validate signature, expiry, issuer, and audience. Explain the alg=none attack on JWTs. How do you prevent algorithm confusion attacks? alg=none Signature skip attack. Algorithm confusion Turning an RS256 public key into an HS256 secret. exp / aud / iss Claims that should be verified. Definition: JWT = header.payload.signature (base64url). Payload is not encrypted, it is only signed. When verifying, pin the algorithm and check exp, iss, aud.

OAuth 2.0: delegated authorization via access tokens. Authorization Code Flow with PKCE prevents interception. OIDC adds id_token (JWT) for authentication on top of OAuth. Walk through the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow with PKCE. Why is PKCE necessary? OAuth 2.0 Delegated authorization (access token). OIDC Authentication on top of OAuth (ID token). PKCE Prevents authorization code interception. Definition: Authorization Code + PKCE flow: the app sends the user to the IdP → receives a code → backend/SPA exchanges code + verifier for a token. OAuth is for authorization; OIDC ID token is for login.

XML-based SSO protocol. IdP authenticates user and sends signed SAML assertion to SP. Used by Okta, Azure AD, OneLogin. Vulnerable to XML signature wrapping and response replay. How does SP-initiated SAML SSO work? What are the security risks in SAML assertions? IdP Identity Provider (Okta, Azure AD). SP Service Provider (your app). Assertion Signed XML containing the user identity. Definition: SAML enterprise SSO: user is redirected from SP to IdP, logs in, IdP sends a signed assertion, SP verifies the signature and creates a session.

WebAuthn/FIDO2: browser-based public key auth, no shared secret. Passkeys sync across devices via iCloud/Google. TOTP: time-based 6-digit codes. Phishing-resistant > phishable. How does WebAuthn work at a technical level? Why are passkeys considered the future of authentication? WebAuthn/FIDO2 Public-key authentication using the browser or OS authenticator. Passkey Synced WebAuthn credential. MFA Something you know + something you have + something you are. Definition: In WebAuthn the private key stays on the device, and the server stores only the public key — phishing-resistant because it is bound to the credential’s origin. TOTP/SMS are weak, and push suffers from fatigue risk.

SDL integrates security into every phase: design (threat model) → code (SAST) → test (DAST) → deploy (scan) → operate (monitor). A bug in design costs $100; in production, $100K+. How do you integrate security into a CI/CD pipeline? What tools do you use at each stage? Shift left Bring security into early phases. SAST / DAST / SCA Code scan / running app scan / dependency scan. Security champion The team's security point person. Definition: SDL: requirements → threat model → secure coding + SAST → DAST/pen-test → release gate → monitoring. Automated checks in CI.

Never store secrets in code, config files, or cleartext env vars. Use HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager for storage, rotation, and just-in-time access with automatic expiry. How do you manage database credentials and API keys in a microservices architecture? Vault / Secrets Manager Central encrypted secrets store. Rotation Change secrets regularly. Dynamic secrets Short-lived DB creds on demand. Definition: No secrets in code/git/Docker images. At runtime, inject from Vault, access via IAM role, rotate, audit. If a leak occurs, revoke immediately.

Scan images for CVEs (Trivy, Grype), run as non-root, use minimal base images (distroless). K8s: Pod Security Standards, Network Policies, OPA Gatekeeper policies. How do you secure a Kubernetes cluster from image build to runtime? Non-root Container user non-privileged. Distroless Minimal image, kam attack surface. Image scan Trivy/Grype CVE scan. Definition: Minimal base image, non-root user, read-only filesystem, capabilities drop, no privileged containers, signed images and registry scanning.

Authenticate every request, authorize every operation, validate every input, rate limit per client. CORS restricts cross-origin access. APIs are the #1 modern attack vector. How would you secure a public REST API serving millions of requests per day? Rate limiting Request caps. Input validation Strict check based on schema. Least data Only necessary fields in response. Definition: Every request authentication, every operation authorization, input schema validation, rate limit, TLS, proper error messages (no stack traces), logging.

SCA scans dependencies for CVEs. SBOM (CycloneDX/SPDX) inventories all components. Artifact signing (cosign) and SLSA levels secure the build pipeline against attacks like SolarWinds. How do you protect against supply chain attacks in your software development process? SCA Software Composition Analysis. SBOM List of components (CycloneDX/SPDX). Lockfile Exact versions pin. Definition: Dependencies contain CVEs, typosquatting, malicious updates. Defense: lockfiles, SCA, SBOM, signed artifacts (Sigstore), minimal deps, private registry.

IAM manages identities and permissions. Service accounts for machines. Policy conditions restrict by IP, time, MFA. Start minimal, add only what is needed. Never use wildcard actions. How do you design IAM policies for a multi-service cloud application? Least privilege Minimum permissions. Role vs user Use service roles, not long-lived keys. Condition IP/MFA/time based policy. Definition: IAM identities (users, roles, service accounts) are assigned policies. Avoid wildcard * , assume roles, use MFA, set permission boundaries, and conduct access reviews.

VPC isolates networks with public/private subnets across AZs. Security Groups (stateful), NACLs (stateless), WAF (L7 SQLi/XSS), and Shield/CloudFront for DDoS protection. Design a VPC architecture for a three-tier web application. What security controls apply at each layer? VPC/subnets Private/public network split. Security Group Stateful instance firewall. NACL Stateless subnet filter. Definition: DBs in a private subnet, only the load balancer is public. SG least-open, NAT egress, VPC endpoints, WAF, flow logs.

Encryption at rest (AES-256 on S3, RDS, EBS) and in transit (TLS 1.3). KMS manages keys with automatic rotation. Envelope encryption: KMS encrypts DEK, DEK encrypts data. How do you implement encryption at rest and in transit for a cloud-native application? At rest Disk/DB encryption. In transit TLS 1.2+/1.3. KMS Key management service, rotation, audit. Definition: Data classification, encryption at rest (KMS keys) and in transit, backups encrypted, tokenization PII, retention policies.

SOC2 (5 trust criteria), HIPAA (PHI protection), GDPR (EU data rights), PCI DSS (card data). Audit logging (CloudTrail), automated evidence collection (Vanta, Drata). How do you design a system that is compliant by default for SOC2 and GDPR? SOC2 Trust criteria audit. GDPR EU data rights. PCI DSS Card data standard. Definition: Compliance frameworks controls and evidence require: access reviews, logging, change management, incident response, data retention, right to erasure (GDPR).

IR phases: Preparation → Detection → Containment → Eradication → Recovery → Postmortem. Runbooks define steps per scenario. Blameless postmortems focus on process failures, not people. Walk through your incident response process for a suspected data breach in a cloud environment. IR phases Prepare, Detect, Contain, Eradicate, Recover, Lessons. Runbook Step-by-step playbook. Blameless postmortem System fix, no blame. Definition: Detect → triage severity → contain (isolate, revoke credentials) → eradicate (root cause) → recover → postmortem. Preserve evidence, maintain a communication plan.

"Never trust, always verify" — no implicit trust based on network location. Micro-segmentation per service. Continuous verification on every sensitive operation. Google BeyondCorp pioneered this. How would you implement Zero Trust architecture in an existing cloud application? Never trust, always verify Do not trust based on network location. Micro-segmentation Small isolated zones. Continuous verification Identity + device posture for every request. Definition: The perimeter model broke (remote work, cloud). In zero trust every request is authenticated + authorized, mTLS, device health, least privilege.

Security is part of every component decision, not bolted on. Patterns: least privilege, defense in depth, fail secure, secure defaults, complete mediation, economy of mechanism. What does "Secure by Design" mean in practice? Give examples of each principle in a real system. Secure by default Safe configuration out of box. Defense in depth Multiple layers. Fail secure Deny on error. Definition: Part of security architecture: minimize attack surface, least privilege, separation of duties, safe defaults, at the input validation boundary.

TLS 1.3: 1-RTT handshake, 3 cipher suites only. AEAD (AES-256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305). ECDHE for perfect forward secrecy. X25519 preferred over P-256 for key exchange. Explain the TLS 1.3 handshake. How does it improve security and performance over TLS 1.2? TLS 1.3 1-RTT handshake, forward secrecy. AEAD Encryption + integrity (GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305). HSTS Header that forces HTTPS. Definition: TLS 1.3 only includes strong cipher suites and provides forward secrecy with ECDHE. Practical: HSTS, certificate automation, internal mTLS, disable TLS 1.0/1.1.

SIEM aggregates logs from all sources, normalizes, correlates, and alerts. SOAR automates incident response. Detection engineering writes rules as code. Median dwell time without SIEM: 204 days. How do you design a security monitoring strategy for a cloud-native application? SIEM Logs aggregate, correlate, alert. SOAR Response automation. Detection rule Alert for a suspicious pattern. Definition: Auth logs, CloudTrail, app logs in one place; rules (impossible travel, many failed logins, new admin) provide alerts; triage and runbooks.

BOLA (formerly IDOR) is the #1 API vulnerability. Attacker accesses objects by manipulating IDs in API calls (e.g., /api/users/123 → /api/users/456). Server doesn't verify ownership. Most common in REST APIs. What is BOLA? How do you prevent it in a multi-tenant API? BOLA Changing the object ID to access another's object. Ownership check On every object access. Unpredictable IDs UUID helps but does not fix it. Definition: GET /orders/123 changed to 124 and you receive another user's order, that's BOLA. Fix: perform a user-ownership/policy check on every object access.

n: Broken Authentication — credential stuffing, session fixation, weak JWT
x: Broken Authentication encompasses weak passwords, no rate limiting on login, credential stuffing, session fixation, and weak JWT implementation (alg:none, no expiry, weak secret). How do you prevent credential stuffing attacks on a login API? What makes a JWT implementation insecure? Credential stuffing Replay of leaked passwords. Session fixation Attacker's session ID on the victim. Rate limit login Per IP + per account. Definition: Weak passwords, no throttling, predictable tokens, long-lived JWT, no MFA. Fix: MFA, breached-password check, lockout/backoff, rotate session ID after login.

n: Broken Object Property Level Authorization — mass assignment, excessive data exposure
x: Mass assignment: API accepts all fields from request body, allowing attackers to set unintended properties (e.g., isAdmin: true). Excessive data exposure: API returns more fields than the client needs. What is mass assignment? How do you prevent it in a REST API? Mass assignment All fields from the request body go into the model. Excessive data exposure Too many fields in the response. DTO Allowlisted fields. Definition: User.update(req.body) allows an attacker to send isAdmin:true . The response includes password hash/internal fields.

n: Unrestricted Resource Consumption — rate limiting, pagination, resource limits
x: APIs without rate limiting are vulnerable to DoS. Lack of pagination allows fetching millions of records. No file size limits enable storage abuse. No query complexity limits enable GraphQL abuse. How do you implement rate limiting for a public API? What are the tradeoffs between different rate limiting algorithms? Rate limit Maximum requests in a time window. Pagination limit Max page size. Cost control Timeouts, payload limits, query depth. Definition: APIs without limits are vulnerable to DoS and bill shock: huge page size, expensive queries, large uploads, SMS/email spam.

n: Broken Function Level Authorization — admin endpoints, vertical privilege escalation
x: Regular users accessing admin functions by calling admin API endpoints directly. Missing authorization checks on function-level operations. Vertical privilege escalation: low-privilege user gains admin access. How do you prevent regular users from accessing admin API endpoints? What is vertical vs horizontal privilege escalation? BFLA Function-level authZ missing. Vertical escalation User → admin functions. Deny by default Role check on every function. Definition: Normal user /api/admin/users or DELETE method call because the UI was only hidden. Fix: server-side role/permission check in a central middleware.

Raw socket(), bind(), listen(), accept() loop — handle multiple concurrent clients without a framework. Covers TCP handshake, partial reads, goroutine-per-connection, graceful shutdown. Design a TCP echo server from raw POSIX sockets. Walk me through bind, listen, accept — and how you would handle 1000 concurrent clients without a framework.

Build HTTP/1.1 on raw TCP. Parse request line, headers, body via Content-Length. Route paths, serve responses, support keep-alive — zero stdlib http. Build an HTTP/1.1 server on raw TCP sockets. How do you parse the request line, headers, and body? What does keep-alive actually do at the wire level?

Recursive DNS resolver: parse DNS packets, walk the hierarchy from root to authoritative, cache by TTL — raw UDP sockets and binary parsing. Explain how a recursive DNS resolver walks from root servers down to authoritative answers. What does the DNS wire format look like?

Single-threaded event loop using epoll/kqueue for I/O multiplexing. Timer min-heap for setTimeout semantics. Handle 1000 concurrent connections in one thread. How does epoll work under the hood? Explain the difference between edge-triggered and level-triggered I/O notification.

on/emit/once/off, error event propagation, setMaxListeners, memory leak detection at 10+ listeners. The observer pattern backbone. Build Node.js EventEmitter from scratch. How does once() auto-remove listeners, and why is the error event special?

require() from scratch: resolution, __dirname, module.exports, caching, circular dependency handling with partial exports. Rebuild Node.js require(). How does module resolution work, and how does caching prevent redundant loads?

n: In-Memory KV Store with File Persistence
x: In-memory hash map + LRU eviction + append-only WAL for crash recovery. GET, SET, DEL, EXPIRE commands. Redis lite without the protocol. Design an in-memory key-value store with WAL for crash recovery. What does the write-ahead log look like, and how do you replay it?

Pool of persistent TCP connections with borrow/return, health check, idle timeout, overflow strategy. Amortize handshake + TLS + auth cost. Build a TCP connection pool. How do you handle borrow and return semantics, idle timeout, and health checks before lending?

HTTP upgrade handshake, WebSocket frame protocol, masking, fragmentation, ping/pong keepalive. Pub/sub broadcast across concurrent connections. Walk me through the WebSocket upgrade handshake. How do you compute the Sec-WebSocket-Accept key from the client challenge?

Signal handling (SIGTERM/SIGINT), connection drain with timeout, health check flip 200→503, worker drain, force-kill fallback. Design production-grade graceful shutdown. How do you drain in-flight requests without dropping connections?

The foundation of Node.js — build a server using only the http module. Build an HTTP server using only Node's built-in http module — GET /hello, POST /echo, 404 handling, JSON responses. Walk me through how you parse the request body from the incoming stream.

Build a command-line tool using fs and process — tests Node fundamentals. Build a CLI tool that takes a file path and prints line count, word count, character count, and the top 5 most frequent words. How do you handle a missing or unreadable file?

A building block used in every Node.js service — caching with expiry. Design an in-memory TTL cache with set/get/delete/clear and stats. Values expire after ttlMs — explain lazy expiry vs active expiry and when you would choose each.

n: Build a Logger with Log Levels
x: Every Node.js app needs a logger — build one that writes to console and file. Build a Logger class with debug/info/warn/error levels, colored console output, and newline-delimited JSON written to a file. How do you make the minimum level configurable at runtime?

Stream-friendly CSV parsing — tests string parsing and edge case handling. Build parseCSV(text) and toCSV(records) that handle quoted fields, commas and newlines inside quotes, and escaped quotes. What is the naive approach and why does it fail?

Configuration management is a real production concern. Build it properly. Build loadConfig() merging defaults → JSON file → env vars → runtime overrides, with nested keys (DB_HOST → config.db.host), type coercion, and required-field validation.

Build your own find command — tests async file system operations. Build walk(dir, options) as an async generator that lazily yields file paths, with extension filters, maxDepth, and ignore patterns. How do you avoid infinite loops with symlinks?

Real-time data push without WebSockets — the simplest live-update mechanism. Build an SSE endpoint at GET /events that pushes a counter every second, detects client disconnects, and supports Last-Event-ID resume. What headers and wire format are required?

RESP wire protocol, core commands (GET/SET/DEL/TTL/INCR/LPUSH), pub/sub fan-out, AOF + RDB persistence. redis-cli should connect and work. Build a Redis-compatible server. How does the RESP wire protocol work, and how do you implement TTL with lazy expiry plus background sweep?

Durable queue with producer/consumer, ack/nack, redelivery timer, dead-letter queue. At-least-once delivery via WAL + visibility timeout. Design a message queue with at-least-once delivery. How does visibility timeout prevent duplicate processing?

Reverse proxy distributing traffic across backends. Round-robin + least-connections, active/passive health checks, connection draining, sticky sessions. Build an HTTP load balancer. Compare round-robin and least-connections algorithms. How do health checks work?

Standalone rate limiter: token bucket + sliding window + fixed window counter. Redis + Lua for atomic distributed counting. Rate limit headers. Design a distributed rate limiter. Compare token bucket, sliding window, and fixed window counter algorithms.

Consistent hash ring with virtual nodes, LRU eviction per node, cache-aside + write-through patterns. Client routes without central coordinator. Design a distributed cache with consistent hashing. How do virtual nodes improve key distribution across nodes?

Cron expression parser, min-heap job queue, distributed lock (SETNX) for exactly-once execution, retry with exponential backoff. Build a distributed cron scheduler. How do you parse cron expressions and compute the next run time?

Protobuf-style wire format with varint + TLV encoding, TCP framing, unary + server-streaming, client stub generation from IDL. Design a minimal RPC framework. How does varint encoding work, and why is length-prefix framing necessary over TCP?

HTTP API for PUT/GET/DELETE objects, bucket management, chunked upload, range requests (206), ETag validation, metadata index. Build an object storage service. How does chunked upload work, and why are range requests important for large objects?

n: URL Shortener — Base62 encoding, collision handling, analytics
x: Generate unique short codes using Base62 (a-z, A-Z, 0-9). Store mapping in DB (short_code → long_url). Handle collisions with retry. Add click analytics (IP, user-agent, timestamp). Use cache (Redis) for hot URLs. 301 vs 302 redirect. How do you generate unique short codes for a URL shortener? How do you handle collisions?

Understand how Express works by building it — middleware chain, params, error handling. Build an Express-like framework: route registration with params (:id), middleware via app.use, next()/next(err), and a 4-argument error handler. How do you convert /users/:id into a matcher?

The backbone of background processing — build a production-grade job queue. Design a JobQueue with configurable concurrency, retry with exponential backoff, status tracking, and lifecycle events. How does a job move through pending → active → completed/failed?

Every production API has one — implement sliding window and token bucket. Build Express rate-limiting middleware with fixed-window and sliding-window strategies, 429 responses with Retry-After, and rate-limit headers. How do you key by client?

Node.js streams are heavily tested at senior level — build a real transform pipeline. Build a streaming file processing pipeline: read a large CSV as a stream, parse, transform, filter, batch into groups of 100, and write JSONL — without loading the file into memory.

Resource management pattern used in every production Node.js service. Design a database ConnectionPool with acquire/release, min/max size, acquire timeout, idle timeout, and health checks. What happens when acquire exceeds max?

Build your own prompting library — tests raw TTY control and keyboard events. Build a prompting library: text, password (masked), select via arrow keys, confirm, and checkbox — using raw-mode stdin. How do you detect arrow key presses?

Build your own chokidar-lite — recursive watching, change types, debouncing. Build watch(dir, options) emitting add/change/delete events with debounce, recursion, ignore patterns, and an initial scan. How do you distinguish add from change?

Implement the WebSocket upgrade handshake and basic framing from scratch. Implement a raw WebSocket server: the HTTP upgrade handshake, Sec-WebSocket-Accept computation, and frame parsing/construction for text messages. Walk me through the accept-key computation.

Redis-lite - a data store with append-only-file durability. Design a KV store with AOF persistence: every mutation appends to a log, replay on restart, SAVE snapshots, TTL support, and keys() wildcard matching.

Product companies run webhook infrastructure - retries, idempotency keys, and a delivery log. Design a WebhookDispatcher with HMAC-signed delivery, per-attempt timeouts, exponential backoff retries, auto-disabling flaky endpoints, and a delivery log with replay.

Payments-grade APIs need idempotency - dedupe retried POSTs by key. Build Express idempotency middleware: a client sends Idempotency-Key, duplicate keys return the stored response instead of re-executing, with a TTL and locking for concurrent duplicates.

Rebuild libuv phases: timers → pending → poll → check → close. Microtask queue, nextTick priority, I/O starvation guard. Rebuild the Node.js event loop phases. How do timers, I/O poll, setImmediate, and close callbacks interact?

Readable/Writable/Duplex/Transform with backpressure, highWaterMark, pipe(). Flowing vs paused mode, drain events. Build Node.js streams from scratch. What is backpressure, and how does highWaterMark control data flow?

Master forks workers, round-robin accept, IPC handle passing, worker health heartbeat, zero-downtime restart via SIGUSR2. Rebuild Node.js cluster from scratch. How does round-robin accept distribute connections across workers?

Generic worker thread pool: task queue, thread lifecycle, SharedArrayBuffer for zero-copy, structured clone messaging, crash respawn. Design a worker thread pool. How does SharedArrayBuffer enable zero-copy data sharing between threads?

n: Chat System — WebSocket, message persistence, presence, delivery receipts
x: WebSocket for real-time messaging. Store messages in DB (PostgreSQL/MongoDB) with conversation_id, sender_id, content, timestamp. Presence service tracks online/offline status. Delivery receipts: sent → delivered → read. Message ordering with sequence numbers. How do you design a chat system backend? How do you ensure message ordering and delivery?

n: Notification System — fanout, multi-channel delivery, preferences
x: Notification service with channels: email (SES/SendGrid), push (FCM/APNs), SMS (Twilio), in-app. User preferences per notification type. Fanout: single event → multiple channel delivery. Queue-based async processing. Delivery status tracking. How do you design a notification system that supports multiple channels (email, push, SMS)?

n: REST API with Auth, CRUD & Validation
x: Build a full production-style API — the most common Node.js senior round problem. Build a Notes REST API: JWT register/login, protected CRUD with ownership checks, request validation, and centralized error handling. How do you implement a JWT by hand?

Offload heavy computation — tests your understanding of Node.js concurrency model. Build a worker-thread pool that distributes CPU-bound tasks, handles worker crashes with requeue, supports cancellation, and reports progress. How does the main thread communicate with workers?

Build the core of a message broker — think mini-Redis pub/sub over TCP. Build a pub/sub server over TCP: SUBSCRIBE/PUBLISH/UNSUBSCRIBE with wildcard channels and per-channel message history. How do you route a publish to matching subscribers?

Combine everything: LRU eviction, TTL expiry, pub/sub invalidation, and HTTP API. Design a CacheServer with an HTTP API combining LRU eviction and TTL expiry, an SSE endpoint for invalidation events, and a stats endpoint. How do LRU and TTL coexist?

Build your own node-cron — parsing cron expressions and scheduling callbacks. Build a cron-style Scheduler parsing expressions like */5 * * * * with ranges and lists, one-time tasks, cancellation, missed-run recovery, and a timezone option.

Parse multi-GB JSON files without loading into memory — a real data engineering problem. Build a streaming JSON parser as a Transform stream: JSONL lines or a streaming array, transform/filter each item, respect backpressure, and recover from malformed lines.

Cache stampede prevention, leader election, mutual exclusion - the lock everyone uses. Design a DistributedLock with SET NX PX semantics, ownership tokens, compare-and-delete release, lease auto-renewal, and retry with backoff.

n: Worker Threads & Clustering — CPU-bound tasks in Node.js
x: Worker Threads run JavaScript in parallel threads with shared memory. Cluster module forks Node.js processes across CPU cores. Explain and build Node.js Worker Threads vs the cluster module: shared memory vs process forking, offloading CPU-bound work, and scaling HTTP servers across cores. When would you use each?

n: Caching Layer — Redis, cache-aside, cache invalidation strategies
x: Redis caching layer for database query results, session data, and frequently accessed data. Design a caching layer: cache-aside vs write-through, TTL and event-driven invalidation, cache stampede prevention with a distributed lock, and the Redis data structures you would use.

Request-scoped state that survives async chains — request IDs, correlation IDs, tenant context. Build a request-context helper using AsyncLocalStorage: assign a requestId (and optional userId/tenantId) per request, propagate it through every async call, and expose get()/set() helpers that any layer can read without passing arguments. How do you wire it into an Express-style middleware?

CLOSED → OPEN → HALF-OPEN state machine so a dead dependency fails fast instead of hanging requests. Build a CircuitBreaker that wraps an async function: calls pass while CLOSED, failures increment a counter that trips the breaker OPEN after a threshold, OPEN fails fast (or returns a fallback), HALF-OPEN after a cooldown allows limited probe calls and closes on success. Emit state-change events.

Publish events reliably by writing to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business change. Build the transactional outbox pattern: in one DB transaction, apply a business change AND insert a row into an outbox table; a relay polls committed outbox rows, publishes each to a queue (or HTTP endpoint), marks it sent, dedupes re-reads, and handles poison rows. Why is this more reliable than queueing inside the transaction?

Prometheus-style counters, gauges, and histograms with a scrape endpoint — the observability staple. Build a small metrics library: counters (monotonic), gauges (settable), histograms (buckets + sum + count), named with labels, exposed at GET /metrics in Prometheus text format, plus default process metrics (event-loop lag, memory, uptime) and per-route HTTP counters/latency.

MemTable (skip list) → SSTable flush, Bloom filter per SSTable, leveled compaction. The write path inside RocksDB and Cassandra. Explain the LSM-tree architecture. How does the write path flow from MemTable to SSTable flush to disk?

B+ tree page layout, WAL for ACID transactions, SQL lexer/parser/executor. File-backed relational DB with CREATE TABLE, INSERT, SELECT. Design a file-backed relational database. How does B+ tree page layout work, and why are leaf nodes linked together?

Content-addressable object store, blob/tree/commit objects, pack files, three-way merge algorithm. Binary-compatible with real Git. How does Git content-addressable object store work? What makes the Merkle DAG tamper-evident?

Lexer → recursive descent parser → AST → bytecode compiler → stack-based VM. Closures, mark-and-sweep GC, basic I/O. Build a programming language interpreter. Walk through the pipeline: lexer, parser, bytecode compiler, and VM execution.

Leader election with randomized timeouts, log replication via AppendEntries, commit quorum, log compaction via snapshotting. Explain the Raft consensus algorithm. How does leader election work, and what safety guarantees does it provide?

Linux namespaces (PID/NET/MNT/UTS/IPC), cgroups v2 resource limits, OverlayFS layers, OCI-compatible create→start→kill→delete. Build a minimal container runtime. What do Linux namespaces isolate, and how do cgroups enforce resource limits?

Same fetch URL called multiple times in one render tree is deduped — automatic within a request lifecycle Request Memoization During a single render, the same URL fetch occurs only once — the rest comes from cache. Layout, page, and 3 components — all calling getUser() ? Only one request will go over the network. The rest will receive the same response. Persistent across requests and deployments. force-cache (default), no-store, revalidate: N Data Cache Server-side persistent cache — stays alive between requests and deployments. force-cache Cache the data (the old default behavior). no-store Fresh data on every request — do not cache. Data Cache is a cache that lives longer than a build/deploy. Data fetched for one user will be served to subsequent visitors as cached (until it is revalidated). Control: fetch(url, { next: { revalidate: 60 } }) — cached for 60 seconds.

Cached HTML + RSC payload at build time for static routes. Invalidated by revalidatePath/revalidateTag Full Route Cache Static routes’ rendered HTML + RSC payload generated at build time and ready. Static vs Dynamic If any dynamic API (cookies, searchParams) is used, the route becomes dynamic — it isn’t cached. Invalidation revalidatePath/Tag deletes the cached route, so the next request is fresh. If a route has no dynamic element, Next builds the full HTML at build time and keeps it. Every visitor gets that ready-made HTML from CDNs — the server doesn’t even run. If any cookies() / headers() / searchParams is used → route becomes dynamic → renders on every request.

Client-side cache of visited route segments. Prefetched on hover. Duration: 30s (dynamic), 5min (static) Router Cache Memory in the browser (client) that stores RSC payloads of visited routes. Prefetch The <Link> fetches the route’s payload in advance on viewport/hover. router.refresh() Requests fresh data for the current route from the server — refreshes the cache. When you navigate to a route, its RSC payload is saved in the browser memory. If you go back to the same route, there will be no network call — instant navigation. <Link> prefetches: static routes get the full payload, dynamic routes only the loading skeleton.

Time-based (revalidate: N), on-demand (revalidatePath, revalidateTag), tags with fetch cache tags Time-based revalidate revalidate: N — after N seconds the cache becomes "stale", and the next request refreshes it. On-demand revalidate revalidatePath() / revalidateTag() — fresh whenever you ask. Cache tag Attach a tag on fetch, then later invalidate the whole group by that name. There are two ways to refresh cached data: time-based ("consider it stale after 60 seconds") and on-demand ("post published? revalidate now"). On-demand is precise — it doesn’t invalidate the entire site, only the related cache.

Measures load performance of the largest image or text block. Target: fetchpriority="high" the browser fetches the LCP image first. Definition: Largest Contentful Paint indicates how quickly the user sees the page’s main content — usually the hero image or a large heading. Good: ≤2.5s, poor: >4s (at the 75th percentile). LCP breaks into four parts: TTFB, resource load delay, resource load duration, element render delay. First

Measures responsiveness — time from user interaction to next visual update. Target: < 200ms. Replaced FID in 2024. INP Approximately the slowest (p98) interaction latency among all page interactions. Target ≤ 200 ms. Long task Work on the main thread longer than 50 ms — blocks input handling. Input delay / processing / presentation The three phases of INP: wait before the handler, handler execution time, and time until the next paint. Definition: Measures the time from an interaction (click/tap/keypress) to the next paint when the screen updates. It replaced FID in 2024 because FID only measured the first interaction and only the delay.

Measures visual stability — unexpected layout shifts during page load. Target: < 0.1. Causes: images without dimensions, injected content, font swap. CLS Cumulative score of unexpected layout shifts. Target ≤ 0.1. Layout shift A visible element changes position without user input. Reserved space Provide width, height, or aspect-ratio in advance for images/ads/embeds. Definition: CLS impact fraction × distance fraction is formed. Shifts that occur within 500 ms of a user click are not counted (they are expected). Common causes: images without dimensions, late-loading ads/banners, font swap, dynamically injected content above.

First pixel of content painted. Target: < 1.8s. Leading indicator for LCP. Affected by TTFB and render-blocking resources. FCP First content pixel (text/image) appears. Target ≤ 1.8 s. Render-blocking Paint is paused until the head's CSS/synchronous JS loads. Leading indicator If FCP is poor, LCP will also be poor. Definition: First Contentful Paint is the first moment when anything (non-white) appears on the page. It depends on TTFB and render-blocking resources.

Server response time. Target: < 800ms. Affected by server processing, CDN, database queries. Foundation for all other metrics. TTFB Time from sending the request to receiving the first byte of the response. Target ≤ 800 ms. CDN / edge Serving from a server close to the user to reduce latency. Cache hit The server/CDN responded without contacting the origin. Definition: TTFB includes DNS, TCP/TLS, redirects, and server processing. It is the baseline for all other metrics — if TTFB is 1.5s, achieving LCP 2.5s is difficult.
